RL School

How reinforcement learning works, in two weeks · v1.0 (2026-10-25)
A two-week course
Understand reinforcement learning, properly.

Fourteen lessons, about 90 minutes each, from "what is a reward" to world models, RL-trained reasoning models, and robots, as of October 2026. Plain English, real numbers, an architecture diagram for every method, interactive widgets, and sources you can check.

How to use this course

  1. One day per sitting. Read the lesson top to bottom. Each one is self-contained but builds on the day before. Week 1 builds the classical machine; Week 2 goes from deep RL to the research frontier.
  2. Play with every widget. The widgets are small, real computations running in your browser: a bandit that actually learns, a grid that actually converges, a PPO objective you can bend. Drag the sliders until the idea clicks.
  3. Look at the architecture. Every method gets a diagram of its parts and what flows between them (networks, buffers, environments, workers). If you can redraw the diagram from memory, you understand the method.
  4. Take the quiz, then mark the day done. Progress is saved on this device only. Nothing is sent anywhere.
  5. Open the sources. The small chips after sentences (like this one Sutton & Barto 2018) link to the original book chapter, paper, blog, or documentation. When you finish the course, read the originals in the Paper Bible.

If you have done LLM School, you already know what a neural network, gradient descent, and a Transformer are; this course assumes that and nothing more. Equations are shown and explained, never proved. Code snippets are ten lines or fewer.

The map

Week 1 builds the machine: rewards, bandits, Markov decision processes, Bellman equations, dynamic programming, learning from experience, Q-learning and DQN, policy gradients. Week 2 is the modern toolkit and where it is used: PPO and SAC, world models, offline RL, exploration and self-play, RL for language models and agents, RL in robots and industry, and the open problems.

Week 1 · Day 1

What is reinforcement learning?

After today you can draw the agent–environment loop, compute a discounted return by hand for any γ, and say precisely why reinforcement learning is not supervised learning.

About 90 min · No prerequisites

Today's big idea

Reinforcement learning is learning what to do from the consequences of what you did. The agent is never told which action was right; after each action it gets a single number, the reward, and its job is to act so that the sum of future rewards is as large as possible. Because nobody hands it the right answers, it has to find them by trying things, and because rewards can arrive long after the action that earned them, it has to work out which of its past actions deserve the credit.

1. Learning from consequences

In the 1890s the psychologist Edward Thorndike put cats in "puzzle boxes" that opened when the cat pulled a loop or pressed a lever. The cats scratched at random until, by accident, they hit the latch; put back in the box, they got out a little faster each time, and after a few dozen trials they went straight to it. Thorndike's Law of Effect summarises it: of several responses to the same situation, those "accompanied or closely followed by satisfaction to the animal" become more firmly connected to the situation, and those followed by discomfort are weakened. Thorndike 1911 Sutton and Barto, whose textbook this course follows, call that sentence "the essence of trial-and-error learning as a principle of learning". Sutton & Barto 2018

Two things in the cat story carry over unchanged to the algorithms of this course. The cat was not shown the solution; it searched for it. And the satisfaction came after a chain of actions, not after each one, so the cat had to connect the reward to the earlier movements that caused it. Sutton and Barto name exactly these two as the "most important distinguishing features" of reinforcement learning: trial-and-error search and delayed reward. Their one-sentence definition is worth memorising: RL is "learning what to do, how to map situations to actions, so as to maximize a numerical reward signal". Sutton & Barto 2018

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Think about teaching a puppy to sit. You do not hand it a textbook. It tries things, and when it does the right one it gets a treat. Sometimes the treat comes a bit late, after it has already done two or three other things, and the puppy has to work out which thing earned it. Reinforcement learning is a computer program doing exactly that: trying things, getting points, and slowly learning which things earn the most points.

2. The agent–environment loop, precisely

Everything in RL is described with two pieces. The agent is the learner and decision maker. The environment is everything the agent interacts with: the game, the robot's body and the room, the stock market, the user reading a chatbot's answer. They talk to each other in a loop of discrete time steps t = 0, 1, 2, …

At step t the agent receives a state St (a description of the situation) and chooses an action At. One step later, as a consequence, it receives a reward Rt+1, a single real number, together with the next state St+1. Then it chooses again. The whole interaction is one long sequence: Sutton & Barto 2018

S0, A0, R1, S1, A1, R2, S2, A2, R3, …

Notice the indices. The reward caused by action At is written Rt+1, not Rt, because reward and next state arrive together, one tick after the action. Some books write Rt for the same quantity; this course follows Sutton and Barto. Sutton & Barto 2018 The agent's rule for choosing actions is its policy π: a deterministic function a = μ(s) or, more often, a probability distribution π(a | s) over actions given the state. OpenAI 2018 Learning, in RL, means improving the policy.

s = env.reset()                 # S_0
done = False
while not done:
    a = policy(s)               # A_t
    s, r, done = env.step(a)    # S_{t+1}, R_{t+1}
    learn(s, a, r)              # the whole course is about this line

Interaction comes in two shapes. In an episodic task the loop breaks into episodes, "such as plays of a game, trips through a maze", each ending in a terminal state after which the environment resets. In a continuing task it "goes on continually without limit", as in process control or "a robot with a long life span". Sutton & Barto 2018 One notation covers both if the end of an episode is treated as an absorbing state that leads only to itself with reward 0 forever. Sutton & Barto 2018

Try it: steer the agent with the arrows. Every move costs −1; the goal pays +10 and ends the episode; the trap pays −10 and also ends it. Watch the trajectory build in exactly the S, A, R order above, and watch the two returns change as you drag γ.

Notice that walking into a wall still costs a step, and that a longer route to the goal has a lower return than a shorter one even though both end with +10: the step cost is how the designer tells the agent that time matters.

3. Reward, return and discount, with a worked example

The reward is always a plain number: "at each time step, the reward is a simple number, Rt ∈ ℝ". Sutton & Barto 2018 But the agent does not maximise the reward it gets right now; it maximises everything it will collect from now on. That total is the return Gt. For an episode ending at step T, the simplest version is the sum:

Gt = Rt+1 + Rt+2 + … + RT

For continuing tasks that sum could be infinite, and even in episodic ones it is useful to care a little less about far-away rewards. So each future reward is multiplied by a discount factor γ (gamma), a number between 0 and 1, raised to the power of how far away it is: Sutton & Barto 2018

Gt = Rt+1 + γ Rt+2 + γ² Rt+3 + … = Σk=0∞ γk Rt+k+1

A reward k steps in the future is worth γk−1 times what it would be worth immediately. With γ = 0 the agent is "myopic", caring only about the next reward; as γ approaches 1 it becomes "farsighted". Sutton & Barto 2018 One line of algebra gives the most useful fact about returns: each return is the next reward plus the discounted return after it, Gt = Rt+1 + γ Gt+1, with GT = 0 at the end of an episode. Sutton & Barto 2018 Day 3 turns that line into the Bellman equation, the backbone of the field.

Worked example. Take the shortest path in the widget above, three steps and then the goal: rewards −1, −1, −1, +10. With γ = 0.9 (so γ² = 0.81, γ³ = 0.729) the return from the start is

G0 = −1 + 0.9·(−1) + 0.81·(−1) + 0.729·10 = −1 − 0.9 − 0.81 + 7.29 = 4.58

With γ = 1 the same path returns 7; with γ = 0 it returns −1. A second example, from David Silver's lectures, shows that the same start can produce very different returns. In his "Student" chain with γ = ½, a student who goes Class 1 → Class 2 → Class 3 → Pass → Sleep collects −2, −2, −2, +10, so G1 = −2 − 2·½ − 2·¼ + 10·⅛ = −2.25; one who goes Class 1 → Facebook → Facebook → Class 1 → Class 2 → Sleep collects −2, −1, −1, −2, −2 and gets −2 − ½ − ¼ − ¼ − ⅛ = −3.125. Silver 2015 Same start, different luck, different returns. The average return from a state is its value, and Day 3 is about computing it.

Two more numbers to keep in your head. If the reward were +1 at every step forever, the return would be the geometric series 1 + γ + γ² + … = 1/(1−γ): exactly 10 for γ = 0.9 and 100 for γ = 0.99. Sutton & Barto 2018 That ratio is a good rule of thumb for the agent's effective horizon: 0.910 ≈ 0.35 and 0.99100 ≈ 0.37, so a reward one horizon away counts for roughly a third of its face value.

Try it: pick a reward pattern (or type your own ten rewards) and drag γ. The bars are the discounted terms γk·rk; the big number is their sum.

Notice how fast the single +10 at step 8 shrinks as γ falls: at γ = 0.9 it is worth 4.3, at γ = 0.5 it is worth 0.04. A small change in γ is a large change in what the agent is willing to wait for.

Analogy

Discounting is interest in reverse. A dollar promised next year is worth less than a dollar today, because you could invest today's dollar and because the promise might not be kept; γ = 0.9 says "a reward one step away is worth 90 cents on the dollar to me". Spinning Up puts it in four words: "cash now is better than cash later". OpenAI 2018 Silver's reasons to discount: it keeps infinite sums finite, encodes uncertainty about the future, matches how animals and people behave, and is mathematically convenient. When every episode is guaranteed to end, γ = 1 is fine. Silver 2015

Common misunderstandings

  • "The agent maximises the reward it gets now." It maximises the return, the discounted sum of all future rewards. Grabbing the biggest immediate reward "can reduce access to future rewards", which is the whole reason the problem is interesting. Sutton & Barto 2018
  • "γ is a fudge factor." It sets the agent's planning horizon (about 1/(1−γ) steps) and it is what makes the return of a never-ending task a finite number.
  • "The reward for At is Rt." In this course it is Rt+1; reward and next state arrive together, one tick later. Check the convention whenever you open a new paper.
  • "A terminal state is worth something." Its value is always zero: nothing can be collected after the episode ends. The +10 for reaching the goal is the reward for the transition into it, not a property of the state. Sutton & Barto 2018

4. The reward hypothesis, and what makes RL hard

Is a single number enough to describe a goal? The field's working assumption says yes. The reward hypothesis: "all of what we mean by goals and purposes can be well thought of as the maximization of the expected value of the cumulative sum of a received scalar signal (called reward)". Sutton & Barto 2018 Richard Sutton's web page gives the same sentence and notes that Michael Littman calls it the reinforcement learning hypothesis. Sutton n.d. It is a hypothesis, not a theorem (Day 14 returns to the awkward cases), but it stretches far: a walking robot rewarded in proportion to forward motion; a maze robot given −1 for every step still inside; a can-collecting robot given +1 per can; a chess program given +1 for a win, −1 for a loss and 0 for everything else, including every move before the end. Sutton & Barto 2018 The chess example is the important one: the reward says what to achieve, never how.

That is also why RL is hard. Silver lists four things that make it unlike the machine learning you already know: Silver 2015

  • No supervisor, only a reward. Nobody says "the right move was e4". The agent learns that a move was good only from a number, often the same number for most moves.
  • Delayed feedback. In chess the only nonzero reward comes at the end. Which of the 40 moves earned the +1? That is the credit assignment problem.
  • Time matters. The data is a sequence, not independent draws; what the agent sees at step 50 depends on what it did at step 49.
  • Your actions change your data. The agent collects its own data, so a policy that never tries a move never learns whether it was good.

The last point creates a dilemma that "does not even arise in supervised and unsupervised learning": exploration versus exploitation. Sutton & Barto 2018 To earn reward, exploit what you know works; to find out whether something else works better, explore, which costs reward now. Day 2 isolates this dilemma and measures what it alone costs.

Going deeper (optional): the objective in one line

Spinning Up writes the goal compactly. A trajectory is τ = (s0, a0, s1, a1, …), its return is R(τ), and a policy's quality is the expected return of the trajectories it produces, J(π) = Eτ∼π[R(τ)]; the optimal policy is π* = argmaxπ J(π). OpenAI 2018 Every algorithm from Day 4 to Day 12 is a different way of climbing J(π): estimate values and act greedily on them, push the policy's parameters up the gradient of J, or learn a model of the environment and plan.

5. RL versus supervised versus unsupervised learning

Sutton and Barto call RL "a third machine learning paradigm, alongside supervised learning and unsupervised learning", and they are explicit that it is not a kind of unsupervised learning: RL "is trying to maximize a reward signal instead of trying to find hidden structure". Sutton & Barto 2018 The table lines the three up.

QuestionSupervisedUnsupervisedReinforcement
What you are givenInputs with correct labelsInputs, no labelsA loop you can act in; a scalar reward per step
Where the data comes fromA fixed dataset, independent samplesA fixed datasetThe agent's own actions; changes as the policy changes
What feedback saysThe right answer for this inputNothingHow good this action turned out, often much later
GoalPredict labels on new inputsFind structure (clusters, density, representations)Maximise expected return
Does exploration matter?NoNoYes: you only learn about actions you try
Typical exampleImage classification; next-token predictionClustering customersPlaying Go; controlling a robot; tuning a chatbot from feedback

The second row is the one that bites in practice: in interactive problems "it is often impractical to obtain examples of desired behavior that are both correct and representative" of the situations the agent will meet. Sutton & Barto 2018 A chess teacher can show you grandmaster games, but not the right move in the strange position you reached by making a mistake. If you did LLM School, you have seen this boundary: pretraining a language model is supervised next-token prediction on a fixed corpus; tuning it from human feedback is RL, because the feedback is a scalar score on text the model itself produced (Day 12).

6. A short history, with dates

1911: Thorndike. The Law of Effect, above, gives RL its psychological ancestor: behaviour followed by satisfaction is repeated, behaviour followed by discomfort is not. Thorndike 1911

1957: Bellman. Richard Bellman's book Dynamic Programming introduced the recursive equation for the value of a decision problem now called the Bellman equation, and his paper "A Markovian Decision Process" introduced the Markov decision process, the formal object behind every lesson in Week 1. Bellman 1957 Sutton & Barto 2018 Day 3 and Day 4 are the Bellman days.

1959: Samuel's checkers. Arthur Samuel's program at IBM improved by playing itself, nudging its evaluation of a position toward the evaluation of the positions that followed, the first implementation of a temporal-difference idea. It learned "to play a better game of checkers than can be played by the person who wrote the program" in "8 or 10 hours of machine-playing time". Samuel 1959 Sutton & Barto 2018

1989: Q-learning. Chris Watkins's thesis "fully brought together" the trial-and-error thread and the optimal-control thread into one algorithm, which Day 6 builds from scratch. Sutton & Barto 2018

1992–1995: TD-Gammon. Gerald Tesauro trained a neural network to play backgammon purely by self-play with temporal-difference learning. Version 2.1 reached "strong master level", within a few hundredths of a point per game of the best humans; the raw-board network had 40 hidden units and trained on 200,000 games. Tesauro 1995 Sutton and Barto date its first success to 1992. Sutton & Barto 2018

2013–2015: DQN. DeepMind's Deep Q-Network combined Q-learning with a convolutional network reading raw Atari pixels. The December 2013 preprint learned 7 games, beating prior methods on 6 and a human expert on 3; Mnih 2013 the February 2015 Nature paper scaled to 49 games with one architecture and one hyperparameter set, "comparable to a professional human games tester". Mnih 2015 Deep RL begins here; see Day 6 and the DQN review.

2016: AlphaGo. Policy and value networks trained on human expert games and then by self-play, combined with tree search. It won 99.8% of games against other Go programs and beat the European champion Fan Hui 5–0, the first program to beat a professional at full-size Go. Silver 2016 See Day 9 and the AlphaGo review.

2019: OpenAI Five and AlphaStar. OpenAI Five became "the first AI system to defeat the world champions at an esports game", beating the Dota 2 champions OG in April 2019 after 10 months of training at about 2 million frames every 2 seconds. Berner 2019 AlphaStar reached Grandmaster level in all three StarCraft II races, above 99.8% of ranked human players, with a league of agents trained against each other. Vinyals 2019 Day 11 covers self-play.

2022: InstructGPT and ChatGPT. InstructGPT (March 2022) fine-tuned GPT-3 on human demonstrations, then applied RL from human feedback on ranked outputs; raters preferred the 1.3B-parameter tuned model to the 175B untuned one. Ouyang 2022 ChatGPT, released on 30 November 2022, used the same family of methods. Wikipedia 2026 Day 12 and the InstructGPT review explain how a preference becomes a reward.

2025: DeepSeek-R1. DeepSeek-R1-Zero was trained "via large-scale reinforcement learning without supervised fine-tuning as a preliminary step" and learned to reason in long chains of thought; R1 performed comparably to OpenAI's o1. DeepSeek-AI 2025 In the Nature version, R1-Zero's accuracy on the AIME 2024 maths competition rose from 15.6% to 77.9% during RL. Guo 2025 As of October 2026 this recipe is the main way frontier labs build reasoning models; see Day 12 and the DeepSeek-R1 review.

Notice the pattern: the ideas (trial and error, Bellman's recursion, temporal differences, self-play) were all in place by 1992. What changed after 2013 was the function approximator, deep networks, and the compute to train them.

8. Architecture

Every method in this course is a particular way of filling in the two boxes below. The first diagram is the loop itself; the second shows where learning sits relative to it.

Read the first diagram left to right. The agent holds a policy, a function from state to action (in Week 2 a neural network; today any rule). The action goes to the environment, which applies its dynamics and sends back two things: the next state and a scalar reward. Nothing else crosses the boundary: no label, no gradient, no description of what the right action would have been. The reward is the whole message.

The second diagram is where the fourteen days differ. Experience, the stream of (S, A, R, S′) tuples the loop produces, feeds a learning algorithm that outputs an improved policy. Day 2's algorithm is a table of running averages; Day 4's needs a model of the environment and no experience at all; Day 6 stores a million tuples in a buffer and trains a network on random batches of them; Day 7 nudges the policy's parameters toward whatever made good trajectories more likely. The loop never changes; the box in the middle does.

Systems view

In practice the two diagrams run on different hardware. The loop (environment simulation and the policy's forward pass) is cheap per step and runs in many parallel copies, usually on CPUs; the learning algorithm batches up their experience and trains on a GPU. How many copies, how large the buffer between them, and how stale the experience is allowed to be are the engineering questions behind Day 6, Day 8 and Day 12, where the numbers are.

Check yourself

Q1. In Sutton and Barto's convention, which reward is the consequence of action At?

Answer 3. The trajectory is S0, A0, R1, S1, …: the reward and the next state arrive together one tick after the action. Some other books write Rt; the convention differs, the idea does not.

Q2. An agent receives +1 at every step forever. With γ = 0.9 its discounted return is…

Answer 2. The geometric series 1 + 0.9 + 0.81 + … sums to 1/(1 − 0.9) = 10. With γ = 0.99 it would be 100. This is also the rule of thumb for the agent's effective horizon.

Q3. Rewards −1, −1, −1, +10 with γ = 0.9. The return from the start is…

Answer 1. −1 − 0.9 − 0.81 + 0.729·10 = 4.58. Option 2 is the undiscounted return (γ = 1); option 4 is γ = 0; option 3 would be the answer if the +10 were not discounted.

Q4. Which statement about RL and supervised learning is correct?

Answer 4. There is no label at all, only a scalar reward, and the data distribution shifts with the policy. Sutton and Barto call RL a third paradigm, distinct from both supervised and unsupervised learning, and note that the exploration–exploitation trade-off "does not even arise" in the other two.

Q5. What did the 2015 Nature DQN paper demonstrate?

Answer 2. DQN (Mnih et al., 2015) played 49 games with the same algorithm, architecture and hyperparameters. Option 1 is AlphaGo (2016), option 3 is TD-Gammon (1992–95), option 4 is DeepSeek-R1-Zero (2025).

Q6. The reward hypothesis says that goals can be expressed as…

Answer 3. "All of what we mean by goals and purposes can be well thought of as the maximization of the expected value of the cumulative sum of a received scalar signal." Cumulative and expected are both essential: the agent maximises the return, not the next reward.

Recap: five things to remember

  1. RL is learning what to do from consequences: trial-and-error search plus delayed reward, with no supervisor telling the agent which action was right.
  2. The loop is St → At → Rt+1, St+1; the agent's rule for choosing actions is the policy π(a | s), and learning means improving it.
  3. The agent maximises the return Gt = Σ γk Rt+k+1, not the next reward. For −1, −1, −1, +10 at γ = 0.9 that is 4.58; for +1 forever it is 1/(1−γ) = 10.
  4. γ sets the horizon (about 1/(1−γ) steps) and keeps infinite sums finite; terminal states are worth zero.
  5. RL is hard because feedback is a delayed scalar, data is sequential, and the agent's own actions choose its data, which forces a trade-off between exploring and exploiting. Day 2 is about that trade-off alone.

Week 1 · Day 2

Bandits: the exploration problem in miniature

After today you can run ε-greedy, UCB and Thompson sampling on a 10-armed testbed, define regret and read a regret curve, and explain why exploration never fully goes away.

About 90 min · Needs Day 1

Today's big idea

Take the loop from Day 1 and delete the state: every step looks the same, and the only thing an action changes is the reward you get right now. What is left is the k-armed bandit, and the only problem left in it is exploration. Every method today is a different rule for the same trade-off: pull the arm that looks best so far, or pull another one to find out whether it is actually better. The cost of that trade-off has a name, regret, and a provable floor: it can grow as slowly as log n, but never slower.

1. The k-armed bandit

Picture a row of k slot machines (one-armed bandits), each with a fixed but unknown payout distribution. Each round you pull one and collect a reward drawn from its distribution. Sutton and Barto's definition: "you are faced repeatedly with a choice among k different options, or actions. After each choice you receive a numerical reward chosen from a stationary probability distribution that depends on the action you selected. Your objective is to maximize the expected total reward over some time period." Sutton & Barto 2018

Each action a has a true action value, the expected reward for pulling it: q*(a) = E[Rt | At = a]. If you knew q*(a) for every arm you would always pull the largest. You do not, so you keep an estimate Qt(a) and try to make it accurate while also collecting reward. Sutton & Barto 2018 The term "action value" is due to Chris Watkins, whose 1989 thesis also contains what may be the first use of ε-greedy. Sutton & Barto 2018

The playground for this lesson is Sutton and Barto's 10-armed testbed: 10 arms whose true values q*(a) are drawn from a normal distribution with mean 0 and variance 1, and whose rewards are normal with mean q*(a) and variance 1. Each run is 1,000 pulls, repeated on 2,000 fresh problems; the book's curves are averages over those runs. Sutton & Barto 2018 The best arm is worth about 1.54 on average, so 1.54 reward per pull is the most any method could hope for.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

There are ten ice-cream shops in town and you have never tried any of them. Every day you can visit one. If you keep going to the one you liked best so far, you might miss a better one. If you keep trying new ones, you eat a lot of mediocre ice cream. The question of the day is: what is the smartest rule for deciding, each morning, where to go?

2. Estimating action values

The natural estimate is the sample average: the mean of all rewards received so far from that arm. Storing every reward would be wasteful. Instead, keep one number per arm and update it. If Qn is the estimate after n−1 rewards and Rn is the n-th reward, then Sutton & Barto 2018

Qn+1 = Qn + (1/n) · [Rn − Qn]

which is exactly the sample mean and "holds even for n = 1". Check it by hand. Arm 1 pays 4, then 2, then 6. Q2 = 4. Q3 = 4 + ½(2 − 4) = 3. Q4 = 3 + ⅓(6 − 3) = 4. The plain average (4 + 2 + 6)/3 is also 4.

The shape of that line is the single most reused pattern in this course, so memorise it in words: NewEstimate ← OldEstimate + StepSize · [Target − OldEstimate]. The bracket is an error; the step size says how far to move toward the target. Sutton & Barto 2018 With step size 1/n you get the exact average, and old rewards matter as much as new ones. With a constant step size α (say 0.1) you get an exponentially recency-weighted average, which forgets the past and is the right choice when arm values drift over time (a nonstationary bandit). Same rewards 4, 2, 6 with α = 0.1 from Q1 = 0: 0 → 0.4 → 0.56 → 1.104. Slow, but it would keep tracking if the arm's true value changed next week. Sutton & Barto 2018

Q, N = [0.0]*k, [0]*k
for t in range(steps):
    if rand() < eps: a = randint(k)        # explore
    else:            a = argmax(Q)         # exploit
    r = pull(a)
    N[a] += 1
    Q[a] += (1/N[a]) * (r - Q[a])          # incremental mean

3. ε-greedy and the testbed numbers

The greedy rule always pulls the arm with the highest current estimate, At = argmaxa Qt(a). It never explores, so if the best arm has a bad first draw it may never be tried again. ε-greedy fixes this with a coin: with probability ε pick an arm uniformly at random; otherwise be greedy. Sutton & Barto 2018

Sutton and Barto's Figure 2.2 compares the two on the testbed. Their text says the greedy method "achieved a reward-per-step of only about 1, compared with the best possible of about 1.54", and "found the optimal action in only approximately one-third of the tasks". ε = 0.1 "explores more, and usually finds the optimal action earlier, but it never selects that action more than 91% of the time". ε = 0.01 "improves more slowly, but eventually would perform better than the ε = 0.1 method". Sutton & Barto 2018 The table gives the numbers from a replication of that figure (500 problems, same setup, averaged over pulls 901–1,000); the book's text states only the greedy row, the rest are read off its figure and reproduced here.

Method (after 1,000 pulls)Reward per pull% pulls on the best armVerdict
Greedy (ε = 0)1.0034%Locks onto a wrong arm two times in three
ε = 0.011.3159%Still improving; would win over a longer run
ε = 0.11.3981%Best at 1,000 pulls; capped at 91%
Best possible≈1.54100%Knowing q* in advance

The 91% ceiling is simple arithmetic: ε = 0.1 spends a tenth of its pulls on random arms, and only one in ten of those lands on the best arm, so the best arm is pulled at most 90% + 1% of the time. That is the first sign of today's theme: a fixed exploration rate pays an exploration tax forever, even after you know the answer.

Try it: the widget runs one 10-armed Gaussian testbed problem with a fixed random seed, so the same problem comes back after every reset. Choose a method, pull a thousand times, and compare the hollow bars (true values) with the filled ones (estimates). Then switch methods and compare the regret curves.

Notice that a single problem is noisier than the table, which averages hundreds; greedy sometimes gets lucky. Notice the shape of the regret curves: ε-greedy is a straight line (a constant fraction of wasted pulls), while UCB and Thompson sampling bend over and flatten. The bad arms' estimates stay rough because they are rarely pulled; that is fine, you do not need to know exactly how bad a bad arm is.

Common misunderstandings

  • "More exploration is always better." ε = 0.1 beats ε = 0.01 over 1,000 pulls and loses to it over a longer run. Sutton & Barto 2018 Once you know the best arm, every exploratory pull is a pure loss.
  • "Greedy is safe because it uses what it knows." On the testbed it finds the best arm only a third of the time. Early bad luck on a good arm is never corrected.
  • "Optimistic initial values solve exploration." Only on stationary problems; their exploratory drive is "inherently temporary" (next section).

4. Optimistic initial values

Here is a trick that explores without a coin. Start every estimate too high, say Q1(a) = +5 when the true values are around 0. Whichever arm is tried first pays less than 5, so its estimate drops and the greedy rule moves on to another arm, which also disappoints, and so on. The learner tours all the arms "being 'disappointed'" before it settles. Sutton & Barto 2018 In the book's Figure 2.3, greedy with Q1 = +5 and α = 0.1 "initially performs worse because it explores more, but eventually it performs better" than ε = 0.1 with Q1 = 0. In the replication, the optimistic method is at 0.58 reward and 30% optimal at pull 100, but reaches 1.50 and 85% by pulls 901–1,000, better than ε-greedy's 1.39 and 81%. Sutton & Barto 2018

The catch is in the mechanism. The drive to explore is spent as the estimates fall to realistic levels; it is "inherently temporary", so if an arm's value changes later the method never re-explores. Sutton and Barto therefore call it "not well suited to nonstationary problems". Sutton & Barto 2018 It is a good trick for stationary problems, not a general solution.

Analogy

Optimism is assuming every ice-cream shop in town is amazing until proven otherwise. You will try all of them, which is exactly what you want in week one. But if the shop you settled on changes owners in year three, your rule gives you no reason to ever look around again. UCB, next, is a version of optimism that never runs out.

5. Upper confidence bounds: optimism that shrinks

ε-greedy explores blindly: a random pull is as likely to land on an arm you already know is terrible as on one you have barely tried. Upper confidence bound (UCB) action selection explores on purpose. It pulls the arm that maximises the estimate plus a bonus for uncertainty: Sutton & Barto 2018

At = argmaxa [ Qt(a) + c · √( ln t / Nt(a) ) ]

Here Nt(a) is how often arm a has been pulled (an arm with N = 0 is pulled first), t is the total number of pulls, and c > 0 sets how much optimism you want. The square-root term "is a measure of the uncertainty or variance in the estimate of a's value". Sutton & Barto 2018 Work one out: at t = 100 with c = 2, an arm pulled 10 times has bonus 2·√(ln 100 / 10) = 2·√0.4605 ≈ 1.36; an arm pulled 50 times has bonus 2·√(4.605/50) ≈ 0.61. Each pull of an arm shrinks its bonus (N grows); each pull of some other arm raises it slightly (ln t grows). No arm is ignored forever, but the attention given to an arm that keeps disappointing falls toward zero, whereas ε-greedy's attention to bad arms is constant.

Try it: one arm's bonus as the run grows. The upper line is an arm you never pull again (N fixed): its bonus creeps up with ln t. The lower line is an arm you pull one time in ten: its bonus shrinks like √(10 ln t / t).

Notice the scales. The ignored arm's bonus grows only logarithmically: from t = 100 to t = 10,000 it rises by a factor of √2, not 100. The regularly pulled arm's bonus heads to zero. UCB's exploration is permanent but ever cheaper.

On the testbed with c = 2, "UCB generally performs better than ε-greedy action selection, except in the first k steps, when it selects randomly among the as-yet-untried actions"; the replication reaches 1.46 reward and 86% optimal by pulls 901–1,000. Sutton & Barto 2018 The curve spikes at pull 11: every arm has been tried once, and the eleventh pull goes to whichever had the luckiest draw, often the best arm. The book's version is UCB1; Auer, Cesa-Bianchi and Fischer introduced it in 2002 with c = √2 and proved that its regret grows only logarithmically in the number of pulls, "uniformly over time" rather than just in the limit. Auer 2002

6. Thompson sampling: explore by sampling your beliefs

The oldest bandit algorithm is also, as of October 2026, one of the most used in practice. William Thompson proposed it in 1933, in a paper about deciding which of two treatments is better while trials are still running. Thompson 1933 The idea: keep a probability distribution over what each arm's value might be, draw one plausible value for each arm, and pull the arm whose draw is highest. Arms you know well produce draws near their true value; arms you know little about produce wild draws that sometimes win, which is exactly when you should try them.

The textbook case is rewards that are 0 or 1 (a click or no click). For each arm k keep a Beta(αk, βk) distribution, starting at Beta(1, 1), which is uniform on [0, 1]. Each round: sample θ̂k ∼ Beta(αk, βk) for every arm, pull xt = argmaxk θ̂k, observe r ∈ {0, 1}, and update only the pulled arm: α ← α + r, β ← β + (1 − r). The posterior mean is α/(α + β) and "the distribution becomes more concentrated as αk + βk grows". Russo 2018 Work one out: arm A has 3 wins and 1 loss, so Beta(4, 2) with mean 0.67; arm B has 1 win and 0 losses, so Beta(2, 1), also mean 0.67. Same mean, but B's distribution is much wider, so B's draw exceeds A's more often than not, and the less-tried arm gets explored without any explicit exploration rule.

Chapelle and Li's 2011 evaluation on simulated bandits and display-advertising data found Thompson sampling "highly competitive" with UCB and ε-greedy and revived interest in it. Chapelle & Li 2011 Russo and colleagues' tutorial flags a common misconception: you sample a plausible success probability for each arm from the posterior, not a predicted outcome of the next pull. Russo 2018 The widget above uses the Gaussian version for its normally distributed rewards: each arm's belief is a normal distribution with mean N·Q/(N+1) and variance 1/(N+1), which narrows by the same logic as the Beta.

7. Regret: the price of not knowing

How do you compare bandit algorithms? Not by total reward, which depends on the problem, but by how much reward you gave up relative to someone who knew the best arm from the start. That quantity is regret. With μ* the best arm's mean and Xt the reward at pull t, the regret after n pulls is Lattimore & Szepesvári 2020

Rn = n·μ* − E[ Σt=1n Xt ]

Regret is never negative, and it is zero only if you already know the best arm. It has a useful decomposition: define the gap Δa = μ* − μa of each arm and let Ta(n) be how many times you pulled it; then Lattimore & Szepesvári 2020

Rn = Σa Δa · E[ Ta(n) ]

Read it as a bill: every pull of a suboptimal arm costs its gap. A good algorithm pulls large-gap arms rarely (they are easy to rule out) and can afford more pulls on arms whose gap is tiny. The goal is sublinear regret, Rn/n → 0: the fraction of pulls wasted goes to zero. ε-greedy with fixed ε fails this test: it wastes about ε·(k−1)/k of its pulls forever, so its regret is a straight line, as you saw in the widget.

How low can regret go? In 1985 Lai and Robbins proved a lower bound, best said in words: for any "reasonable" algorithm (one that does well on every problem, not just this one), regret must grow at least like a constant times log n, where the constant depends on the gaps and on how hard each suboptimal arm is to tell apart from the best. Lattimore & Szepesvári 2020 Auer and colleagues summarise: Lai and Robbins "were the first to show that regret must grow at least logarithmically in the number of plays", and UCB1 matches that rate; Auer 2002 so does Thompson sampling. Chapelle & Li 2011

This answers the lesson's title. Why does exploration never fully go away? Because log n keeps growing. A method whose regret flattened to a constant would have to stop exploring, and any method that stops exploring can be fooled by some problem on which an arm it gave up on was actually best. The best you can do is explore less and less, at the rate your confidence justifies, which is exactly what the shrinking UCB bonus and the narrowing Thompson posterior implement.

Going deeper (optional): the UCB1 regret bound

Auer, Cesa-Bianchi and Fischer's Theorem 1 states that for rewards in [0, 1], UCB1 with c = √2 has expected regret after n pulls of at most 8·Σi: μi<μ* (ln n)/Δi + (1 + π²/3)·Σj Δj. Auer 2002 The first term is the log n growth; notice that arms with a small gap contribute more, since 1/Δi is large: they are pulled more often, but each pull is cheap. The Lai–Robbins floor has the same log n shape with a smaller constant, Σi Δi/D(pi‖p*), where D is the KL divergence between arm i's reward distribution and the best arm's. Chapelle & Li 2011 Day 11 brings the same optimism-in-the-face-of-uncertainty idea to full RL, where the "arms" are whole states and the bonus becomes an exploration reward.

8. Contextual bandits in the real world

Real decisions come with side information. Sutton and Barto's version: suppose that each round you are handed a bandit task to play but also "some distinctive clue about its identity (but not its action values)", say the machine's colour. Then you can learn a policy from clue to action, "if red, select arm 1; if green, select arm 2". Sutton & Barto 2018 This is the contextual bandit (the book calls it associative search): a context x arrives, you pick an action, you see a reward for that action only. It is "intermediate between the k-armed bandit problem and the full reinforcement learning problem" because the action affects the immediate reward but not the next context. Sutton & Barto 2018 Remove that last restriction, let actions change what comes next, and you are back to the full loop of Day 1, which is Day 3.

This is where the lesson meets production systems. In 2010 Li, Chu, Langford and Schapire framed the choice of which story to show on the Yahoo! front page as a contextual bandit, with user features as context and the click as reward. Evaluated offline on over 33 million logged events, their algorithm achieved "a 12.5% click lift compared to a standard context-free bandit algorithm". Li 2010 Chapelle and Li ran Thompson sampling with a logistic-regression click model on display-advertising data and found it competitive there too. Chapelle & Li 2011 The same logic applies to the A/B test: a fixed 50/50 split keeps sending half your users to the losing version for the whole experiment, while a bandit shifts traffic toward the winner as evidence accumulates; Steven Scott made this Bayesian case for business experiments in 2010. Scott 2010 Whenever a system picks among a few options for a stream of users and gets quick feedback (headlines, ads, recommendations, prices), there is a bandit underneath.

9. Architecture

A bandit agent is the smallest possible RL agent, so its diagram is the smallest too. The top row is the k-armed case; the bottom row shows what changes when a context arrives.

Read the top row left to right. The agent's entire memory is a table with one row per arm: an estimate Q(a) and a count N(a) (for Thompson sampling, the two Beta parameters play both roles). The selection rule reads the table and emits one action; it is the only place the three methods differ. The environment draws a reward from the chosen arm and sends it back; the update rule writes it into the one row that was pulled, using the incremental-mean line from Section 2. There is no state, so nothing carries from one step to the next except the table.

The bottom row is the contextual version. A context x (user features, time of day) arrives before each decision. A table cannot index a continuous context, so it becomes a model f(x, a) that predicts each action's reward in this context, with an uncertainty estimate for UCB or a posterior over its weights for Thompson sampling: a linear model per article in Li 2010, logistic regression in Chapelle & Li 2011. The reward still arrives for the chosen action only, which is the defining feature of a bandit: you never learn what the other headline would have done.

Systems view

Everything in the top row fits in a few kilobytes: ten estimates, ten counts, one rule. The widget on this page runs 1,000 pulls faster than the page can redraw. The cost in production is elsewhere: the Yahoo! system was evaluated offline on more than 33 million logged events, which required an unbiased way to replay a logged policy's data for a new one, Li 2010 and Chapelle and Li's advertising evaluation was run over a 4-day test period. Chapelle & Li 2011 Logging, delayed feedback (a click can arrive seconds after the page is shown) and offline evaluation are the engineering of bandits; the algorithm is the easy part.

Check yourself

Q1. An arm pays 4, then 2, then 6. Using Qn+1 = Qn + (1/n)(Rn − Qn), its estimate after the three pulls is…

Answer 2. Q2 = 4, Q3 = 4 + ½(2−4) = 3, Q4 = 3 + ⅓(6−3) = 4, identical to (4+2+6)/3. Option 4 is what you get with a constant step size α = 0.1 starting from 0.

Q2. Why can ε-greedy with ε = 0.1 never pull the best of 10 arms more than 91% of the time?

Answer 4. 90% greedy pulls plus 10% × 1/10 random pulls that happen to hit the best arm gives 91% at most, even with perfect estimates. The exploration tax of a fixed ε is paid forever.

Q3. At t = 100, with c = 2, the UCB bonus of an arm pulled 10 times is about…

Answer 1. 2·√(ln 100 / 10) = 2·√0.4605 ≈ 1.36. Option 2 is the bonus for an arm pulled 50 times; option 3 is ln 100 itself.

Q4. "Sublinear regret" means that…

Answer 3. Rn/n → 0. The total still grows, at least like log n by the Lai–Robbins bound, so mistakes never stop; they just become rare. Regret is never negative.

Q5. In Beta–Bernoulli Thompson sampling, what do you sample for each arm every round?

Answer 2. You draw θ̂k ∼ Beta(αk, βk) and pull the largest draw. Sampling the mean (option 4) would be greedy and never explore; sampling an outcome (option 1) is the misconception Russo et al. warn against.

Q6. Which method's exploration is "inherently temporary", making it unsuitable for arms whose values drift?

Answer 4. Optimism is spent as the inflated estimates fall to realistic levels; afterwards the method is plain greedy. UCB's bonus and Thompson's posterior keep exploring (less and less), and ε-greedy keeps exploring at a constant rate.

Recap: five things to remember

  1. A k-armed bandit is RL with no state: k actions, unknown mean rewards q*(a), one pull per round. Only exploration is left.
  2. Estimates update as NewEstimate ← OldEstimate + StepSize·[Target − OldEstimate]; step size 1/n gives the exact mean, a constant α forgets the past.
  3. On the 10-armed testbed greedy gets about 1.00 reward per pull and finds the best arm a third of the time; ε = 0.1 gets about 1.39 and is capped at 91% optimal; the best possible is about 1.54.
  4. UCB adds a bonus c·√(ln t / N(a)) that shrinks for pulled arms and creeps up for ignored ones; Thompson sampling draws a plausible value from each arm's posterior and pulls the largest draw. Both explore less and less, never zero.
  5. Regret Rn = Σa Δa E[Ta(n)] is what you lose to the best arm; Lai and Robbins (1985) proved it must grow at least like log n, so exploration never fully goes away. Contextual bandits add side information and run headline, ad and A/B systems in practice (Yahoo!: 12.5% click lift).

Sources

  1. Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, 2nd edition — Sutton & Barto, MIT Press, 2018. Chapter 2 is today's lesson: sections 2.1–2.7 and 2.9, Figures 2.2–2.4.
  2. Finite-time Analysis of the Multiarmed Bandit Problem — Auer, Cesa-Bianchi & Fischer, Machine Learning 47, 2002. UCB1 and its logarithmic regret bound (Theorem 1).
  3. On the likelihood that one unknown probability exceeds another in view of the evidence of two samples — W. R. Thompson, Biometrika 25, 1933. The origin of Thompson sampling.
  4. An Empirical Evaluation of Thompson Sampling — Chapelle & Li, NIPS 2011. The paper that brought Thompson sampling back; Algorithm 1 and the display-advertising experiments.
  5. A Tutorial on Thompson Sampling — Russo, Van Roy, Kazerouni, Osband & Wen, 2018. Algorithm 3.2 (BernTS) and the "common misconception" in Section 3.
  6. Bandit Algorithms — Lattimore & Szepesvári, Cambridge University Press, 2020 (free PDF). Chapter 4 for regret and its decomposition (Lemmas 4.4–4.5), Chapter 16 for the Lai–Robbins lower bound (Theorem 16.2).
  7. A Contextual-Bandit Approach to Personalized News Article Recommendation — Li, Chu, Langford & Schapire, WWW 2010. LinUCB and the Yahoo! front-page result.
  8. A modern Bayesian look at the multi-armed bandit — Steven L. Scott, Applied Stochastic Models in Business and Industry 26, 2010. Bandits as a replacement for fixed-split experiments.

Week 1 · Day 3

Markov decision processes and the Bellman equations

After today you can define states, actions, transitions, policies and the two value functions V and Q, write down the Bellman expectation and optimality equations, and check them by hand on a small grid.

About 90 min · Needs Day 2

Today's big idea

Once the situation can change, "how good is this action" depends on where it leaves you. The Markov decision process is the model that makes this precise, and the Bellman equation is the one-line consequence: the value of a state equals the reward you expect now plus the discounted value of where you expect to be next. Every RL algorithm in this course is a way of solving that equation approximately.

1. The Markov property: what a "state" must contain

In Day 2 the world never changed: every pull of a bandit arm faced the same situation. Today the situation moves. A chess move changes the board; a step in a maze changes where you stand. The word for "the situation right now" is state, and the whole theory rests on one requirement about it.

A state St has the Markov property when the probability of what happens next depends only on it, not on how you got there. In David Silver's phrase, "the future is independent of the past given the present". Silver 2015

P[ St+1 | St ] = P[ St+1 | S1, S2, …, St ]

If this holds, the history may be thrown away: the state is a sufficient statistic of the future. Sutton and Barto put the burden on the designer: "The state must include information about all aspects of the past agent–environment interaction that make a difference for the future." It is "a restriction not on the decision process, but on the state". Sutton & Barto 2018

A concrete test. A ball flies through the air. If your state is "position", you cannot predict the next position: a ball at the same point could be rising or falling, so position alone is not Markov. If your state is "position and velocity", the next position is predictable (up to noise) and the history adds nothing: Markov. Choosing a state is choosing what to remember.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

In a board game you do not need to know every move that was ever played to pick your next move. You just look at the board. The board is the "state": it already contains everything from the past that still matters. If a game rule said "you cannot move a piece you moved three turns ago", then the board alone would not be enough, and you would have to add that memory to your state.

2. The MDP: states, actions, and p(s′, r | s, a)

A Markov decision process (MDP) is the bandit problem plus a Markov state that your actions change. Richard Bellman introduced the model in 1957 in a short paper titled "A Markovian Decision Process". Bellman 1957 A finite MDP has four ingredients and one number:

  • S, a finite set of states.
  • A, a finite set of actions (possibly different in each state).
  • R, a finite set of possible rewards, which are real numbers.
  • The dynamics p, a single function that gives the probability of every (next state, reward) pair given the current state and action.
  • The discount γ between 0 and 1, from Day 1.

p(s′, r | s, a) ≐ Pr{ St = s′, Rt = r | St−1 = s, At−1 = a },   with   Σs′ Σr p(s′, r | s, a) = 1

That one function p is the whole environment. From it you can derive anything else: the transition probability p(s′ | s, a) = Σr p(s′, r | s, a), and the expected reward r(s, a) = Σr r Σs′ p(s′, r | s, a). Sutton & Barto 2018 Silver writes the same thing as a tuple ⟨S, A, P, R, γ⟩ with transitions Pass′ and rewards Ras kept separate; Silver 2015 the book's four-argument form also lets the reward depend on where you landed.

Two sanity checks. A bandit is an MDP with a single state. A terminal state (game over, goal reached) is one from which every action returns to itself with reward 0, so its value is 0 by definition.

3. Policies, V, and Q

A policy is the agent's rule for acting: "a mapping from states to probabilities of selecting each possible action", written π(a | s) = Pr{At = a | St = s}. Sutton & Barto 2018 A deterministic policy is the special case where one action gets probability 1 in each state; you can write it as a function a = π(s). A stochastic policy spreads probability over several actions. The equiprobable random policy, π(a | s) = 1/|A| for every a, will be our test case all day.

Given a policy, two questions have well-defined answers. How good is it to be in state s and then follow π? That is the state-value function V. How good is it to be in s, take action a, and only then follow π? That is the action-value function Q. Both are expected returns, where the return Gt = Rt+1 + γRt+2 + γ²Rt+3 + … is the discounted sum you met in Day 1.

vπ(s) ≐ Eπ[ Gt | St = s ]     qπ(s, a) ≐ Eπ[ Gt | St = s, At = a ]

The two are tied together in both directions. V is the policy-weighted average of Q, because the first thing that happens in s is that π picks an action. And Q is the environment-weighted average of "reward plus discounted V of the next state", because after the action the environment picks (s′, r):

vπ(s) = Σa π(a | s) qπ(s, a)     qπ(s, a) = Σs′, r p(s′, r | s, a) [ r + γ vπ(s′) ]

The term "action value" is Chris Watkins's, from the 1989 thesis behind the Q-learning review. Sutton & Barto 2018 V has one number per state, Q one per state–action pair, and Q is the one you can act on directly: comparing q(s, a) across actions tells you what to do without knowing the dynamics.

4. The Bellman expectation equation

Substitute the second formula of section 3 into the first and you get an equation that mentions only vπ:

vπ(s) = Σa π(a | s) Σs′, r p(s′, r | s, a) [ r + γ vπ(s′) ]   for every s

This is the Bellman expectation equation. Here is the derivation in words, with no algebra. The return has a recursion: whatever happens, Gt = Rt+1 + γ Gt+1, because the sum from tomorrow onward is the sum from today onward with one reward peeled off and the rest discounted once more. Take the expectation of both sides given St = s. The left side is vπ(s). On the right, the expected first reward and the expected value of the next state are both averages over the two random choices that happen in one step: π chooses a, then the environment chooses (s′, r). Weighting every branch by its probability gives the double sum. Sutton and Barto read it as: "the value of the start state must equal the (discounted) value of the expected next state, plus the reward expected along the way". Sutton & Barto 2018

The same substitution the other way round gives the equation for Q, in which the policy appears one step later: qπ(s, a) = Σs′, r p(s′, r | s, a) [ r + γ Σa′ π(a′ | s′) qπ(s′, a′) ]. OpenAI 2018

Two facts about this equation carry the rest of the course. First, it is linear in the unknowns vπ(s): n states give n linear equations in n unknowns, which is how the book produced the gridworld numbers in section 7. Sutton & Barto 2018 Second, it is a consistency condition, not a procedure: it says what must be true of vπ and leaves open how to find it. Algorithms are different answers to "how".

Analogy

Think of value as the total candy you will collect from here on if you keep walking your usual route, with candy far down the road counting a little less. The Bellman equation says: candy-from-here = candy-on-this-square + 0.9 × candy-from-the-next-square. You do not need to walk the whole route to check a value; you only need to look one square ahead. That one-step look is called a backup, because information is backed up from the next state to this one.

5. The Bellman optimality equation

Policies can be compared: π is at least as good as π′ when vπ(s) ≥ vπ′(s) in every state. This is only a partial order (two policies may each win in different states), but the central theorem of MDPs is that it always has a top: "There is always at least one policy that is better than or equal to all other policies." That is an optimal policy π*, and all optimal policies share the same optimal value functions: Sutton & Barto 2018

v*(s) ≐ maxπ vπ(s)     q*(s, a) ≐ maxπ qπ(s, a)     q*(s, a) = E[ Rt+1 + γ v*(St+1) | St = s, At = a ]

Now the key move. Under an optimal policy, the value of a state must equal the value of the best action from it, because an optimal policy would never knowingly take a worse one. So in the backup diagram the policy's averaging level turns into a maximum, and we get the Bellman optimality equations:

v*(s) = maxa Σs′, r p(s′, r | s, a) [ r + γ v*(s′) ]

q*(s, a) = Σs′, r p(s′, r | s, a) [ r + γ maxa′ q*(s′, a′) ]

Because of the max, these are nonlinear: n equations in n unknowns that matrix algebra cannot solve. But for a finite MDP the system has a unique solution v*, and once you have it, acting well is easy. Any policy that is greedy with respect to v*, picking the action that maximises the bracket above, is optimal: "a one-step-ahead search yields the long-term optimal actions". With q* you do not even need the one-step search; the best action is read straight off the table. Sutton & Barto 2018 Silver adds that an optimal deterministic policy always exists: π*(a | s) = 1 for a = argmaxa q*(s, a). Silver 2015

So why is RL not just "solve the optimality equation"? Solving it exactly needs known dynamics, Markov states, and enough compute, and compute fails first. Backgammon has about 1020 states, and solving its Bellman equation exactly "would take thousands of years"; RL methods settle for approximate solutions. Sutton & Barto 2018 The rest of this course is about the approximations.

Common misunderstandings

  • "Markov means the environment is simple or deterministic." It means only that the state carries everything that predicts the future. Dice, noise and huge state spaces are all allowed; it is a restriction on the state, not on the process.
  • "v*(s) is the reward you get in s." It is the expected discounted sum of all future rewards under the best behaviour. In the optimal gridworld of section 7, state A is worth 24.4 even though its reward is 10, because the +10 can be collected again every five steps.
  • "The Bellman equation is an algorithm." It is a condition that vπ satisfies. Dynamic programming, temporal-difference learning and Q-learning are different algorithms for solving it, exactly or approximately.
  • "The optimal policy is unique." The optimal values are unique. Several policies can achieve them; the book's optimal gridworld shows cells with two or three equally good arrows.
  • "Reward and next state are independent." The book's four-argument p(s′, r | s, a) models them jointly on purpose; in the 3-state MDP below, the risky action's reward depends on where it lands.

6. A 3-state MDP solved by hand

Here is an MDP small enough to solve on paper. Two non-terminal states, Start and Mid, one terminal state Goal, two actions everywhere, and γ = 0.9.

StateActionOutcome
Startsafe→ Mid, reward 0, probability 1
Startrisky→ Goal, reward +10, probability 0.5; → Start, reward −1, probability 0.5
Midsafe→ Goal, reward +5, probability 1
Midrisky→ Goal, reward +8, probability 0.8; → Start, reward 0, probability 0.2

Guess that the optimal policy is "risky in both states" and write the optimality equation for each state under that guess. Goal is terminal, so v*(Goal) = 0.

v(Start) = 0.5·[10 + 0] + 0.5·[−1 + 0.9·v(Start)]   ⇒   0.55·v(Start) = 4.5   ⇒   v(Start) = 8.18

v(Mid) = 0.8·[8 + 0] + 0.2·[0 + 0.9·8.18] = 6.4 + 1.47 = 7.87

Now check the guess with the q* table, using q*(s, a) = Σ p [r + γ v*(s′)]:

Stateq*(s, safe)q*(s, risky)Greedy actionv*(s) = max
Start0 + 0.9·7.87 = 7.090.5·10 + 0.5·(−1 + 0.9·8.18) = 8.18risky8.18
Mid5 + 0 = 5.000.8·8 + 0.2·(0 + 0.9·8.18) = 7.87risky7.87

In both states the greedy action is the one we assumed, so the values satisfy the optimality equation: max(7.09, 8.18) = 8.18 and max(5.00, 7.87) = 7.87. The solution is unique, so these are v* and q*, and "always risky" is optimal. For comparison, the equiprobable random policy gives vπ(Start) = 6.56 and vπ(Mid) = 6.29, lower than v* in every state, as the partial order promises.

Try it: pick a policy below. The widget solves the two-equation linear system for vπ, computes qπ for all four state–action pairs, and highlights the action that is greedy with respect to qπ.

Notice that for "random" and "always safe", the greedy action disagrees with the policy in at least one state: that is the signal that a better policy exists. For "always risky" the greedy action is the policy itself, which is the hand check above. "Always safe" scores 4.50 at Start: the walk Start → Mid → Goal collects 0 then +5, and 0.9 × 5 = 4.5.

A computer does the same check by repeating the optimality backup until nothing changes; this is value iteration, which Day 4 treats properly:

P = {("Start","safe"):  [(1.0,"Mid",0)],  ("Start","risky"): [(0.5,"Goal",10),(0.5,"Start",-1)],
     ("Mid","safe"):    [(1.0,"Goal",5)], ("Mid","risky"):   [(0.8,"Goal",8), (0.2,"Start",0)]}
v = {"Start": 0.0, "Mid": 0.0, "Goal": 0.0}            # Goal is terminal: stays 0
for sweep in range(100):                               # Bellman optimality backup
    for s in ("Start", "Mid"):
        v[s] = max(sum(p*(r + 0.9*v[s2]) for p, s2, r in P[(s, a)]) for a in ("safe", "risky"))
print(round(v["Start"], 2), round(v["Mid"], 2))        # 8.18 7.87

7. Sutton and Barto's 5×5 gridworld

The book's Example 3.5 is the standard test case for everything in this lesson. Sutton & Barto 2018 The state is one of 25 cells. Four actions move north, east, south or west with reward 0; a move off the grid leaves the position unchanged and costs −1. From A (top row, second column) every action pays +10 and teleports the agent to A′ at the bottom of that column; from B (top row, fourth column) every action pays +5 and teleports to B′, two rows below. Nothing is terminal; the game runs forever with γ = 0.9.

For the equiprobable random policy, solving the 25 linear expectation equations gives these values (rows top to bottom):

col 1col 2 (A/A′)col 3col 4 (B/B′)col 5
row 13.38.84.45.31.5
row 21.53.02.31.90.5
row 30.10.70.70.4−0.4
row 4−1.0−0.4−0.4−0.6−1.2
row 5−1.9−1.3−1.2−1.4−2.0

Three things to read off. A is worth 8.8, less than its immediate reward of 10, because the teleport drops the agent at A′ on the bottom edge, where a random walker keeps bumping into the wall at −1 each time. B is worth 5.3, more than its +5, because B′ sits in the middle of the grid with positive value. And you can check any cell by hand with the expectation equation. Take the centre cell (row 3, column 3, value 0.7). Its neighbours are 2.3 to the north, 0.4 east, −0.4 south, 0.7 west, and all four rewards are 0, so

v = ¼ · 0.9 · (2.3 + 0.4 − 0.4 + 0.7) = 0.675 ≈ 0.7

which matches to the one decimal the table shows. Sutton & Barto 2018

Example 3.8 solves the same grid for v*. The optimal agent walks to A, collects +10, is teleported to A′, walks four cells back up the column and repeats:

col 1col 2 (A/A′)col 3col 4 (B/B′)col 5
row 122.024.422.019.417.5
row 219.822.019.817.816.0
row 317.819.817.816.014.4
row 416.017.816.014.413.0
row 514.416.014.413.011.7

Check the optimality equation at A. Every action from A does the same thing, so the max is trivial: v*(A) = 10 + 0.9 · v*(A′) = 10 + 0.9 · 16.0 = 24.4. Check B the same way: 5 + 0.9 · 16.0 = 19.4. The column under A shows the discount at work: 24.4 × 0.9 = 22.0, × 0.9 = 19.8, × 0.9 = 17.8, × 0.9 = 16.0, so v*(A′) = 0.9⁴ · v*(A). Sutton & Barto 2018

Try it: every cell starts at 0. Press "One backup" to apply the Bellman equation once to all 25 cells at the same time, then keep pressing, or "Run to convergence". Switch between the random policy (expectation equation) and the optimal policy (optimality equation). Tap any cell to see its backup written out with its four neighbours.

Notice that after one backup only A, B and the edge cells are non-zero: information travels one cell per backup. The random-policy grid needs about 220 synchronous backups to settle to twelve decimals, the optimal grid about 285, but both match the book's tables to one decimal long before that. The centre cell's backup shows the four-neighbour sum from above (0.67 from the unrounded values, 0.675 from the book's rounded ones); A in optimal mode shows 10 + 0.9 · 16.0.

Going deeper (optional): why repeated backups converge

The right-hand side of a Bellman equation is an operator on value tables. Because γ < 1, applying it to two different tables brings their largest difference down by a factor of at least γ (it is a contraction), and a contraction has exactly one fixed point, reached by repeated application from any start. That is the uniqueness claim of section 5 and the reason "Run to convergence" is safe to press. With γ = 1 and no terminal state the argument fails, which is why the gridworld, which never ends, needs γ < 1 to have finite values at all.

8. Partial observability: when you cannot see the state

Everything above assumed the agent sees St. Often it sees only a clue. A partially observable MDP (POMDP) is, in Silver's words, "an MDP with hidden states. It is a hidden Markov model with actions". The tuple gains an observation set O and an observation function Z, which gives the probability of each observation given the true next state and the action. Silver 2015 Sutton and Barto describe the same setting as an environment that "would emit not its states, but only observations", and define the agent's state as whatever summary of the history it keeps, St = f(Ht). Sutton & Barto 2018

The clean fix is the belief state: a probability distribution over the hidden states given everything observed so far. "The belief state b(Ht) satisfies the Markov property", so a POMDP is an ordinary MDP whose states are beliefs. Silver 2015 The cost is that beliefs are continuous and high-dimensional, so in practice agents use cheaper summaries, and "the states of real agents will not be Markov but may approach it as an ideal." Sutton & Barto 2018

The most famous cheap summary is in the 2013 DQN paper. A single Atari screen shows where the ball is but not which way it is moving; the authors say "the task is partially observed and many emulator states are perceptually aliased, i.e. it is impossible to fully understand the current situation from only the current screen". Their fix makes the state the recent history: the preprocessing is applied "to the last 4 frames of a history" and the frames are stacked "to produce the input to the Q-function". Mnih 2013 Four frames carry position, velocity and acceleration, close enough to Markov for Pong and Breakout. The DQN review covers what the network did with them.

9. Architecture

An MDP is a graph with two kinds of nodes. Here is the 3-state MDP of section 6 drawn that way, with the optimal actions highlighted.

Read it left to right. A state node branches into one dot per action; which dot you take is the policy's business. Each dot branches into outcomes; which one happens is the environment's business, with probabilities from p. Every value in this lesson is a number attached to a node: V to circles, Q to dots. A backup diagram (section 4) is this graph cut out around one node and read one level down.

The second picture shows which objects each equation relates.

Today both arrows are computed exactly: p is known and the state table is small. From Day 4 onward one or both become approximate: dynamic programming keeps p but iterates; temporal-difference methods drop p and sample it; deep RL replaces the value table with a network. The diagram does not change, only how faithfully each box is computed.

Systems view

Everything today runs on your phone's CPU in microseconds. The 5×5 gridworld has 25 states and 100 state–action pairs, so one synchronous sweep is 100 evaluations of r + γ v(s′), and the 220 to 285 sweeps to convergence are about 25,000 multiplications. The problem at scale is not the per-state cost but the number of states: backgammon's 1020 would make a single sweep impossible, which is why no later method in this course visits every state. Sutton & Barto 2018

Check yourself

Q1. A ball is flying through the air. Which description of the state is Markov?

Answer 3. Position and velocity predict the next position; the history adds nothing, so it is a sufficient statistic. Position alone is not Markov (rising and falling look identical). The full history is Markov too, but trivially and wastefully; Markov does not require keeping everything, only everything that matters.

Q2. What is the main mathematical difference between the Bellman expectation equation and the Bellman optimality equation?

Answer 1. The expectation equation averages over actions with π, which is linear in v and can be solved as a linear system (that is how the book got the random-policy gridworld). The optimality equation replaces the average with a max, so it is nonlinear. Both equations exist in V and Q forms, both use γ, and both allow stochastic policies.

Q3. In the optimal 5×5 gridworld, v*(A′) = 16.0 and every action from A pays +10 and teleports to A′ with γ = 0.9. What is v*(A)?

Answer 4. v*(A) = 10 + 0.9 × 16.0 = 24.4. The value is far more than the +10 reward because the agent collects it again every five steps; 26.0 forgets the discount.

Q4. Under the equiprobable random policy, state A in the gridworld is worth 8.8, less than its reward of 10. Why?

Answer 2. The +10 is received in full (it is Rt+1, not discounted), but v(A′) = −1.3 under the random policy, and 10 + 0.9 × (−1.3) = 8.8. Every action from A collects the reward, so the policy cannot "skip" it.

Q5. You are handed the exact q*(s, a) table for an MDP. What else do you need to act optimally?

Answer 3. Any policy greedy with respect to q* is optimal, and q* already contains the one-step lookahead. With only v* you would need p to look one step ahead. A deterministic optimal policy always exists.

Q6. Why did the 2013 DQN agent stack the last four Atari frames as its input?

Answer 2. The paper says the task "is partially observed" and a single screen cannot "fully understand the current situation". Stacking frames puts velocity and acceleration into the input, turning a POMDP into something close to an MDP.

Recap: five things to remember

  1. A state is Markov when it contains everything about the past that predicts the future; this is a requirement on the state you choose, not on the world.
  2. A finite MDP is states, actions, rewards, the dynamics p(s′, r | s, a), and γ. A policy π(a | s) chooses actions; vπ(s) and qπ(s, a) are expected returns, with vπ(s) = Σa π(a | s) qπ(s, a).
  3. Bellman expectation: vπ(s) = Σa π Σs′, r p [r + γ vπ(s′)]. It is linear, one equation per state, and a consistency condition rather than an algorithm.
  4. Bellman optimality: v*(s) = maxa Σs′, r p [r + γ v*(s′)]. Nonlinear, unique solution, and any policy greedy with respect to v* (or q*, with no lookahead) is optimal. Check: v*(A) = 10 + 0.9 × 16.0 = 24.4; 3-state MDP v* = (8.18, 7.87).
  5. When the state is hidden you have a POMDP; the belief state restores the Markov property in theory, and stacking recent observations (DQN's four frames) approximates it in practice.
