Week 1 · Day 7

Policy gradients and actor–critic

After today you can derive the REINFORCE update from the log-derivative trick, explain why a baseline cuts variance without adding bias, read the GAE formula and set λ, and say what A3C and A2C changed in 2016.

About 90 min · Needs Day 6

Today's big idea

Instead of learning a value for every action and acting greedily, you can give the policy its own parameters and climb the expected return directly. The policy gradient theorem says the climbing direction is "make the actions you took more likely, in proportion to how well things turned out". Everything after that, baselines, advantages, critics, GAE, parallel workers, is about measuring "how well" with less noise and less waiting.

1. Why learn the policy directly

Every method so far, from tabular Q-learning to DQN on Day 6, learned an action value Q(s,a) and then acted by taking the arg max. That works when actions are few and discrete. It breaks in two common situations.

Continuous actions. A robot arm chooses seven joint torques, each a real number. There is no finite list to take the max over, and maximising a neural network over its input at every step is an optimisation problem in itself. A parameterised policy π(a|s,θ) sidesteps this: the network outputs the action distribution directly. The standard choice is a Gaussian whose mean μ(s,θ) and standard deviation σ(s,θ) are network outputs, so the density is π(a|s,θ) = 1/(σ√(2π)) · exp(−(a − μ)²/(2σ²)); σ is kept positive by outputting its logarithm. Sutton & Barto 2018

Stochastic policies that are better than any deterministic one. Sutton and Barto's short-corridor example makes the point. A tiny gridworld has three non-terminal states, but the agent cannot tell them apart, and in the middle state "left" and "right" are swapped. Any ε-greedy policy scores about −44 per episode at best, while a policy that chooses "right" with probability about 0.59 scores about −11.6. No value-plus-arg-max method can express "go right 59% of the time"; a softmax policy can, and gradient ascent finds it. Sutton & Barto 2018

There is a third, quieter reason. Changing θ by a small amount changes the action probabilities by a small amount. With a Q-table, a tiny change in two values can flip the arg max and change the policy completely. Smoothness is what makes the convergence story for policy gradients cleaner, and it is the thread that leads to Day 8.

So define the objective: J(θ) is the expected return of the policy with parameters θ, and the update is plain gradient ascent, θ ← θ + α ∇J(θ). The whole question is how to estimate ∇J(θ) from samples. Achiam 2018

2. The policy gradient theorem and the log-derivative trick

The difficulty: J(θ) depends on θ twice. The policy picks actions, and the actions decide which states you visit. Differentiating through the state distribution looks hopeless, because you do not know the environment's dynamics. The policy gradient theorem says you never need to. For a policy π(a|s,θ) with on-policy state distribution μ(s),

∇J(θ) ∝ Σs μ(s) Σa qπ(s,a) ∇π(a|s,θ)

Plain words: how often you are in each state, times how good each action is there, times how to make that action more likely. The derivative of μ(s) with respect to θ does not appear. In the episodic case the constant of proportionality is the average episode length; in the continuing case it is exactly 1. Sutton & Barto 2018

The trajectory version of the same result is easier to turn into code, and it rests on one identity, the log-derivative trick: for any probability P(τ|θ), ∇P = P · ∇log P. Write J as an expectation over trajectories τ, move the gradient inside, apply the trick, and you are back to an expectation that you can sample:

∇J(θ) = Eτ∼πθ[ ∇θ log P(τ|θ) · R(τ) ]

Now expand log P(τ|θ). It is the sum of log ρ₀(s₀), log π(at|st) for every step, and log P(st+1|st,at) for every step. Only the policy terms contain θ, so the start-state and transition terms vanish under ∇θ. That is the trick's payoff: you never model the environment, you only differentiate your own network. Achiam 2018

∇J(θ) = Eτ[ Σt ∇θ log πθ(at|st) · R(τ) ]

Read it as an instruction: run the policy, then for every action you took, nudge its log-probability up, scaled by the return of the whole trajectory. Good episodes push all of their actions up; bad episodes (negative return) push all of theirs down. A sample estimate from a batch D of trajectories is just the average: ĝ = (1/|D|) Στ Σt ∇log π(at|st) R(τ). Achiam 2018

Analogy

Think of a weighted maximum-likelihood problem. Supervised learning says "increase log p(label | input)" for every example, weight 1. The policy gradient says the same for every (state, action) pair you experienced, but the weight is the return. Weights can be negative, which supervised learning never has, and the "dataset" was generated by the very model you are updating, so it goes stale the moment θ changes. Those two differences are the whole of RL's extra difficulty.

3. REINFORCE, with a softmax update you can check

REINFORCE is the algorithm you get by using the formula above with the return from each time step onward. Ronald Williams published it in 1992 in Machine Learning; it is the ancestor of every method in this week and the next. Sutton & Barto 2018 The per-step update, written the way Sutton and Barto box it, is

θ ← θ + α γt Gt ∇ ln π(At|St,θ)

where Gt is the discounted return from step t to the end of the episode. The gradient of ln π equals ∇π/π. Sutton and Barto explain the division: ∇π is the direction in parameter space that most increases the probability of repeating At, and dividing by π(At|St) stops actions that are already frequent from winning merely because they get updated more often. Sutton & Barto 2018 See the REINFORCE review for the original paper.

for episode in range(num_episodes):
    states, actions, rewards = run_episode(policy)        # one full rollout
    G = 0
    for t in reversed(range(len(rewards))):               # returns, back to front
        G = rewards[t] + gamma * G
        logp = policy.log_prob(states[t], actions[t])
        theta += alpha * (gamma ** t) * G * grad(logp)    # the REINFORCE step

A worked softmax step. Take two actions with a softmax over two logits, both 0, so π(right) = 0.5. For a softmax, the gradient of log π(a) with respect to the logits is onehot(a) − π. You take "right" and the episode returns G = +10; α = 0.01.

  • ∇logits log π(right) = [1 − 0.5, 0 − 0.5] = [0.5, −0.5].
  • Update: logits ← [0, 0] + 0.01 × 10 × [0.5, −0.5] = [0.05, −0.05].
  • New π(right) = σ(0.05 − (−0.05)) = σ(0.1) ≈ 0.525. "Right" got more likely, as it should.

Now the same episode, but suppose you knew that a typical return from this state is 12, and you use G − 12 = −2 as the weight instead: logits ← [−0.01, 0.01], π(right) ≈ 0.495. The same +10 is now evidence against "right", because it was below expectation. That is the baseline idea in miniature, and it is the subject of the next section.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

You play a game of darts and remember every throw. If you win the game, you try to repeat all of those throws a little more next time; if you lose, a little less. That is REINFORCE. It works, but slowly, because sometimes you win with bad throws (luck) and lose with good ones. The fix in the next section is to stop asking "did I win?" and start asking "did I do better than I usually do?"

4. High variance, and the baselines that fix it

REINFORCE is a Monte Carlo method: it waits for the real return. The return is a sum of many random rewards, and the same return is credited to every action in the episode, including the irrelevant ones. The GAE paper states the consequence precisely: with the full return the estimator is unbiased regardless of how good your value function is, "but it has high variance due to the sum of terms". Schulman 2016 High variance means you need many episodes before the average points the right way.

Two fixes cost nothing in bias. The first is reward-to-go: an action at time t cannot have caused rewards before t, so weight it by R̂t = Σt'≥t rt' instead of the whole-episode return. The expectation is unchanged because Ex∼Pθ[∇log Pθ(x)] = 0 for any distribution (the "expected grad-log-prob" lemma), so the dropped terms average to zero. Achiam 2018

The second is the baseline: subtract any function b(s) of the state from the weight. Sutton and Barto's one-line proof: Σa b(s) ∇π(a|s,θ) = b(s) ∇ Σa π(a|s,θ) = b(s) ∇1 = 0. So the baseline "leaves the expected value of the update unchanged, but it can have a large effect on its variance". Sutton & Barto 2018 The usual choice is b(s) = V(s), the state value, learned by regressing a second network onto the observed returns with a mean-squared-error loss. Achiam 2018

θ ← θ + α (Gt − b(St)) ∇ ln π(At|St,θ)

Why does it help so much? Imagine two actions whose returns both land somewhere in [90, 110]. Without a baseline every update is a push of size about 100 in a random direction; the signal (the 5-point difference between the actions) is buried under a 100-point offset. With b = 100 the pushes are ±10 and point toward the better action.

Try it: the widget below has three arms paying 100, 105 and 95 on average, each with ±10 of noise, and a uniform softmax policy. Press "Sample batch", then switch the baseline on and off and change N.

Notice that the two estimates have the same target (0, +1.67, −1.67) but the baseline-free one is swamped: with the seeded N = 20 batch its variance is about 230 times larger, and even at N = 200 it still gets the sign of an arm wrong while the baseline version lands within 0.1 of the truth. The learned baseline starts at zero and improves across presses; that is what the critic will do online in the next section.

Common misunderstandings

  • "A baseline biases the gradient toward the baseline's opinion." It does not. As long as b depends only on the state, not the action, the expected update is identical. Only the spread changes.
  • "Policy gradient is supervised learning on the good actions." The weights can be negative, and the data were produced by the policy you are changing, so a batch is only valid for the parameters that produced it. Supervised learning has neither property.
  • "Lower variance is always better." Reward-to-go and state baselines are free. The methods in sections 5 to 7 trade variance for bias, and the trade has to be tuned.

5. Advantage and actor–critic

Using V(s) as a baseline gives the weight Gt − V(st). Replace the sampled return by its expectation given the action and you get Q(s,a) − V(s), which has a name: the advantage Aπ(s,a). It answers "how much better than the policy's average is this particular action in this state?" The general policy gradient is E[Σt ∇log π(at|st) Φt] with Φt any of R(τ), R̂t, R̂t − b(st), Qπ(st,at) or Aπ(st,at); all have the same expectation, and the advantage has the lowest variance of the exact ones. Achiam 2018

You cannot observe A exactly, but you can estimate it with the value network you already have. Sutton and Barto: methods that learn both a policy and a value function "are often called actor–critic methods, where 'actor' is a reference to the learned policy, and 'critic' refers to the learned value function". Sutton & Barto 2018 The simplest version, one-step actor–critic, uses the TD error as the advantage estimate:

δt = Rt+1 + γ V(St+1,w) − V(St,w)    θ ← θ + α δt ∇ ln π(At|St,θ)    w ← w + αw δt ∇V(St,w)

The same number δt trains both networks: for the actor it says "better or worse than expected"; for the critic it is the semi-gradient TD(0) error you met in the bootstrapped targets of Day 6. Because δt is available after one step, the update is fully online. You no longer wait for the episode to end, which also makes continuing tasks possible. Sutton & Barto 2018 The price is bias: if V is wrong, δt is wrong in a consistent direction, whereas the Monte Carlo return is noisy but honest.

The critic never chooses anything. It only scores what the actor did. If that sounds like a coach shouting "better than I expected" or "worse than I expected" after each move, that is exactly the intended picture.

6. A3C and A2C: the CPU turning point

In February 2016 Mnih and colleagues at DeepMind published A3C, Asynchronous Advantage Actor-Critic. Mnih 2016 Its algorithmic content is modest: an actor–critic whose advantage uses k-step bootstrapping, A(st,at) = Σi=0k−1 γi rt+i + γk V(st+k) − V(st), with k at most tmax = 5, plus an entropy bonus β H(π(·|s)) added to the policy objective with β = 0.01, which the paper says "improved exploration by discouraging premature convergence to suboptimal deterministic policies". Mnih 2016

The systems content is what changed the field. DQN needed a replay buffer to break correlations between consecutive samples, which forces off-policy learning. A3C instead ran 16 actor-learner threads on one multi-core CPU, with no GPU, each with its own copy of the environment. Every thread acts for up to 5 steps, computes gradients locally, and pushes them into a shared set of parameters with shared RMSProp (decay 0.99) and no locks, in the style of Hogwild!. Different threads explore different states at the same moment, so the gradient stream is decorrelated without any replay. Mnih 2016

Method (57 Atari games, human starts)Training timeMeanMedian
DQN8 days on a GPU121.9%47.5%
Dueling Double DQN8 days on a GPU343.8%117.1%
Prioritized DQN8 days on a GPU463.6%127.6%
A3C, feed-forward1 day on 16 CPU cores344.1%68.2%
A3C, feed-forward4 days on 16 CPU cores496.8%116.6%
A3C, LSTM4 days on 16 CPU cores623.0%112.6%

The scores are human-normalised, from Table 1 of the paper. Mnih 2016 One day on a CPU matched eight GPU-days of Dueling Double DQN on the mean, and four days beat every DQN variant on the mean. Going from 1 to 16 threads sped A3C up about 12.5 times, less than the 24.1 times of one-step Q-learning but enough. Mnih 2016 The same recipe trained a TORCS driver, MuJoCo continuous controllers and a 3D maze agent with an LSTM. The A3C review goes through the figures.

A2C is the synchronous version of the same update: the N environments step in lockstep, their N × T samples are stacked into one batch, one gradient is computed and applied, then everyone continues. There is no separate algorithm here; the PPO paper simply calls it "advantage actor critic" and uses it as a baseline. Schulman 2017 Synchronous batching wastes a little time waiting for the slowest environment but makes the GPU useful again and is deterministic, which is why nearly every modern implementation is A2C-shaped.

for update in range(num_updates):
    batch = [env.rollout(policy, T) for env in envs]          # N envs × T steps, in lockstep
    R_hat = kstep_returns(batch, V, gamma)                    # bootstrap with V(s_{t+k}) at the segment end
    A_hat = R_hat - V(batch.states)                           # advantage estimate (or GAE)
    policy_loss = -(logp(batch) * A_hat).mean() - beta * entropy(batch).mean()
    value_loss  = ((V(batch.states) - R_hat) ** 2).mean()
    optimizer.step(policy_loss + value_loss)

7. GAE: one knob between TD and Monte Carlo

Section 5 used the one-step TD error as the advantage (low variance, biased by whatever V gets wrong). Section 4 used the full return minus V (unbiased, high variance). A3C's k-step estimator sits in between at a fixed k. Generalized Advantage Estimation, published by Schulman and colleagues in 2015 and presented at ICLR 2016, replaces the hard cut-off with an exponentially weighted average of all the k-step estimators. Schulman 2016 Define the TD residual δt = rt + γV(st+1) − V(st). Then

ÂtGAE(γ,λ) = Σl=0∞ (γλ)l δt+l

Two endpoints make the knob readable. At λ = 0 the sum collapses to δt: the one-step TD error, which the paper calls "much lower variance" but biased unless V is exact. At λ = 1 the telescoping sum of discounted residuals equals Σl γl rt+l − V(st): the discounted return minus the baseline, unbiased and noisy. Schulman 2016 Intermediate λ is a bias–variance dial, and λ is not a discount: γ defines what return you are optimising; λ only changes how you estimate the advantage of that return.

A three-step check by hand. With γ = 0.99 and λ = 0.95, γλ = 0.9405. Suppose the residuals are δ = [1.0, 0.5, −0.2]. Then Â0 = 1.0 + 0.9405 × 0.5 + 0.9405² × (−0.2) = 1.0 + 0.470 − 0.177 ≈ 1.293. At λ = 0 the answer is 1.0; at λ = 1 it is 1.0 + 0.99 × 0.5 + 0.9801 × (−0.2) ≈ 1.299.

Try it: the widget below has a 10-step trajectory with fixed rewards and a half-decent critic. Slide λ and watch Â0 move from the one-step TD error to the Monte Carlo value; then lower γ.

Notice that at γ = 0.99, Â0 is 0.084 at λ = 0 (the critic thought step 0 was about as good as expected), 2.16 at λ = 0.95 and 3.13 at λ = 1 (the trajectory earned far more than the critic's V(s₀) = 1.5 promised). The big negative δ at step 5 and the big positive ones at steps 6 to 8 only reach Â0 once λ lets the later residuals in. The weights (γλ)l printed under the chart are the whole mechanism.

In practice, the paper's experiments found intermediate λ in [0.9, 0.99] usually best. Cart-pole learned fastest with λ in [0.92, 0.98] at γ = 0.99; the 3D biped liked γ in [0.99, 0.995] and λ in [0.96, 0.99]; the quadruped did best at γ = 0.995, λ = 0.96. Schulman 2016 The pair γ = 0.99, λ = 0.95 became the default that Day 8's PPO inherited, and PPO uses the truncated form of the sum, stopping at the end of each T-step rollout segment. Schulman 2017

Going deeper (optional): why the λ = 1 endpoint is exactly Monte Carlo minus V

Write out Σl γl δt+l = Σl γl rt+l + Σl γl+1 V(st+l+1) − Σl γl V(st+l). The two V sums are the same series shifted by one term, so everything cancels except the first V(st), leaving the discounted return minus V(st). Any error in V drops out, which is why λ = 1 is unbiased. For λ < 1 the cancellation is incomplete, and the leftover depends on V's accuracy; the GAE paper shows that if V were exactly the true value function, every λ would be unbiased, so the bias you pay is precisely the critic's error, discounted by γλ. Schulman 2016

8. Architecture

Read the left panel top to bottom. An observation enters a shared trunk (A3C's Atari trunk is a 16-filter 8×8 stride-4 convolution, a 32-filter 4×4 stride-2 convolution and a 256-unit fully connected layer). It splits into a policy head (a softmax over actions, or μ and log σ for a Gaussian) and a value head (one scalar). Mnih 2016 The sampled action goes to the environment; the reward and next state come back and, with two value estimates, form δ. The actor loss −δ log π(a|s) pushes the action up or down; the critic loss δ² pulls V toward the bootstrapped target; both gradients land in the same trunk parameters, so the value task also shapes the features the policy uses. An entropy term, when present, attaches to the policy head.

The right panel is the systems wrapper. A global parameter vector lives in shared memory. Each worker copies it, acts in its private environment for up to tmax = 5 steps, computes k-step advantages and gradients locally, and adds them to the global parameters without waiting for anyone. Workers are always slightly out of date with respect to each other, and A3C simply tolerates that. Mnih 2016 A2C replaces the asynchrony with a barrier and a single batched update, which is the shape that Day 8's PPO keeps.

Systems view

A3C's headline run used 16 actor-learner threads on a single multi-core CPU and no GPU at all, γ = 0.99, shared RMSProp with decay 0.99. On the 57-game Atari benchmark one day of this matched Dueling Double DQN's 8 GPU-days on the human-normalised mean (344.1% vs 343.8%), and the 16-thread setup was about 12.5 times faster than one thread. There is no replay memory to size; the only state besides the networks is each worker's current 5-step segment. On MuJoCo tasks the paper reports good solutions in under 24 hours, typically in a few hours. Mnih 2016

Check yourself

Q1. In REINFORCE, why is the update proportional to ∇π(At|St) divided by π(At|St), that is, to ∇ ln π?

Answer 3. Frequently chosen actions appear in more updates; dividing by their probability compensates, so the expected update equals the true gradient. The transition probabilities vanish for a different reason (they do not depend on θ).

Q2. You subtract a state-dependent baseline b(s) from the return in the policy gradient. What happens to the expected gradient?

Answer 1. Σa b(s) ∇π(a|s) = b(s) ∇1 = 0, so the expectation is unchanged. The widget's "variance ratio" tile is the effect that remains.

Q3. In the two-action softmax example, the agent took "right" with π(right) = 0.5, got G = +10, and used baseline b = 12 with α = 0.01. What happened to π(right)?

Answer 4. G − b = −2, so the logits move to [−0.01, 0.01] and π(right) = σ(−0.02) ≈ 0.495. A return below expectation counts as evidence against the action. Without the baseline the same episode gave 0.525.

Q4. What does the critic do in an actor–critic method?

Answer 2. The critic learns V(s) and supplies the TD error δ; it never picks actions. Choosing the arg max of a value is what DQN did on Day 6, not what an actor–critic does.

Q5. Set λ = 0 in GAE. What is Ât?

Answer 3. Only the l = 0 term survives ((γλ)⁰ = 1), leaving δt: low variance, biased by the critic's error. λ = 1 gives the Monte Carlo return minus V.

Q6. According to Table 1 of the A3C paper, how did one day of A3C on 16 CPU threads compare with Dueling Double DQN after 8 days on a GPU, on the human-normalised mean over 57 games?

Answer 2. The one-day feed-forward A3C scored 344.1% mean against 343.8% for Dueling Double DQN. The 623.0% figure is the LSTM variant after four days; 121.9% is the original DQN.

Recap: five things to remember

  1. Policy gradient methods parameterise π(a|s,θ) and climb J(θ) directly; this handles continuous actions and lets the optimum be stochastic, which value-plus-arg-max cannot express.
  2. The log-derivative trick turns ∇J into E[Σt ∇log π(at|st) · (how good)]; environment dynamics drop out because they do not depend on θ. REINFORCE (Williams 1992) uses the sampled return as "how good".
  3. Reward-to-go and any state-only baseline b(s) leave the expected gradient unchanged and cut variance, often by orders of magnitude; the natural baseline is a learned V(s).
  4. Actor–critic uses the TD error δ = r + γV(s') − V(s) as an online advantage estimate, trading some bias for far less variance and no waiting; A3C (2016) ran this on 16 CPU threads and matched 8 GPU-days of DQN in one day; A2C is its synchronous twin.
  5. GAE's λ dials between the one-step TD error (λ = 0) and Monte Carlo minus V (λ = 1); γ = 0.99, λ = 0.95 is the default that PPO inherited. λ is not a discount.

Sources

  1. Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter 13: Policy Gradient Methods — Sutton & Barto, MIT Press, 2018. The policy gradient theorem, the short-corridor example, the REINFORCE and one-step actor–critic boxes, and the Gaussian policy.
  2. Intro to Policy Optimization — Achiam, OpenAI Spinning Up, 2018. The cleanest written derivation of the log-derivative trick, reward-to-go, and the baseline identity.
  3. Vanilla Policy Gradient — OpenAI Spinning Up, 2018. Pseudocode for the advantage-weighted gradient with a fitted value baseline.
  4. Simple statistical gradient-following algorithms for connectionist reinforcement learning — Williams, Machine Learning 8(3–4):229–256, 1992. The REINFORCE paper.
  5. Asynchronous Methods for Deep Reinforcement Learning — Mnih et al., DeepMind, ICML 2016. A3C: 16 CPU threads, tmax = 5, entropy β = 0.01, Table 1 and Table 2 for the numbers quoted above.
  6. High-Dimensional Continuous Control Using Generalized Advantage Estimation — Schulman, Moritz, Levine, Jordan & Abbeel, ICLR 2016. Equations 16–18 and Section 7's λ ranges.
  7. Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms — Schulman et al., OpenAI, 2017. For the truncated GAE (eq. 11) and the use of A2C as a baseline; read fully on Day 8.

Week 2 · Day 8

Trust regions: TRPO, PPO, and SAC

After today you can explain why an unconstrained policy step can wreck training, write down PPO's clipped objective and fill in its worked table, list the implementation details that make PPO work, contrast it with maximum-entropy SAC for continuous control, and pick between them for a given problem.

About 90 min · Needs Day 7

Today's big idea

A policy gradient is only a local direction: the data that produced it were collected by the policy you are about to change. Step too far and the next batch comes from a worse policy, and the loop can collapse. TRPO fixes this with a hard KL constraint and second-order machinery; PPO gets most of the benefit with a one-line clip. For continuous control with expensive samples, a different family (DDPG, TD3, SAC) reuses old data from a replay buffer and, in SAC, pays the agent for staying random.

1. Why big policy steps collapse

On Day 7 the update was θ ← θ + α ĝ. Nothing told you how big α could be. In supervised learning a too-large step costs you one bad batch; the data do not care. In on-policy RL the data are the policy's own behaviour. A step that overshoots changes which states the agent visits, the next batch is collected by that worse policy, its advantages are estimated by a critic trained on the old states, and the following step can be worse still. One number from the PPO paper shows the size of the effect: on seven MuJoCo tasks, scored so that 0 is a random policy and 1 is the best result seen, the plain surrogate objective with no clipping or penalty averaged −0.39, worse than random, while the same code with clipping at ε = 0.2 averaged 0.82. Schulman 2017

The TRPO paper gives the theory. Let Lπ(π̃) be the surrogate objective: the expected advantage of a new policy π̃ measured on states visited by the old policy π. Its Theorem 1 says the true performance of π̃ is bounded below by

η(π̃) ≥ Lπ(π̃) − C · DKLmax(π, π̃),   C = 4εγ / (1−γ)²

where ε is the largest advantage in absolute value. Schulman 2015 Plain words: the surrogate is a good proxy for real improvement only while the new policy stays close to the old one, as measured by KL divergence. Move far and the penalty term swallows any surrogate gain. The region where you may trust the surrogate is the trust region.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Learning to ride a bike, you lean a little at a time and see what happens. If you lean a lot at once you fall over, and now you are learning from the ground instead of from the bike. PPO is a rule that says "never change what you would do by more than a little bit per practice session". SAC, later today, is a different rule: "you get points for treasure, and also points for trying new paths".

2. TRPO: a KL leash, and what it costs

Trust Region Policy Optimization, submitted in February 2015, turns the bound into an algorithm. With the probability ratio r(θ) = πθ(a|s) / πθk(a|s), the surrogate is L(θk,θ) = E[r(θ) · Aπθk(s,a)], and the update is

θk+1 = argmaxθ L(θk,θ)   subject to   D̄KL(θ ‖ θk) ≤ δ

using the average KL over visited states rather than the theory's per-state maximum, which is impractical, and a hard constraint rather than a penalty because the theoretically justified penalty coefficient gives "very small steps". The paper used δ = 0.01 for all experiments. Schulman 2015

Solving that constrained problem is where the cost lives. Expand L to first order (gradient g) and the KL to second order (Hessian H, the Fisher information matrix). The solution is the natural gradient step θk+1 = θk + √(2δ / gᵀH⁻¹g) · H⁻¹g. H has as many rows as the network has parameters, so it is never formed or inverted; instead Hx = g is solved with conjugate gradient using Hessian-vector products (the paper ran 10 CG iterations and computed Fisher-vector products on 10% of the batch), and a backtracking line search shrinks the step by a factor αj until the KL constraint holds and the surrogate actually improves. Schulman 2015 Achiam 2018

A step by hand. With δ = 0.01 and gᵀH⁻¹g = 4, the scale is √(2 × 0.01 / 4) = √0.005 ≈ 0.0707 along H⁻¹g. If the resulting KL came out at 0.013, above δ, the line search would try 0.8 × 0.0707, then 0.64 × 0.0707, until KL ≤ 0.01 and the surrogate is positive.

TRPO worked: it learned swimming, hopping and walking in MuJoCo where natural gradient without the trust region failed to produce hopping or walking, and it played seven Atari games from pixels with a 33.5k-parameter convolutional policy. Schulman 2015 But every update needs a conjugate-gradient solve and a line search, it does not sit naturally with shared actor–critic networks, noisy architectures or dropout, and it is a lot of code. The TRPO review has the details. The question that produced PPO was: can a first-order method get the same stability?

3. PPO's clipped objective, with a worked table

Proximal Policy Optimization (July 2017) keeps TRPO's ratio rt(θ) = πθ(at|st) / πθold(at|st), which equals 1 at the old parameters, and replaces the constraint with a clipped objective:

LCLIP(θ) = Êt[ min( rt(θ) Ât,  clip(rt(θ), 1−ε, 1+ε) Ât ) ]

with ε a hyperparameter, "say, ε = 0.2". The paper's own description: clipping "removes the incentive for moving rt outside of the interval [1−ε, 1+ε]", and taking the minimum makes the result "a lower bound (i.e., a pessimistic bound) on the unclipped objective". Around θold the clipped and unclipped objectives agree to first order, so the gradient at the start of an update is the ordinary policy gradient. Schulman 2017

Work through one sample at a time with ε = 0.2, so the band is [0.8, 1.2]:

Ârtr · Âclip(r) · ÂLt = minGradient w.r.t. r?
+21.02.02.02.0yes (the starting point)
+21.53.01.2 × 2 = 2.42.4no: clipped flat, stop pushing this action up
+20.61.20.8 × 2 = 1.61.2yes: the unclipped term is the minimum, and it pulls r back up
−21.5−3.01.2 × (−2) = −2.4−3.0yes: unclipped, keeps pushing the probability down
−20.6−1.20.8 × (−2) = −1.6−1.6no: already made it unlikely enough
−10.9−0.9−0.9−0.9yes (inside the band)

The pattern to memorise: the objective goes flat exactly when the update would move r further in the direction the advantage already favours, beyond the band. It is never flat when the move would hurt. That asymmetry is what "pessimistic bound" means in practice, and it is why PPO can take several gradient steps on the same batch without running away.

Try it: the widget draws one term of LCLIP as a function of r. Set Â = +2 and drag r past 1.2, then set Â = −2 and drag it below 0.8.

Notice the plateau appears on one side only, and which side flips with the sign of Â. Inside the band the solid line sits on the dashed one: ordinary policy gradient. Outside the band on the "harmful" side the solid line still follows the dashed one, so a step that lowered the probability of a good action is corrected at full strength. The paper's Figure 1 is this plot for Â > 0 and Â < 0. Schulman 2017

The paper also tried an adaptive KL penalty, LKLPEN = Êt[rtÂt − β KL[πold, πθ]], halving β when the measured KL fell below dtarg/1.5 and doubling it above 1.5 dtarg. It scored 0.74 against clipping's 0.82 and the paper says it "performed worse than the clipped surrogate objective". Schulman 2017 The KL idea did not die, though: it returns as the per-token KL penalty in RLHF in section 5.

Common misunderstandings

  • "PPO enforces a trust region." It removes the incentive to move r outside the band for each sample. Nothing bounds the KL between old and new policy; implementations that want a bound add early stopping on an approximate KL (Spinning Up stops at 0.01) as a separate mechanism. Achiam 2018
  • "ε = 0.2 means the policy can change by at most 20%." Only each sample's ratio is clipped, only in the direction its advantage favours, and the minimum keeps the full gradient when a move is harmful. The policy as a whole can drift further.
  • "TD3's and SAC's twin critics average their two estimates." They take the minimum. Pessimism is the whole point.
  • "Off-policy always beats on-policy." Only per environment step. With cheap, parallel simulators PPO often wins on wall-clock, and it handles discrete actions, which SAC as published does not.

4. PPO in practice: the details that matter

The full PPO loss adds a value term and an entropy bonus, which matters when policy and value share a network:

Lt = Êt[ LtCLIP(θ) − c1 (Vθ(st) − Vttarg)² + c2 H[πθ](st) ]

Advantages are the truncated GAE from Day 7, computed over each T-step segment and bootstrapped with V at the segment's end. Schulman 2017 Algorithm 1 is the whole method: N actors each run πθold for T steps and compute Â; then optimise L for K epochs over minibatches of size M ≤ NT; then set θold ← θ and throw the batch away. The MuJoCo settings were T = 2048, Adam at 3 × 10⁻⁴, 10 epochs, minibatch 64, γ = 0.99, λ = 0.95. The Atari settings were T = 128 with 8 actors, 3 epochs, minibatches of 32 × 8, ε = 0.1, c1 = 1, c2 = 0.01, with both the learning rate (2.5 × 10⁻⁴) and ε annealed linearly to 0 over training. Schulman 2017

for k in range(iters):
    batch = rollout(envs, policy_old, T)                    # N·T samples, log π_old stored
    adv, ret = gae(batch, V, gamma=0.99, lam=0.95)           # truncated GAE, bootstrap at segment end
    for epoch in range(K):
        for mb in minibatches(batch, M, shuffle=True):
            ratio = exp(policy.logp(mb) - mb.logp_old)
            L_clip = min(ratio * mb.adv, clip(ratio, 1-eps, 1+eps) * mb.adv).mean()
            loss = -L_clip + c1 * ((V(mb.s) - mb.ret) ** 2).mean() - c2 * policy.entropy(mb.s).mean()
            adam.step(loss, grad_clip=0.5)
    policy_old = policy.copy()

Those equations are a small part of why PPO works. In March 2022 Huang, Dossa, Raffin, Kanervisto and Wang published "The 37 Implementation Details of Proximal Policy Optimization" in the ICLR Blog Track, reverse-engineering OpenAI's reference ppo2 code. Their 13 core details include: a vectorised architecture that learns from N × M samples per rollout; orthogonal weight initialisation with gain √2 in hidden layers, 0.01 for the policy head and 1 for the value head; Adam's ε set to 10⁻⁵ rather than the default 10⁻⁸; linear learning-rate annealing to zero; GAE with λ = 0.95 and value bootstrapping; shuffled minibatch updates (4 minibatches × 4 epochs on Atari, 32 × 10 on MuJoCo); advantage normalisation per minibatch; the clipped surrogate (ε 0.1 Atari, 0.2 MuJoCo); clipping the value loss around the old value; one combined loss with entropy coefficient 0.01 on Atari and 0 on MuJoCo; a global gradient-norm clip of 0.5; and separate 64-unit tanh networks for policy and value on simple tasks. Huang 2022 Nine more details are Atari preprocessing (no-op resets, frame skip 4, 84×84 grayscale, sign-clipped rewards, 4-frame stacks) and nine are continuous-control specifics (state-independent log-std initialised to 0, observation normalisation and clipping at ±10, reward scaling by a running standard deviation). Huang 2022

Not every detail earns its place. The blog notes that Engstrom et al. (2020) "find no evidence that the value function loss clipping helps" and Andrychowicz et al. (2021) "suggest value function loss clipping even hurts performance", yet it ships in the reference code. Huang 2022 The lesson for you: when a PPO run fails, check the code-level details (initialisation, normalisation, Adam ε, gradient clipping) before touching the objective.

Analogy

TRPO is a surveyor who measures the exact distance to the cliff edge before every step: safe, but slow and heavy with instruments. PPO is a hiker with a rule of thumb: "never take a step you would not be happy to retrace", enforced per footfall by the clip. SAC, in section 6, is a different hiker altogether: one who is paid by the metre of new ground covered as well as by the view at the end.

5. Why PPO became the default

PPO's paper results were good rather than spectacular. On the seven MuJoCo tasks it beat TRPO, cross-entropy method, vanilla policy gradient and A2C at one million steps; on 49 Atari games with three seeds it "won" 30 games on average reward across training versus 18 for ACER and 1 for A2C, while on final-100-episode reward ACER won 28 to PPO's 19. So PPO learned fastest, and ACER finished slightly higher; the abstract's claim is that PPO is "much simpler". Schulman 2017 Simplicity won. Three practical reasons: PPO is first-order only, so it works with any network and any optimiser; it has one clip knob instead of a constrained solver; and its rollout–update loop parallelises across as many environments as you can afford. Two systems proved the last point at scale.

OpenAI Five. The Dota 2 agent that beat the world champions OG 2–0 on 13 April 2019 was trained with PPO and GAE. Its policy was a single-layer LSTM with 4096 units holding about 84% of the parameters; the optimisers consumed batches of around two million frames every two seconds; training ran for the equivalent of 180 days spread over 10 months because of restarts and reverts, consuming roughly 770 ± 50 petaflop/s-days through the April 2019 match, on 480 to 1,536 optimiser GPUs, 500 to 1,440 rollout GPUs and 80,000 to 172,800 rollout CPUs. Berner 2019 An algorithm that needed a Hessian-vector solve per update would not have survived that pipeline.

RLHF. InstructGPT (March 2022) fine-tuned a supervised model with PPO against a learned reward model, adding "a per-token KL penalty from the SFT model at each token to mitigate over-optimization of the reward model", and optionally mixing in pretraining gradients (PPO-ptx). The 1.3-billion-parameter InstructGPT was preferred by human raters over the 175-billion-parameter GPT-3. Ouyang 2022 Here the "environment" is a language model emitting tokens, actions are discrete, rollouts are cheap in parallel, and the policy is a Transformer with billions of parameters: PPO's conditions exactly. The InstructGPT review follows this story into the second week.

6. Off-policy continuous control: DDPG → TD3 → SAC

PPO discards every batch after K epochs. If each environment step is expensive, a real robot, a slow physics simulator, you want to keep the data. That is the off-policy family, which extends Q-learning from Day 6 to continuous actions and learns from a replay buffer.

DDPG (September 2015) is "deep Q-learning extended to continuous actions": a deterministic actor μθ(s) and a critic Qφ(s,a). The critic minimises the squared Bellman error against the target r + γ(1−d) Qtarg(s', μtarg(s')); the actor maximises Qφ(s, μθ(s)) by back-propagating through the critic; target networks move by Polyak averaging; exploration comes from adding noise to the actions. One architecture and one hyperparameter set solved more than 20 simulated physics tasks, some from pixels. Lillicrap 2015 Achiam 2018 Its weakness is overestimation: the actor hunts for whatever action the critic over-rates.

TD3 (February 2018) makes three fixes. Clipped double-Q: train two critics and use the smaller of the two target values, y = r + γ(1−d) mini=1,2 Qtarg,i(s', a'). Delayed policy updates: update the actor and targets once per d = 2 critic updates. Target policy smoothing: add clipped noise to the target action, a' = clip(μtarg(s') + clip(ε, −c, c), alow, ahigh) with ε ∼ N(0, 0.2) and c = 0.5, so the critic cannot exploit a sharp spike. Fujimoto 2018 On HalfCheetah at one million steps TD3 reached 9636.95 against 3305.60 for DDPG and 1795.43 for PPO. Fujimoto 2018

SAC (January 2018; the version with automatic temperature, December 2018) changes the objective itself. Maximum-entropy RL asks the agent to maximise reward plus a bonus for the entropy of its own policy:

J(π) = Σt E[ r(st,at) + α H(π(·|st)) ]

The temperature α "determines the relative importance of the entropy term against the reward". Haarnoja 2018 This is not the entropy regulariser of A3C or PPO. Those add entropy to the loss; SAC puts it in the reward, so it changes Q and V themselves through a soft Bellman equation, Q(s,a) = E[r + γ(Q(s',a') − α log π(a'|s'))]. The policy that maximises this objective at one state is π(a|s) ∝ exp(Q(s,a)/α), and the actor is trained to match it by minimising a KL divergence. Achiam 2018 SAC keeps TD3's twin critics (the paper: "two Q-functions significantly speed up training, especially on harder tasks"), uses a stochastic tanh-squashed Gaussian actor sampled with the reparameterisation trick, and in the 2018 follow-up learns α automatically by holding the policy's entropy near a target H̄ = −dim(A), for example −6 on HalfCheetah; the same follow-up dropped the separate state-value network as unnecessary. Haarnoja 2018 Haarnoja 2018b

Try it: the widget below has a one-dimensional action with two rewarding regions, Q = 1.0 near a = +0.6 and Q = 0.7 near a = −0.5. Slide the temperature.

Notice that at α = 0.05 virtually all the mass (99.6%) sits on the right peak and the entropy is −1.75 nats, a near-deterministic policy. At α = 0.2 the second peak is alive with about a quarter of the mass. By α = 1.0 the density is nearly flat and the entropy approaches ln 2 = 0.693, the maximum for actions in [−1, 1]. Automatic temperature tuning is a controller on this slider: if the policy's entropy is above the target, α falls; below it, α rises.

The α gradient by hand. With H̄ = −6 and a policy whose current entropy is −4 (more random than the target), the temperature loss J(α) = E[−α log π(a|s) − α H̄] has derivative E[−log π] − H̄ = (−4) − (−6) = +2, so gradient descent lowers α: less reward for randomness. At entropy −8 the derivative is −2 and α rises. Haarnoja 2018b Why bother? The January 2018 SAC needed a hand-tuned reward scale per task (5 for Hopper, Walker, HalfCheetah and Ant; 20 for Humanoid-v1) because scaling the reward is the same as changing α, and Figure 3 of that paper showed SAC "is sensitive to reward scaling since it is related to the temperature". Automatic α removes the knob. Haarnoja 2018

Results: in the 2018 benchmarks DDPG "fails to make any progress on Ant-v1, Humanoid-v1, and Humanoid (rllab)", while SAC "performs consistently across all tasks" and "learns considerably faster than PPO". Haarnoja 2018 On real hardware, SAC taught a Minitaur quadruped to walk from 160,000 environment steps (about 400 episodes, roughly two hours of real time), with the gait generalising to slopes, obstacles and stairs; a Dynamixel claw learned to rotate a valve in about three hours from joint angles and about 20 hours (300k steps) from 32×32 images. Haarnoja 2018b The SAC review covers both papers.

Going deeper (optional): why "stochastic" helps SAC beyond exploration

The January 2018 paper's Figure 2 compares SAC with a deterministic variant on Humanoid (rllab): the deterministic version is unstable across seeds while the stochastic one trains smoothly, which the authors read as "stochasticity can stabilize training". Haarnoja 2018 The entropy term smooths Q, so the actor cannot climb a narrow erroneous spike the way DDPG does (TD3's target smoothing is a hand-built version of the same idea), and a policy that keeps a second mode alive, as the widget shows at moderate α, can still switch to it if the critic later finds it was underrated.

7. Choosing PPO versus SAC

As of October 2026 these two are the workhorses of model-free deep RL, and the choice is mostly about where your samples come from.

QuestionFavours PPOFavours SAC (or TD3)
Are actions discrete?Yes: PPO handles discrete and continuous actions, including language tokensSAC as published is continuous-only
Are environment steps cheap and parallel?Yes: game engines, physics farms, LLM rollouts; OpenAI Five pushed ~2M frames per 2 sNo: real robots, slow simulators; Minitaur walked after 160k steps
What matters more, wall-clock or sample count?Wall-clock with many envs; on-policy data are used K times and discardedSamples; a 10⁶-transition replay buffer is reused for many updates
What are the stability knobs?ε, epochs, minibatch size, entropy coefficient, LR annealing, grad clipα (automatic in modern SAC), τ = 0.005, reward scale (removed by auto-α)
Does it parallelise?Natively: N actors × T steps per updateThe reference design takes one gradient step per environment step and "does not support parallelization"

Sources for the table: PPO paper and Dota report for the PPO column, SAC papers and Spinning Up for the SAC column. Schulman 2017 Berner 2019 Haarnoja 2018b Achiam 2018 Rule of thumb: PPO when simulation is cheap or actions are discrete; SAC or TD3 for continuous control when every sample costs real time. The HalfCheetah numbers make the sample-efficiency gap concrete: at one million steps TD3's 9637 against PPO's 1795 in the TD3 paper's Table 1. Fujimoto 2018 But if you can run ten thousand HalfCheetahs at once, those million steps take minutes and the comparison flips to wall-clock, where PPO is hard to beat.

8. Architecture

Read the PPO band left to right. N environments, usually on CPU, run the frozen policy πθold for T steps and record states, actions, rewards, the old log-probabilities and the critic's values. The rollout buffer holds N × T samples (8 × 128 on Atari, 1 × 2048 on MuJoCo in the paper). GAE turns rewards and values into advantages and return targets, bootstrapping with V at each segment's end. The learner then runs K epochs over shuffled minibatches: ratio from the stored log-probabilities, clipped loss, value loss, entropy, one Adam step per minibatch with the gradient norm clipped at 0.5. Finally θold ← θ, the buffer is emptied, and the loop repeats. The data are used K times (3 to 10) and never again. Schulman 2017 Huang 2022

The SAC band has more boxes but a steadier rhythm. The actor outputs a mean and log-standard-deviation, samples a tanh-squashed action, and the transition goes into a replay buffer of 10⁶ transitions. Each update samples a batch of 256: the actor proposes ã' at s', the two target critics are evaluated there, and the smaller value minus α log π(ã'|s') forms the target y for both critics' squared-error losses. The actor update samples ã at s with the reparameterisation trick and climbs minj Qφj(s,ã) − α log π(ã|s), with gradients flowing through the critics into θ. α is nudged toward holding the policy entropy at H̄, and the target critics follow the critics with τ = 0.005. Networks are two 256-unit ReLU layers, Adam at 3 × 10⁻⁴, γ = 0.99, one gradient step per environment step. Haarnoja 2018b Achiam 2018

Systems view

PPO's loop separates cleanly into rollout workers (CPU, or rollout GPUs when the policy is a 4096-unit LSTM) and an optimiser (GPU). OpenAI Five ran 480 to 1,536 optimiser GPUs, 500 to 1,440 rollout GPUs and 80,000 to 172,800 rollout CPUs, consuming about two million frames every two seconds, for the equivalent of 180 training days spread over 10 months. Berner 2019 SAC's loop is serial by design: one environment step, one gradient step, so a single GPU or even a CPU keeps up with a real robot; the Minitaur learned to walk in about two hours of real time (160k steps), and the valve task took about three hours from joint angles and about 20 hours from pixels. Haarnoja 2018b The replay buffer at 10⁶ transitions is the only large memory structure in either method, and PPO does not have one.

Check yourself

Q1. In the PPO paper's MuJoCo comparison (0 = random, 1 = best), what did the unclipped surrogate score, and what did clipping at ε = 0.2 score?

Answer 2. The unconstrained surrogate averaged −0.39, below a random policy, while ε = 0.2 clipping scored 0.82. The adaptive KL penalty scored 0.74 and ε = 0.3 scored 0.70.

Q2. With ε = 0.2, Â = +2 and rt = 1.5, what is the clipped objective term and its gradient with respect to r?

Answer 4. r·Â = 3.0 but clip(1.5) = 1.2 gives 2.4; the minimum is 2.4, a constant in r, so the gradient is zero: no incentive to push this action further up.

Q3. Which statement about PPO's clipping is correct?

Answer 1. Clipping is per-sample and one-sided; nothing bounds the overall KL, which is why some implementations add early stopping on approximate KL. On the harmful side of the band the unclipped term is the minimum and the gradient stays active.

Q4. How does SAC's entropy term differ from the entropy bonus in A3C or PPO?

Answer 3. In maximum-entropy RL the objective is Σ E[r + α H(π)]; the entropy is part of what the critic estimates, giving the soft Bellman equation and the target y = r + γ(min Q_targ − α log π). A3C and PPO add entropy as a regulariser on the policy loss only.

Q5. TD3 and SAC use two critics. How do they combine the two estimates when forming the target?

Answer 2. Clipped double-Q takes mini Qtarg,i, a deliberately pessimistic estimate that counters the overestimation DDPG suffers when the actor exploits critic errors.

Q6. You must train a controller for a physical quadruped where each hour of experience costs an engineer's afternoon. Which choice does today's lesson support?

Answer 4. Expensive, serial, continuous-action samples are SAC's home ground; the Minitaur learned to walk from 160k environment steps in about two hours of real time. PPO's strength is cheap, parallel simulation, and TRPO and A2C are on-policy too.

Recap: five things to remember

  1. On-policy data go stale the moment θ changes, so an unconstrained policy step can collapse training: the unclipped surrogate scored −0.39 against 0.82 for PPO's clipping on MuJoCo.
  2. TRPO maximises the surrogate E[r·A] under an average-KL constraint δ = 0.01, solved with conjugate gradient and a line search; correct but second-order and heavy.
  3. PPO's LCLIP = E[min(r·Â, clip(r, 1−ε, 1+ε)·Â)] is a pessimistic bound that goes flat only when a step would push a ratio further in the direction its advantage already favours; it allows K epochs of minibatch updates on one batch. Code-level details (init, Adam ε, normalisation, grad clipping) carry much of its performance.
  4. PPO became the default because it is first-order, has one knob, and parallelises: OpenAI Five (up to 172,800 rollout CPUs, 180 training days) and InstructGPT's RLHF both used it.
  5. DDPG → TD3 → SAC is the off-policy continuous-control line: replay buffer, twin critics with a minimum, target smoothing, and in SAC an entropy term inside the reward with an automatically tuned temperature. Choose PPO for cheap parallel simulation or discrete actions, SAC or TD3 when samples are expensive.

Week 2 · Day 9

Model-based RL and world models

After today you can explain what a learned model of the environment buys an agent (planning, sample efficiency) and what it costs (compounding error), trace how Dyna-Q, MuZero and Dreamer each use one, and state exactly what Dreamer 4 did and did not do in Minecraft from offline data alone.

About 90 min · Needs Day 8

Today's big idea

A model-free agent learns only from the steps it actually takes. A model-based agent also learns how the world answers its actions, then rehearses inside that model: thousands of imagined steps for every real one. The prize is sample efficiency. The price is that the rehearsal is only as good as the model, and a one-step model's errors feed back into its own input, so imagination must be kept short.

1. Model-free versus model-based: the trade

A model of the environment is anything the agent can use to predict how the environment will respond to an action. A distribution model gives the probabilities p(s′, r | s, a); a sample model just produces one plausible next state and reward. Sutton and Barto define planning as any process that takes a model as input and produces or improves a policy. Sutton & Barto 2020

Everything you have met so far, Q-learning, DQN, PPO, SAC, is model-free: values and policies are fitted directly to real transitions. Model-based methods also learn, or are given, a model, and use it to generate simulated experience. The trade:

PropertyModel-freeModel-based
Real steps neededmany (DQN: tens of millions of frames)far fewer; the model is reused for many updates
Where errors come fromnoisy value estimatesa wrong model, and the errors compound over imagined steps
Compute per real stepone updateone update plus n planning updates or a search
What transfers to a new rewardnothing; relearnthe model; only the planner has to change

The second row is the whole lesson: a model turns compute into data, but a model that is 1% wrong per step is far more than 1% wrong after fifty steps. Every method today is a different answer to that tension.

2. Dyna-Q: learning and planning with the same line of code

Richard Sutton's Dyna (1990) is the simplest model-based method. Sutton & Barto 2020 After each real step (S, A, R, S′) a Dyna-Q agent does three things: the ordinary Q-learning update; a model update that just remembers "S, A led to R, S′" (the environment is assumed deterministic); and n planning steps, each picking a previously seen state–action pair at random and applying the same Q-learning update to what the model remembers about it. With n = 0 Dyna-Q is exactly one-step Q-learning.

Q[S][A] += alpha * (R + gamma * max(Q[S2]) - Q[S][A])   # (d) direct RL
model[(S, A)] = (R, S2)                                 # (e) model learning
for _ in range(n):                                      # (f) planning
    s, a = random.choice(list(model))                   #   a seen state-action pair
    r, s2 = model[(s, a)]
    Q[s][a] += alpha * (r + gamma * max(Q[s2]) - Q[s][a])   # the same update

The textbook maze makes the payoff concrete: 47 states, four deterministic moves, reward +1 only for reaching G, γ = 0.95, α = 0.1, ε = 0.1, Q initialised to 0, shortest path 14 steps. Averaged over 30 runs, n = 0 needed about 25 episodes to reach near-optimal performance, n = 5 about 5, and n = 50 only 3. All three took about 1,700 steps in the first episode: planning cannot help before the model has seen the goal once. Sutton & Barto 2020

Try it: pick n, press Run, then tick "compare all three". The widget runs the same maze with the same constants, averaged over 10 seeded runs.

Notice that the n = 50 curve is flat from episode 3 while n = 0 is still above 100 steps at episode 10. The maze arrows show the greedy action wherever Q is above zero: planning updates propagate value back toward S long before the real walk does.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Two kids learn a maze. One only learns from real steps. The other closes her eyes after every real step and replays fifty moves she remembers, thinking "that corner led here, so this corner must be good too". After one real walk she knows most of the route; the first kid needs twenty-five.

3. Planning with search: MCTS in four steps

Dyna plans in the background, improving a value table for every state. Decision-time planning spends its compute on the one state the agent is in right now. The dominant algorithm since 2006 is Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS), which took computer Go from weak amateur to 6-dan strength in a decade. Sutton & Barto 2020 Each iteration has four steps:

Selection walks down the existing tree with a tree policy that balances promising moves against under-explored ones (usually an upper-confidence rule, UCB). Expansion adds one child node. Simulation plays the game out from there with a cheap rollout policy, often random moves. Backup sends the result up the path, updating each node's visit count and mean value. After hundreds of iterations the root's visit counts are a good policy. The catch: every edge of the tree needs a simulator. AlphaGo and AlphaZero (Day 11, AlphaGo review) were handed the true rules. The next question was whether the simulator could be learned.

Analogy

Choosing a chess move by MCTS is playing many quick imaginary games from the current position, spending more of them on the lines that are going well, and then playing the move you spent most of your imagination on.

4. Search with a learned model: MuZero

MuZero (DeepMind, preprint November 2019, Nature December 2020) runs AlphaZero's search without ever being told the rules. It learns three networks. The representation function h turns the observation history into a root hidden state s⁰. The dynamics function g maps (sk, a) to a predicted reward rk and the next hidden state sk+1. The prediction function f maps any hidden state to a policy pk and a value vk. MCTS runs entirely in hidden-state space: one g call and one f call per simulation, 800 simulations per move for board games and 50 for Atari. Schrittwieser 2019

Nothing forces the hidden state to look like a board. It is trained only so that, unrolled K = 5 steps along the actions actually played, the predicted policies match the search policies, the values match the observed returns and the rewards match the observed rewards. The model is a value-prediction device, not a simulator: it wastes no capacity on pixels that never affect the score. Schrittwieser 2019

On 57 Atari games MuZero reached a median human-normalised score of 2041% and a mean of 4999%, against 1921% and 4025% for the previous best, R2D2, after 20 billion frames (about 12 hours of training). In Go, chess and shogi it matched AlphaZero's Elo and slightly exceeded it in Go. Schrittwieser 2019 Its Go strength rose by more than 1000 Elo as thinking time went from 0.1 s to 50 s per move, and in Ms. Pac-Man even 6 or 7 simulations per move, fewer than there are actions, still worked. DeepMind 2020 More in the MuZero review.

5. Learning in imagination: PlaNet, Dreamer, DreamerV3

MuZero plans at decision time. The Dreamer family, from Danijar Hafner and colleagues, uses its model the Dyna way: to generate training data for an actor–critic in the background. The model is a world model, a network that predicts the future in a compressed latent state rather than in pixels.

PlaNet (November 2018) introduced the recurrent state-space model (RSSM): a latent with a deterministic part h, carried by a GRU, and a stochastic part z, sampled each step, so the model can represent both what it knows and what it is unsure about. It planned in this latent space and solved pixel-based control with far fewer episodes than model-free agents. Hafner 2018 Dreamer (December 2019) replaced the planner with an actor and critic trained purely on imagined latent trajectories. Hafner 2019 DreamerV2 (October 2020) switched to discrete latents (32 categorical variables with 32 classes each) and a 15-step horizon, and became the first agent to reach human-level Atari by learning entirely inside a separately trained world model: gamer-normalised median 2.15 against Rainbow's 1.47, on one GPU in about 10 days. Hafner 2020

DreamerV3 (preprint January 2023, Nature 2 April 2025) made world models general: one fixed set of hyperparameters across 8 domains and more than 150 tasks, and six model sizes from 12M to 400M parameters, where bigger models score higher and need less data. Hafner 2023 Nature 2025 The main trick is predicting rewards and values in symlog space:

symlog(x) = sign(x) · ln(|x| + 1), symexp(x) = sign(x) · (e|x| − 1)

which is nearly the identity near zero and squashes large magnitudes, so one network handles rewards of 1 and of 10,000 without per-task tuning. The headline result was Minecraft: every DreamerV3 run collected a diamond from scratch within 100M environment steps, with no human data and no curriculum, the first algorithm to do so. Hafner 2023 See the Dreamer review.

Try it: step through one turn of Dreamer's loop. In step 4, drag the error slider and watch the imagined frames rot with horizon.

Notice that imagination never produces pixels; the decoded frames are shown only so you can see the error. With 0.10 error per step the k = 15 frame is wrong about 79% of the time, which is why Dreamer stops at 15 or 16 steps and lets the critic estimate the rest.

6. Dreamer 4: diamonds from offline data alone

Dreamer 4 (Hafner, Yan and Lillicrap, 29 September 2025) swaps the RSSM for a Transformer. A tokenizer (about 400M parameters) compresses each frame to continuous tokens; a block-causal dynamics model (about 1.6B, total about 2B) attends spatially within a frame and causally across frames, interleaved with actions. Shortcut forcing trains the dynamics model on noised tokens, conditioned on both noise level and step size, to predict the clean tokens directly, so each generated frame needs only K = 4 forward passes and the model runs interactively on one GPU. Hafner 2025

Training has three phases: pretrain the world model on video with or without actions; add policy and reward heads trained by behaviour cloning; then freeze the Transformer and train the policy on imagined rollouts with a sign-of-advantage objective. The data was the VPT contractor set, 2,541 hours of Minecraft video with recorded actions, which the authors contrast with the 270,000 hours of YouTube video VPT used, hence their "100× less data" claim. Training ran on 256 to 1,024 TPU-v5p chips. Hafner 2025

Now the result, stated carefully. On the offline diamond challenge the agent reached more than 90% success up to the stone pickaxe, 29% for the iron pickaxe, and obtained diamonds in 0.7% of episodes: over 20,000 mouse and keyboard actions from pixels. A fine-tuned VPT managed sticks in 53% of episodes and rarely iron; a Gemma-3 vision-language-action baseline reached the iron pickaxe 11% of the time and never a diamond. Hafner 2025 What this is: the first agent to get a diamond with zero environment interaction, the whole policy learned from a fixed dataset plus imagination. What it is not: a reliable diamond miner (DreamerV3 online did it in every run), proof that the agent understands Minecraft mechanics rather than recombining recorded play, or a result on tasks beyond the 17 tested. As of October 2026 commentary still debates that second point.

7. Generative environments and other cousins

Push a world model to full video fidelity and it stops being an agent's internal tool and becomes an environment in its own right. DeepMind's Genie (February 2024) trained an 11B-parameter model on 30,000 hours of platformer video with no action labels, inferring 8 latent actions, at about 1 frame per second. Bruce 2024 Genie 3 (5 August 2025) generates playable 3D worlds from a text prompt at 720p and 24 frames per second in real time, stays consistent for several minutes, and accepts "promptable world events" such as a change of weather; DeepMind used it to test its SIMA agent. Stated limits: a small action space, weak multi-agent interaction, minutes rather than hours. DeepMind 2025 Project Genie (29 January 2026) put Genie 3 in a web app for US Google AI Ultra subscribers, capped at 60-second generations. Google 2026

Two other designs matter. TD-MPC2 (October 2023) is MuZero's decoder-free idea for continuous control: latent dynamics, a reward head and five Q-functions, with sampling-based planning in latent space; one hyperparameter set covered 104 tasks across four domains, and a single 317M-parameter agent learned 80 tasks spanning different robots and action spaces. Hansen 2023 DayDreamer (June 2022) ran Dreamer on four physical robots with no simulator: a quadruped learned to roll over, stand and walk in about one hour and adapted to pushes within about ten minutes. Wu 2022

Common misunderstandings

  • "Model-based means the agent is given the physics." MuZero and Dreamer learn their models from pixels. AlphaZero is the one that was handed a perfect simulator.
  • "A world model must reconstruct the image." MuZero and TD-MPC2 never decode a pixel; they predict only what planning needs: reward, value, policy, next latent.
  • "Dyna is a different algorithm from Q-learning." It is Q-learning applied to both real and remembered transitions; n = 0 recovers Q-learning exactly.
  • "Genie is an RL agent." Genie 3 is an environment generator. An agent such as SIMA is trained inside it.
  • "More imagination is always better." Model errors compound; Dreamer stops at 15–16 steps and MBPO showed long rollouts hurt.

8. Compounding error, and why robots care

A one-step model with a small error produces, after k imagined steps, a state that was never real, and each further prediction is made from that unreal input. This is compounding model error, and there are four standard defences. Keep horizons short: Dreamer imagines 15 or 16 steps and bootstraps with the critic. Branch from real states: MBPO (June 2019) starts every short rollout from a replay-buffer state and argues from a bound that long rollouts are not worth their bias. Janner 2019 Predict clean targets rather than noise, as Dreamer 4's shortcut forcing does. And train the model for value prediction instead of pixel accuracy, as MuZero and TD-MPC2 do, so errors in irrelevant detail cost nothing.

Going deeper (optional): why the critic saves the horizon

Dreamer's actor target is a λ-return over the imagined trajectory: imagined rewards for the first steps, then the critic's value at the horizon. Lengthening the horizon trades critic error for model error; the best trade is a tuned constant, which is why every Dreamer paper reports H = 15 or 16 rather than "as long as possible". Hafner 2020

Why does this matter most for robots? Because a robot's real steps are the expensive ones: slow, wearing, sometimes dangerous, and impossible to parallelise across 1,000 copies of the hardware. A world model turns one hour of walking data into millions of imagined steps, which is what DayDreamer showed. As of October 2026 the open questions are whether Transformer world models trained on video (Dreamer 4, Genie 3) can supply those imagined steps for real manipulation, and how to detect that imagination has drifted off the real world before a policy trained on it is deployed. Day 10 takes up the related problem of learning from fixed datasets.

9. Architecture

Read the top row left to right. A replayed frame enters the encoder, which produces the stochastic latent z_t; the GRU updates the deterministic state h_t from the previous h, z and action. Three heads read (h_t, z_t): the decoder reconstructs the frame, which exists only to force the latent to keep useful detail; the reward and continue heads predict the two numbers the agent needs. The KL term pulls the dynamics predictor's guess ẑ, made from h alone, toward what the encoder saw. Hafner 2023 Bottom row: start from a replayed latent, let the actor choose, let the dynamics predictor produce the next (h, ẑ), score it with the reward and continue heads, repeat 16 times. The critic regresses onto λ-returns of that imagined trajectory and the actor is updated to raise them. Then the actor acts for real, and the new transition refills the replay buffer that feeds the top row.

Left to right again: the observation history enters the representation function h and becomes a root hidden state s⁰. From any hidden state, f reads off a policy and a value. g takes a hidden state and an action and returns a reward and the next hidden state, which feeds straight back into g. Training unrolls five steps along the actions actually played and matches the three outputs to their targets. At play time the same g and f are what MCTS expands: the tree at top-left is the figure of section 3 with every node replaced by a hidden vector. Schrittwieser 2019

Systems view

MuZero on board games trained on 16 TPUs while 1,000 TPUs ran self-play; on Atari, 8 training and 32 acting TPUs, 20B frames in about 12 hours, 50 simulations per move. Schrittwieser 2019 DreamerV2 ran one Atari game on a single GPU for about 10 days (200M frames). Hafner 2020 DreamerV3 scaled from 12M to 400M parameters with imagination horizon 16, and Minecraft episodes ran up to 36,000 steps (30 minutes). Hafner 2023 Dreamer 4: about 2B parameters, 192-frame context of 256 spatial tokens each, 256–1,024 TPU-v5p for training, K = 4 passes per generated frame, interactive on one GPU at inference. Hafner 2025 DayDreamer needed no cluster at all: one robot, one workstation, one hour. Wu 2022

Check yourself

Q1. In the Dyna maze with n = 50 planning steps, roughly how many episodes did the agent need to reach near-optimal performance, compared with about 25 for n = 0?

Answer 3. Sutton and Barto report about 25, 5 and 3 episodes for n = 0, 5 and 50. The first episode is the same length for all n because the model knows nothing useful until the goal has been reached once.

Q2. What is the main difference between how MuZero and AlphaZero search?

Answer 1. Both run MCTS with 800 simulations per move on board games. The difference is what a node contains: a real board for AlphaZero, a hidden vector produced by g for MuZero, which was never told the rules.

Q3. A colleague says: "A good world model must reconstruct the frames accurately, otherwise planning in it is meaningless." Which fact contradicts this?

Answer 4. MuZero's hidden state is trained only to predict policy, value and reward; TD-MPC2 is likewise decoder-free. Reconstruction is one way to shape a latent, not a requirement for planning.

Q4. Dreamer imagines 15–16 steps ahead rather than, say, 500. Why?

Answer 2. Each imagined state is produced from the previous imagined state, so error accumulates. Short horizons plus a critic for the tail (and MBPO's branched rollouts) are the standard remedy.

Q5. Which statement about Dreamer 4's Minecraft result is accurate?

Answer 3. The 100M-step online result belongs to DreamerV3; 270,000 YouTube hours is VPT's dataset, which Dreamer 4 contrasts with its 2,541 contractor hours. The diamond rate is 0.7%, a first for offline-only learning but far from reliable.

Q6. symlog(x) = sign(x) · ln(|x| + 1). What is symlog(e − 1), where e ≈ 2.718?

Answer 2. ln((e − 1) + 1) = ln(e) = 1. The function is close to the identity near zero and grows only logarithmically, which lets one critic handle rewards of very different scales.

Recap: five things to remember

  1. A model turns compute into data: Dyna-Q with n = 50 planning updates per real step learned the maze in 3 episodes instead of 25, using the same Q-learning update on remembered transitions.
  2. MCTS plans at decision time in four steps (selection, expansion, simulation, backup); MuZero runs it over learned hidden states with three networks h, g, f and matched AlphaZero without being told the rules (Atari median 2041%).
  3. Dreamer learns an RSSM world model from pixels and trains its actor–critic entirely on 15–16-step imagined latent trajectories; DreamerV3 solved 150+ tasks with one hyperparameter set and mined Minecraft diamonds from scratch within 100M steps.
  4. Dreamer 4 (September 2025) learned a 2B-parameter Transformer world model from 2,541 hours of offline Minecraft data and reached diamonds in 0.7% of episodes with no environment interaction: a first, not a solved task.
  5. Model error compounds with horizon. Short rollouts, branching from real states, clean-target prediction and decoder-free latents are the defences, and they matter most where real steps are expensive: robots.
