Week 2 · Day 10

Offline RL and generative policies

After today you can explain why learning from a fixed dataset breaks ordinary Q-learning, what conservatism (CQL, IQL) does about it, how Decision Transformer and diffusion or flow policies turn control into sequence modelling and generation, and when offline beats online.

About 90 min · Needs Day 9

Today's big idea

Every method so far could try things. Offline RL cannot: it gets a log of someone else's behaviour and has to produce a better policy without a single new interaction. The Bellman max then asks about actions the log never contains, and a network's guesses for those actions are exactly the ones the max will pick. Every working offline method either refuses to trust unseen actions (CQL, IQL) or stops asking the question altogether and treats control as generating plausible, high-return trajectories (Decision Transformer, diffusion and flow policies).

1. The offline setting: a log, and no second chances

In offline RL (older name: batch RL) you are handed a fixed dataset D of transitions (s, a, r, s') that some behaviour policy πβ produced, and you must output a policy without ever touching the environment during training. Levine 2020 D comes from robot fleets that logged years of teleoperation, hospital records of treatments and outcomes, click logs, an earlier agent's replay buffer, or gameplay video with actions, which is how Dreamer 4 learned Minecraft in Day 9 from 2,541 hours of recorded play. Hafner 2025

You accept the handicap because exploration is sometimes unsafe, expensive or impossible: nobody lets a learning agent try random treatments on patients, and a real robot collects in a week what a simulator produces in minutes. The hope is that the log already contains what a good policy needs, and that RL can extract it the way a Transformer extracts grammar from text. Levine 2020

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Imagine learning to cook only by watching other people's cooking videos. You never get to taste your own food until the exam. If the videos only ever show pasta and soup, you have no idea whether chocolate in the soup is a brilliant idea or a disaster. A careful student assumes "if nobody in the videos tried it, treat it as bad" and sticks to combining the best moves they actually saw. That careful student is offline RL.

2. Distribution shift and extrapolation error

Why not just run DQN on the dataset? Off-policy methods are supposed to learn from any data. The trouble is the target. Q-learning updates toward r + γ maxa' Q(s', a'), and the max ranges over all actions, including ones the behaviour policy never took in s'. For those, Q(s', a') is not an estimate but a guess by a function approximator extrapolating beyond its data. Fujimoto, Meger and Precup named this extrapolation error in December 2018 and showed that DQN and DDPG on a fixed batch often get worse the longer they train. Fujimoto 2018 Online, the agent would try the over-valued action, fail, and correct. Offline, nothing corrects the guess; the max systematically picks the most over-estimated action and feeds the error into every state that leads there.

A tiny example you can check by hand. One state, five actions. The true values are Q = (4, 6, 5, 3, 2), so action 2 is best. The dataset contains actions 1–3 only (say 12, 20 and 8 samples), with rewards that are the true values plus a little noise. A fitted Q-network reproduces the seen actions roughly right, Q̂ ≈ (4.1, 5.9, 5.2, ?, ?), and fills in the two blanks with whatever its weights happen to produce, say Q̂(4) = 7.5 and Q̂(5) = 8.2. Greedy on Q̂ chooses action 5, whose true value is 2. Its regret, the gap between the best true value and the one you got, is 6 − 2 = 4. Behaviour cloning would have copied the most common action (action 1, regret 2). Anything that pushes the two blanks down lets the argmax land on action 2 and the regret drops to 0.

Try it: press "Fit Q" to fit a noisy estimator to the dataset. Watch which action the greedy policy picks, then raise α, the conservative penalty, and fit again.

Notice that with α = 0 the greedy action is usually 4 or 5: the estimator's blind guesses for unseen actions are noisy, and the max selects whichever guess landed high. Raising α pushes those guesses down (and nudges well-covered actions up), so the choice falls back onto action 2, the best action the data actually supports. Press "Fit Q" several times at each α: conservatism is about what happens on average over many possible fits.

3. Behaviour cloning versus offline RL

The simplest thing to do with a log is behaviour cloning (BC): supervised learning of a from s, ignoring rewards. It never prefers an action the data lacks, but it can only reproduce the behaviour policy, so mediocre operators yield a mediocre policy. Offline RL uses the rewards to do two things BC cannot: pick the best actions rather than the average when several appear in the same state, and stitch fragments of different trajectories, the first half of one route and the second half of another, into a path no demonstrator ever completed. Levine 2020 The AntMaze benchmarks test exactly this: an ant robot must reach a goal, but the dataset contains only aimless wandering. BC scores 0 on antmaze-medium-play; CQL reaches 61.2. Kumar 2020

When the data is already expert, BC is hard to beat: hopper-medium-expert gives BC 111.9 and CQL 111.0. Kumar 2020 Look at the data first. Expert demonstrations call for imitation; mixed-quality logs call for RL.

4. CQL: a Q-function that under-estimates on purpose

Conservative Q-Learning (CQL, June 2020) keeps the ordinary Bellman regression and adds one penalty term designed so that the learned Q is a lower bound on the true value. The CQL(H) objective is

minQ α · Es∼D[ log Σa exp Q(s,a) − Ea∼π̂β[Q(s,a)] ] + ½ E(s,a,s')∼D[ (Q(s,a) − B̂πQ̂(s,a))² ]

Read the bracket as "soft-max of Q over all actions minus the average Q over the actions the data contains". It is never negative, and it is small only when no unseen action is valued above the seen ones. Minimising it pushes Q down wherever the soft-max is being driven by an unseen action and pushes Q up on dataset actions. The second term is the usual Bellman error. The trade-off knob is α: too small and extrapolation returns; too large and Q is flattened toward the data and the policy collapses to BC. Kumar 2020 In the widget above the penalty α·(1/5 − π̂β(a)) is this idea with a uniform policy in place of the soft-max.

The payoff shows on mixed-quality data. In CQL's Table 1 (D4RL normalised scores), walker2d-mixed scores 26.7 against the best prior method's 11.3, about 2.4×; hopper-mixed 48.6 against 25.3 (1.9×); walker2d-medium-expert 98.7 against 11.3; and antmaze-medium-play 61.2 where every baseline scores 0.0. On Atari with only 1% of a DQN replay buffer, Q*bert reached 14,012 versus 383.6 for QR-DQN, about 36×. The abstract summarises it as 2–5× higher final return on mixed datasets. Kumar 2020 The CQL review walks through the proof sketch.

Analogy

A restaurant critic who has only eaten the pasta and the soup refuses to rate the mystery dish above anything they actually tasted. They may miss a hidden gem, but they never send you to a dish nobody has tried. CQL is that critic; α is how stubborn they are.

5. IQL: never ask about unseen actions

Implicit Q-Learning (IQL, October 2021) takes the opposite route: instead of penalising unseen actions, it never evaluates them. It replaces the max over actions with a state-value network V(s) fitted only on actions in the data, using expectile regression:

L2τ(u) = |τ − 1(u < 0)| · u² LV = E(s,a)∼D[ L2τ( Q(s,a) − V(s) ) ] LQ = E[ ( r + γ V(s') − Q(s,a) )² ]

With τ = 0.5 the expectile loss is plain squared error and V is the mean of Q over dataset actions. With τ above 0.5, errors where Q is above V are weighted τ and errors below are weighted 1 − τ, so V creeps up toward the best actions in the data without ever naming an action outside it. Check it on three samples Q = {2, 4, 9}: the mean is 5; the τ = 0.9 expectile v solves 0.9·(9 − v) = 0.1·((v − 2) + (v − 4)), which gives v ≈ 7.9. The policy is then extracted by advantage-weighted regression, Lπ = E[ exp(β(Q − V)) · log π(a|s) ], a BC loss that weights dataset actions by how much better than V they were (weights clipped at 100). The paper uses τ = 0.7, β = 3 on MuJoCo locomotion and τ = 0.9, β = 10 on AntMaze. Kostrikov 2021

On the stitching-heavy AntMaze tasks IQL totals 378.0 against CQL's 303.6; on locomotion the two are level (692.4 against 698.5); overall 1070.4 against 1002.1. Because IQL's training signal only ever touches dataset actions, it is also unusually easy to continue training online afterwards. Kostrikov 2021

6. D4RL and the normalised score

Offline results depend entirely on which dataset you were given, so D4RL (April 2020) published standard ones: Maze2D and AntMaze (umaze, medium, large; play and diverse), Gym-MuJoCo (hopper, halfcheetah, walker2d with random, medium, expert, medium-replay and medium-expert data), Adroit hand manipulation, FrankaKitchen, Flow traffic and CARLA driving. Fu 2020 Every number in Sections 4 and 5 is a normalised score:

scorenorm = 100 × (score − random) / (expert − random)

So 0 is a random policy, 100 is the expert that generated the expert data, and scores above 100 are possible. If random play returns −5 and the expert 100, a policy returning 47 gets 100 × 52 / 105 ≈ 49.5. Fu 2020 The medium-replay (CQL's "mixed") and medium-expert sets, which mix policies of different quality, are where methods separate.

7. Decision Transformer: control as autocomplete

In June 2021 two papers one day apart asked whether offline RL needs a value function at all. Decision Transformer (DT) writes each trajectory as a token stream with three tokens per timestep, the return-to-go R̂t = Σt'≥t rt' (the reward still to come), the state st and the action at, and trains a causal GPT to predict each action from everything before it. Each token type has its own linear embedding (a CNN for images), a learned per-timestep embedding is added to all three tokens of a step, and the loss is mean squared error or cross-entropy on action tokens only. Chen 2021 No Bellman update, no max over actions, no extrapolation error: the model only says which actions went with high returns in the data.

At test time you type the return you want: set R̂ high, feed the state, read out the action, act, subtract the reward received from the target, repeat. Ask for 90 and the model autocompletes a trajectory that looks like the 90-return trajectories it saw. Chen 2021 The companion Trajectory Transformer models the whole trajectory (states, actions and rewards, discretised) and plans with beam search over high-reward continuations. Janner 2021

On D4RL, DT averages 74.7 against CQL's 63.9 (without Reacher). On Atari, trained from 1% of a DQN replay buffer, DT beats CQL on Breakout (267.5 against 211.1) but loses heavily on Q*bert (15.4 against 104.2). Its clearest win is Key-to-Door, where picking up a key early only pays off at a door much later: with 10K trajectories DT succeeds 94.6% of the time against CQL's 13.3% (71.8% against 13.1% with 1K), because attention credits the key directly. Cutting the context to one timestep collapses Breakout from 267.5 to 73.9 and Pong from 106.1 to 2.5. Chen 2021 The Decision Transformer review has the full tables.

Common misunderstandings

  • "Offline RL is just behaviour cloning." BC copies the average demonstrator and ignores rewards. Offline RL selects the best actions and stitches trajectories: CQL 61.2 on antmaze-medium-play, BC 0.
  • "Just run DQN on the dataset." Without a penalty or constraint, Q-values on unseen actions grow with nothing to correct them, and the policy chases them (BCQ, 2018).
  • "Decision Transformer learns a value function." It conditions on a desired return instead. That makes it sensitive to the target you type and weak at stitching sub-trajectories that never co-occurred, which is where CQL and IQL beat it on AntMaze.
  • "Diffusion policies are too slow for control." With 10 DDIM steps Diffusion Policy runs in about 0.1 s on an RTX 3080; π0 emits 50-step action chunks with 10 flow steps at up to 50 Hz.

8. Diffusion Policy and flow-matching policies

Imitation has its own failure. When demonstrators push a block around an obstacle, half go left and half go right; a Gaussian head trained by mean squared error learns the average, straight into the obstacle. Diffusion Policy (March 2023) represents π(a|o) as a conditional denoising process over an action sequence: start from Gaussian noise AK and apply K steps of

Ak−1 = α ( Ak − γ εθ(Ot, Ak, k) + N(0, σ²I) ), k = K, …, 1

where εθ is a network trained, exactly as in image diffusion, to predict the noise added to a ground-truth action sequence, and α, γ, σ follow the noise schedule. Because the output is a sample rather than a mean, the policy goes left on one run and right on the next, never straight. Chi 2023 The network sees the last To = 2 observations, predicts Tp = 16 actions, executes the first Ta = 8 and re-plans, a receding horizon that keeps motion smooth and reactive. Training uses 100 DDPM steps; inference with DDIM at 10–16 steps takes about 0.1 s on an RTX 3080. Chi 2023

Across 12 simulated tasks from 4 benchmarks (plus 3 bimanual) it beat the previous state of the art by 46.9% on average; on real Push-T it succeeded 95% of the time against 20% for an LSTM with a Gaussian-mixture head and 0% for implicit behaviour cloning (humans: 100%). Chi 2023 The Diffusion Policy review has the per-task table.

Try it: press "Add noise" to draw a random action, then "Denoise step" repeatedly, or "Run K steps". The two shaded circles are the two demonstrated routes; the cross is where an MSE-trained policy would aim.

Notice that the dot wanders in its first steps and then commits to one of the two modes; different starting noise ends in different modes, roughly half each. The MSE cross sits between them, a point no demonstrator ever chose. Set K = 2 and press "20 samples": with so few steps, many runs stall between the modes, because each large step approximates a two-humped distribution with one Gaussian. By K = 10 almost every run commits.

Flow-matching policies replace noise prediction with a velocity field vθ(Aτ, o, τ) and integrate an ordinary differential equation from noise to action. π0 (October 2024) does this on a vision-language model: a 3B-parameter PaliGemma backbone reads images and an instruction, a roughly 300M-parameter "action expert" attends to it and outputs the velocity, and 10 Euler steps (step size 0.1) turn noise into a 50-step action chunk at up to 50 Hz. It was trained on more than 10,000 hours of data from 7 robot configurations across 68 tasks, laundry folding and table bussing among them. Black 2024

Going deeper (optional): why multimodality kills the MSE head

Minimising E[(a − μ(o))²] over demonstrations makes μ(o) the conditional mean E[a|o]. If a is "left" or "right" with probability ½ each, the mean is the midpoint, which has probability zero under the demonstrations. A Gaussian-mixture head needs the number of modes fixed in advance and collapses in high dimensions; energy-based (implicit) policies represent any shape but are hard to train and sample. Diffusion and flow models represent arbitrary multimodal distributions with one network and a plain regression loss, which is why they took over robot imitation after 2023. Chi 2023

9. RL fine-tuning of generative policies

Imitation gets a diffusion policy to the level of its demonstrators; to go further you want policy-gradient RL, and here a problem appears. PPO needs log π(a|s) for the action it took, but for a diffusion or flow policy the probability of the final action is a marginal over every possible denoising path, and nobody can compute it. DPPO (September 2024) sidesteps this with a two-layer MDP: inside each environment step t sits a chain of denoising states aK → aK−1 → … → a0, and each denoising step is itself an "action" with a Gaussian likelihood you can write down. Reward arrives only when a0 hits the environment; PPO runs on the denoising steps, and in practice only the last few are fine-tuned. Ren 2024 On Robomimic Transport from state it passed 90% success, the first RL method past 50%, and in a sim-to-real one-leg furniture assembly it reached 80% (16 of 20) where a Gaussian policy fine-tuned the same way scored 0%. Ren 2024

Flow policies are harder still: their sampler is deterministic, so there is no per-step Gaussian to take a log of. πRL (October 2025) offers two fixes: Flow-Noise adds a small learnable noise network at each integration step, making the per-step likelihood exact; Flow-SDE converts the ODE into a stochastic differential equation with the same marginals. Either way, PPO on the denoising MDP lifted π0 on LIBERO from 57.6% to 97.6% (Flow-Noise) or 96.1% (Flow-SDE), and π0.5 from 77.1% to 98.3% or 97.9%; on 4,352 ManiSkill pick-and-place tasks π0 went from 38.4% to 77.8% and π0.5 from 40.1% to 89.7%. Chen 2025 The pattern mirrors Day 9 and the LLM world: pretrain a large generative model on logs, then let RL sharpen it.

# DPPO-style fine-tuning: policy gradient on denoising steps, not on the final action
for t in env_steps:
    a_k = noise()                       # a^K
    for k in range(K, 0, -1):
        mean = denoiser(obs, a_k, k)    # Gaussian step: log-prob is tractable
        a_k = mean + sigma[k] * randn()
        logp[k] = gaussian_logp(a_k, mean, sigma[k])   # used by PPO's ratio
    reward = env.step(a_k)              # only a^0 touches the world

10. When offline beats online

Offline wins when interaction is unsafe or expensive (healthcare, driving, physical robots), when a large log already exists (recommenders, robot fleets, game replays), and when the data comes from many mediocre operators whose good fragments can be stitched into something better than any one of them. Levine 2020 Online wins when a cheap, faithful simulator exists and the task needs behaviour the data does not contain: no amount of conservatism finds a trick nobody in the log ever tried. The 2024–2025 robot results point at the hybrid now standard: imitation or offline RL on logs for a competent generative policy, then a short online RL phase to fix its failure modes, as DPPO and πRL do. 11. Architecture

Three diagrams, one per family. Boxes filled in the accent colour are trained; plain boxes are fixed data or fixed arithmetic.

Read left to right. In the first diagram data flows one way, from the dataset into the networks, and the policy is a by-product of the learned values; the dashed environment box is the whole point. In the second nothing is a value: the Transformer is a language model whose vocabulary happens to be returns, states and actions. In the third the trained parts are the encoder and the noise network; the schedule, the sampling loop and the receding-horizon bookkeeping are fixed arithmetic, which is why the same trained network runs with 100 DDPM steps or 10 DDIM steps.

Systems view

Offline training is a supervised-learning workload: no simulators, no actors, a dataset on disk and a GPU. Inference is where the clocks matter. Diffusion Policy predicts 16 actions per call and executes 8, so a 0.1 s DDIM call (10 steps, RTX 3080) controls a robot at 10 Hz. Chi 2023 π0 runs a 3.3B-parameter model amortised over 50-step chunks at up to 50 Hz. Black 2024 Decision Transformer's Atari runs used 1% of a DQN replay buffer, 500 thousand of 50 million transitions per game, and its cost grows with context length since each timestep adds 3 tokens. Chen 2021 RL fine-tuning (DPPO, πRL) brings simulators and rollouts back, but starting from a competent policy needs far fewer of them than learning from scratch.

Check yourself

Q1. Why does running plain DQN on a fixed dataset tend to get worse the longer it trains?

Answer 3. Fujimoto et al. (2018) called this extrapolation error: Q-values on actions outside the data are unconstrained guesses, the max selects the highest, and the error propagates. Online, trying the action would correct it; offline, nothing does.

Q2. In the CQL(H) objective, what does the penalty term α·[log Σa exp Q(s,a) − Ea∼π̂β Q(s,a)] do when minimised?

Answer 1. The bracket is "soft-max over all actions minus mean over seen actions"; it is non-negative and shrinks only when unseen actions are not valued above seen ones. The Bellman term stays. The result is a lower bound, not an upper bound.

Q3. IQL fits V(s) with an expectile loss. With τ = 0.9 and dataset Q-values {2, 4, 9} at one state, V ends up…

Answer 4. Errors above V are weighted 0.9, errors below 0.1, so V moves toward the best in-data values without reaching the max: 0.9(9 − v) = 0.1((v − 2) + (v − 4)) gives v ≈ 7.9. τ = 0.5 would give the mean, 5.

Q4. Decision Transformer reached 94.6% on Key-to-Door with 10K trajectories, against CQL's 13.3%. What explains the gap?

Answer 2. DT has no value function at all; it conditions on return-to-go and attends across the whole trajectory, so long-range credit assignment is a single attention lookup. The context ablation (Breakout 267.5 → 73.9 at K = 1) shows the context is what matters.

Q5. Demonstrators avoid an obstacle by going left half the time and right half the time. A policy trained with a mean-squared-error head will…

Answer 3. MSE regression learns the conditional mean, which sits between the two modes at a point no demonstrator chose. Diffusion Policy samples from the full distribution instead, which is why it reached 95% on Push-T against 20% for an LSTM-GMM policy.

Q6. Why can you not fine-tune a diffusion policy by applying REINFORCE to the final action a0?

Answer 1. Each denoising step has a Gaussian likelihood you can write down, so PPO runs on the "denoising MDP" nested inside the environment MDP. Flow policies need an extra trick (Flow-Noise or Flow-SDE) because their sampler is deterministic.

Recap: five things to remember

  1. Offline RL learns from a fixed log with no interaction. The Bellman max then asks about actions the log lacks, and the network's guesses for them are exactly what the max selects: extrapolation error (BCQ, 2018).
  2. CQL adds α·[log Σ exp Q − mean Q on data] so that Q lower-bounds the truth; it gives 2–5× higher returns on mixed data and 61.2 against 0 on antmaze-medium-play. IQL never queries unseen actions, fitting V as an upper expectile (τ = 0.7 or 0.9) and extracting the policy by advantage-weighted regression; AntMaze 378.0 against CQL 303.6.
  3. D4RL normalised score = 100 × (score − random) / (expert − random); 0 is random, 100 is the expert.
  4. Decision Transformer drops values entirely: three tokens per step (return-to-go, state, action), a causal GPT, type the return you want. Key-to-Door 94.6% against 13.3%, but it cannot stitch and depends on the target you ask for.
  5. Diffusion and flow policies generate action chunks from noise, so they can represent multimodal demonstrations (Push-T 95%, +46.9% average; π0 on more than 10,000 hours). RL fine-tuning works by putting PPO on the denoising steps, not the final action: πRL took π0 from 57.6% to 97.6% on LIBERO.

Sources

  1. Offline Reinforcement Learning: Tutorial, Review, and Perspectives on Open Problems — Levine, Kumar, Tucker & Fu, 2020. The definition of the setting, why it matters (healthcare, robotics), and the distribution-shift problem in full.
  2. Off-Policy Deep Reinforcement Learning without Exploration — Fujimoto, Meger & Precup, ICML 2019 (arXiv Dec 2018). Names extrapolation error and introduces batch-constrained Q-learning (BCQ).
  3. Conservative Q-Learning for Offline Reinforcement Learning — Kumar, Zhou, Tucker & Levine, NeurIPS 2020. The CQL(H) objective, the lower-bound argument, and Table 1 with the D4RL numbers quoted today.
  4. Offline Reinforcement Learning with Implicit Q-Learning — Kostrikov, Nair & Levine, ICLR 2022 (arXiv Oct 2021). Expectile regression, advantage-weighted extraction, τ and β settings, AntMaze totals.
  5. D4RL: Datasets for Deep Data-Driven Reinforcement Learning — Fu, Kumar, Nachum, Tucker & Levine, 2020. The benchmark suite and the normalised-score formula.
  6. Decision Transformer: Reinforcement Learning via Sequence Modeling — Chen et al., NeurIPS 2021. Token layout, evaluation loop, Atari and D4RL tables, Key-to-Door and context ablations.
  7. Offline Reinforcement Learning as One Big Sequence Modeling Problem — Janner, Li & Levine, NeurIPS 2021. The Trajectory Transformer: model everything, plan with beam search.
  8. Diffusion Policy: Visuomotor Policy Learning via Action Diffusion — Chi et al., RSS 2023 (extended IJRR 2024). Eq. 4, the horizons T_o/T_p/T_a, the 46.9% average gain, Push-T 95%, Fig. 3 on multimodality.
  9. π0: A Vision-Language-Action Flow Model for General Robot Control — Black et al., Physical Intelligence, 2024. Flow matching on a PaliGemma backbone, more than 10,000 hours of data, 50-step action chunks.
  10. Diffusion Policy Policy Optimization — Ren et al., 2024. The two-layer denoising MDP, PPO over denoising steps, Transport and real furniture-assembly results.
  11. πRL: Online RL Fine-tuning for Flow-based Vision-Language-Action Models — Chen et al., Oct 2025. Flow-Noise and Flow-SDE, LIBERO and ManiSkill numbers.
  12. Training Agents Inside of Scalable World Models — Hafner, Yan & Lillicrap, Sep 2025. Dreamer 4: the offline Minecraft result referenced from Day 9.

Week 2 · Day 11

Exploration, self-play, and multi-agent RL

After today you can explain why Montezuma's Revenge defeated DQN, how curiosity, RND and Go-Explore fixed it, how self-play went from TD-Gammon to AlphaZero, and why learning alongside other learners is harder than it looks.

About 90 min · Needs Day 10

Today's big idea

Reward-maximising agents only improve on what they have already stumbled into. When rewards are rare, you have to manufacture a reason to go somewhere new: a bonus for novelty, a memory of where you have been, or an opponent who is exactly as good as you. Self-play is the cleanest version of that last trick, and it stops being clean the moment more than two players, or cooperation, enter the game.

1. Hard exploration: the game that scored zero

By 2015 DQN (Day 6, the DQN review) was superhuman on dozens of Atari games, yet on Montezuma's Revenge it scored 0.02 points after 200 million frames and saw only two rooms. Bellemare 2016 The first level is a maze of 24 rooms, and the first points need a long chain: climb down a ladder, jump a skull, take a key, climb back, open a door, and one wrong step kills you. Random actions never complete that chain, so the agent never sees a reward, so there is no gradient. This is hard exploration: rewards so sparse or so far away that undirected noise cannot reach them.

ε-greedy (Day 6) and entropy bonuses (Day 7) are undirected: they explore equally everywhere, including places visited a thousand times. In a 30-cell corridor with one reward at the end, ε-greedy with all Q-values at zero is a random walk, which needs on the order of 30² ≈ 900 steps to reach the end. Montezuma is that corridor with ladders and skulls.

2. Count-based bonuses and pseudo-counts

The oldest fix is to pay the agent for visiting rare states. Keep a table N(s) of how many times each state has been visited and add an exploration bonus to the reward:

r⁺(s) = β / √N(s)

A fresh state pays β; one visited 100 times pays β/10. Because the bonus is a reward, Q-learning propagates it backwards and the agent learns to steer toward the frontier rather than wander. The catch is the table: in pixel space every frame is new, N(s) = 1 forever, and the bonus is flat.

Bellemare and colleagues derived a pseudo-count from a density model ρ over frames instead: if ρ(x) is the model's probability of frame x and ρ′(x) the probability after training on x one more time, then N̂(x) = ρ(x)(1 − ρ′(x)) / (ρ′(x) − ρ(x)) behaves like a visit count, and they used the bonus β(N̂ + 0.01)^−1/2 with β = 0.05. Bellemare 2016 Plugged into DQN, the agent visited 15 rooms of Montezuma within 50 million frames against 2 without the bonus, averaging 2,461 points at that stage, 3,439 at 100 million frames, with a best run of 6,600. Bellemare 2016

Try it: the corridor below has one reward at the far end. Run 200 steps with plain ε-greedy, reset, then run 200 steps with the count bonus switched on.

Notice the shape of the visit counts. ε-greedy piles them near the start (cell 15 is the furthest it gets in 200 steps; it needs about 1,100 steps to touch cell 29 once). The count bonus spreads visits down the corridor, reaches the reward at step 82 and keeps returning. The policy did not change; only what counts as reward.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Imagine a huge house where the only candy is in the last room. Wandering at random, you keep ending up in the same three rooms by the front door. Now every room has a sticker machine: a whole sticker the first time you enter, half a sticker the fourth time, almost nothing after that. Suddenly the far rooms are the interesting ones, and on the way you bump into the candy. RND, below, is a sticker machine that still works when every room looks slightly different each visit.

3. Curiosity: ICM and RND

A second idea replaces counts with prediction error: be curious about what you cannot yet predict. The Intrinsic Curiosity Module (ICM) trains a forward model to predict the next state's features from φ(st) and at, and pays the agent the error:

rit = (η/2) · ‖ φ̂(st+1) − φ(st+1) ‖²

The trick is in φ: an inverse model trains it to predict at from (φ(st), φ(st+1)), so φ keeps only what the agent's actions can influence and ignores leaves blowing in the wind. On sparse-reward VizDoom ICM reached a 100% mean score where plain A3C got 0%, and in Super Mario with the game reward removed it crossed more than 30% of level 1 on curiosity alone. Pathak 2017

Random Network Distillation (RND, the RND review) is simpler and became the standard. Take two networks of the same shape. The target f is randomly initialised and frozen forever; the predictor f̂ is trained by mean-squared error to copy f's output on observations the agent has seen. The intrinsic reward is the copying error:

rit = ‖ f̂(ot+1) − f(ot+1) ‖²

On familiar observations the predictor has learned the target's output, so the bonus is small; on a new one the error is large. Because the target is a fixed deterministic function, a flickering screen is not forever surprising: the predictor can learn it and the bonus decays. That kills the noisy-TV problem of pixel-prediction curiosity, where any source of randomness is infinitely interesting. Observations are whitened and clipped to [−5, 5], the bonus is divided by its running standard deviation, and PPO gets two value heads: episodic extrinsic, non-episodic intrinsic. Burda 2018

After roughly 1.97 billion frames RND averaged 8,152 on Montezuma's Revenge against 2,497 for plain PPO and 400 for dynamics-prediction curiosity, above the average human score of 4,753, with a best return of 17,500 and the best agents finding 22 of the 24 rooms on level 1; a recurrent variant with 1,024 parallel environments averaged 10,070. Burda 2018 It was the first agent past the average human without demonstrations.

Common misunderstandings

  • "Curiosity means rewarding surprising pixels." Raw pixel-prediction error gets stuck staring at anything random. ICM predicts only controllable features; RND predicts a fixed deterministic function, so noise becomes learnable and stops paying. Burda 2018
  • "RND trains both networks." Only the predictor trains. If the target also moved, the error would never settle and the bonus would mean nothing.
  • "Go-Explore is another intrinsic reward." It uses no bonus at all. It is an explicit archive of places plus a rule for returning to them.
  • "AlphaGo learned Go without humans." The 2016 AlphaGo started from human expert games; the tabula-rasa system is AlphaGo Zero, a year later. Silver 2017

4. Go-Explore and Agent57: remember, return, then explore

Go-Explore's authors diagnosed two failures bonuses cannot cure. Detachment: the bonus in an area is consumed, the agent drifts elsewhere, and forgets how to get back to the frontier. Derailment: even if it remembers, the noise needed to find new things knocks it off the long, precise path back. Ecoffet 2021

Go-Explore separates the two jobs. It keeps an archive of cells, where a cell is a frame downscaled to 11 × 8 greyscale pixels with 8 intensity levels, so that many nearby frames share a cell. Each iteration: pick a cell (favouring rarely chosen ones), return to it with no noise (in 2019, by restoring the emulator state), then explore randomly from there, adding new cells and better routes to the archive. Phase 2 robustifies the best trajectories into a policy by imitation learning that starts near the end and works backwards. Ecoffet 2019

Without game-specific knowledge it averaged 43,763 on Montezuma's Revenge, against a previous intrinsic-motivation best of about 11,500 mean and a human expert's roughly 34,900. With hand-written cell features (room, level, keys) it averaged 666,474, and one run reached 18,003,200 points, past the human world record of 1,219,200. On Pitfall, where every previous RL method scored 0 or less, it averaged 59,494. Ecoffet 2019 The Nature version replaced state restoration with a goal-conditioned policy, solved every previously unsolved Atari game, and transferred to a sparse-reward robot task. Ecoffet 2021

One line on Agent57 (2020): episodic novelty × RND-style lifelong novelty, a family of policies from curious to greedy, and a bandit choosing among them gave the first agent above the human baseline on all 57 Atari games. Badia 2020

MethodYearWhere the drive to explore comes fromMontezuma's Revenge
DQN2015ε-greedy noise only≈ 0 points, 2 rooms
Pseudo-counts2016density model → count → β/√N̂15 rooms at 50M frames; 3,439 mean at 100M
ICM2017forward-model error in controllable featurestested on VizDoom and Mario, not Montezuma

Analogy

Go-Explore is how people actually play a hard video game: keep save-points, load the furthest one, try something different, keep the new save if it got you somewhere new. The learned policy comes last, once a route is known to exist.

5. Self-play: from TD-Gammon to AlphaZero

Board games have the opposite problem: the reward is clear but you need an opponent at your level, and a too-strong one teaches nothing. Self-play has the agent play copies of itself, so the opponent is always exactly as good as you and improves as fast: a free, automatic curriculum.

The idea predates deep learning. Gerald Tesauro's TD-Gammon (1992–1995) trained a small multilayer network by TD(λ) from self-play alone, starting from random weights, about 200,000 games for the 40-hidden-unit version; version 2.1 finished a 40-game series near parity with Bill Robertie, one of the world's best players. Tesauro 1995

AlphaGo (the AlphaGo review) brought the recipe to Go with three parts: a policy network, trained first on human expert games and then by self-play policy gradient; a value network predicting the winner from self-play positions; and Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS, Day 9), which uses the policy to choose which moves to look at and the value network plus fast rollouts to score positions. It won 99.8% of games against other Go programs and beat the European champion Fan Hui 5–0 in October 2015. Silver 2016 In March 2016 it beat Lee Sedol 4–1 in Seoul before more than 200 million viewers; its move 37 in game two had a one-in-10,000 chance of being played by a human. DeepMind 2016

Then DeepMind removed the humans. AlphaGo Zero (October 2017) starts from random play with only the rules, uses one network with a policy head and a value head, and drops the rollouts: MCTS scores leaves with the value head alone. The search becomes the teacher: at every position MCTS produces a visit distribution π better than the raw policy p, and the network is trained to make p match π and v match the game result z. After 3 days it beat the version that beat Lee Sedol 100–0; after 40 days and about 5 million games on 4 TPUs it passed AlphaGo Master, the strongest previous version. Silver 2017 DeepMind 2017

AlphaZero (preprint December 2017, Science December 2018) ran the same algorithm, unchanged, on chess and shogi. From random play it overtook Stockfish after 4 hours, the shogi program Elmo after 2 hours, and AlphaGo Lee after 30 hours; against Stockfish it won 155 and lost 6 of 1,000 games. It searched about 60 thousand positions per second against Stockfish's 60 million, a thousand times fewer, because the network makes the search selective. It played on 4 first-generation TPUs and 44 CPU cores. DeepMind 2018

Try it: the widget below is the MCTS half of that loop on tic-tac-toe, with random rollouts instead of a value head. Set the simulations per move and play 100 games, or press Sweep for the whole curve.

Notice the win rate rising with simulations: against a random opponent from about 83% at 10 simulations to about 96% at 500; against the 1-ply opponent from about 61% to 95%. The player never changes; it only thinks longer. In AlphaZero the network replaces the rollouts and the improved search becomes the training target, so thinking longer today makes the network stronger tomorrow.

Going deeper (optional): the AlphaZero loss

Each self-play move stores (s, π, z): the position, the MCTS visit distribution, and the final result from that player's view. The network fθ(s) = (p, v) is trained on

L = (z − v)² − πᵀ log p + c‖θ‖²

MCTS selects children by PUCT, Q(s,a) + U(s,a) with U ∝ p(a) · √N(s) / (1 + N(s,a)): the prior steers the search, the value scores leaves without rollouts, and because π comes from searching with the current network, network and search improve each other. Silver 2017 MuZero (Day 9) keeps this loop and learns the rules too.

6. Multi-agent RL: why it is harder than it looks

Two-player zero-sum games are the easy case of multi-agent learning. Four things break when you leave it.

Non-stationarity. Every method so far assumes the environment does not change while you learn. Other learning agents are part of your environment, so, as the MADDPG paper puts it, "the environment becomes non-stationary from the perspective of any individual agent". Lowe 2017 A replayed transition from last month was generated against an opponent who no longer exists; the Markov assumption behind Q-learning and replay quietly fails.

What "optimal" means. With several players the standard answer is a Nash equilibrium: a strategy for every player such that nobody can do better by changing only their own. In rock-paper-scissors it is one third each; any deviation can be exploited. In two-player zero-sum games the equilibrium is the minimax solution and self-play converges toward it, which is why AlphaZero's recipe works. In general-sum games, with teammates or negotiation, there can be many equilibria with different payoffs, and "play the equilibrium" is not a complete instruction. That is why Cicero, below, models how humans play instead of solving the game.

Who sees what. Centralised training, decentralised execution (CTDE): during training each agent's critic sees every agent's observations and actions, which makes its world stationary again; at execution each actor uses only its own observation, so the team runs with no central brain. MADDPG is the actor-critic (Day 7) version. Lowe 2017

Who you train against. Playing only your latest self can cycle: beat A with B, forget A, relearn A. Population-based training keeps 10 to 80 agents, periodically has the bottom 20% copy the weights and hyperparameters of the top 20%, then perturbs the hyperparameters by ×0.8 or ×1.2; it lifted UNREAL on DMLab from 93% to 106% human-normalised. Jaderberg 2017 AlphaStar's league adds exploiter agents whose only job is to find weaknesses in the main agents. Vinyals 2019

Three systems show the scale this took; as of October 2026 they remain the landmarks:

  • OpenAI Five (Dota 2, five against five). One run, 180 days of training spread over 10 months (June 2018 to April 2019) with more than 20 "surgeries" that changed model or environment without restarting. It beat the world champions OG 2–0 on 13 April 2019, then won 99.4% of 7,257 public games in the four-day OpenAI Five Arena, with a 17-hero pool. Berner 2019
  • AlphaStar (StarCraft II). Seeded by imitating human games (already better than 84% of players), then trained in the league; Grandmaster in all three races, above 99.8% of ranked players on Battle.net, playing anonymously with a human camera view and at most 22 actions per 5 seconds. Vinyals 2019
  • Cicero (Diplomacy, seven players, natural-language negotiation). A 2.7-billion-parameter dialogue model fine-tuned on more than 40,000 human games, plus a planner (piKL) that predicts human moves and improves on them while staying human-like. Over 40 games on webDiplomacy.net it scored more than double the average and placed in the top 10%. Meta 2022

7. Architecture

Left to right: the environment emits an observation and the real reward rext. The observation is normalised and sent through the frozen target f and the trainable predictor f̂; their squared difference, divided by its running standard deviation, is rint. PPO receives both streams: the extrinsic head treats rext as episodic, the intrinsic head treats rint as non-episodic (curiosity about a room should not reset when you die), and the two advantages are summed. The dashed gradient stops at the predictor: the target never changes, so observations the predictor has fit stop paying.

Top row: a position enters one residual network with two heads. MCTS runs 800 simulations, each selecting a path by PUCT (Q plus a bonus U proportional to the prior p), expanding a leaf, sending it through the network for a fresh (p, v), and backing v up to the root; the output is the visit distribution π, from which the move is played. Bottom row: each finished game writes (s, π, z) for its positions into a buffer; training pushes p toward π and v toward z; the new parameters go back to the self-play workers. Better network, better search, better targets.

Bottom to top: each actor maps its own observation to its own action. During training all observations and actions flow up into one critic, which can attribute a team outcome to each agent's choice and send a policy gradient back down. At execution the top box is deleted and the actors run independently, which is what makes the result deployable on separate robots or players.

Systems view: what ran where

RND's headline run lasted about 1.97 billion frames; the recurrent variant ran 1,024 parallel environments. Burda 2018 AlphaGo Zero's 40-day run played about 5 million games on 4 TPUs; AlphaZero played its matches on 4 first-generation TPUs plus 44 CPU cores. DeepMind 2017 DeepMind 2018 OpenAI Five was the extreme: a 159-million-parameter policy, 84% of it one 4,096-unit LSTM, fed batches of about 2 million frames every 2 seconds by up to 172,800 rollout CPUs into up to 1,536 optimiser GPUs, roughly 770 petaflop/s-days over 10 months. Berner 2019 The pattern: cheap simulators on many CPU cores, one learner on accelerators, and the gap between them is the engineering.

Check yourself

Q1. Why did DQN score essentially zero on Montezuma's Revenge?

With ε-greedy noise the agent saw two rooms and almost never a reward; without rewards, Q-learning has no signal. Bellemare 2016 reports 0.02 points after 200 million frames.

Q2. In RND, which network is trained?

The predictor learns to copy the frozen target on visited observations. Where it has succeeded, the error (and the bonus) is small; new observations still produce large error.

Q3. RND averaged 8,152 on Montezuma's Revenge. How does that compare with the average human score reported in the same paper?

Burda 2018 gives the average human as 4,753; RND was the first to pass it without demonstrations. 34,900 is the human expert figure quoted by Go-Explore, and 43,763 is Go-Explore's own mean.

Q4. What is the key difference between Go-Explore and a curiosity bonus?

"First return, then explore." Returning without noise fixes derailment; the archive fixes detachment. The 43,763 mean used no domain knowledge and no demonstrations.

Q5. What did AlphaZero search per second compared with Stockfish, and who won?

The network makes the search selective: fewer positions, better chosen. Those are the DeepMind 2018 figures for the Science version.

Q6. "Multi-agent RL is just several single-agent learners running at once." What is wrong with this?

Lowe 2017: "the environment becomes non-stationary from the perspective of any individual agent". CTDE restores a stationary view for the critic during training only.

Recap: five things to remember

  1. Hard exploration is a missing-signal problem: on Montezuma's Revenge DQN saw two rooms and scored about zero because random actions never reached the first reward.
  2. Novelty can be a reward. Counts (β/√N), pseudo-counts from a density model, and prediction error (ICM, RND) all turn "I have not been here" into gradient; RND's frozen-target trick reached 8,152 against the human 4,753 and 22 of 24 rooms.
  3. Go-Explore replaces bonuses with memory: archive cells, return to them without noise, then explore; 43,763 on Montezuma and 59,494 on Pitfall, where RL had scored nothing.
  4. Self-play is an automatic curriculum; AlphaGo Zero and AlphaZero close the loop by training one network on its own search results, beating Stockfish after 4 hours with a thousand times fewer positions per second.
  5. Beyond two-player zero-sum games, "optimal" blurs into Nash equilibria, other learners make the environment non-stationary, and the fixes are centralised critics (CTDE), populations and leagues, and, for Cicero, modelling humans rather than solving the game.

Week 2 · Day 12

RL for language models and agents: RLHF → RLVR → agentic RL

After today you can explain how a reward model is trained, write down the RLHF-PPO, DPO and GRPO objectives and what each gives up, describe how DeepSeek-R1 learned to reason from 0/1 rewards and why its 2025–26 successors changed the advantage, read a scaling curve for RL compute, and set up a multi-turn tool-use episode as an RL problem.

About 90 min · Needs Day 8

Today's big idea

A language model is already a policy: its next-token distribution. Everything today is one recipe applied three times. Sample responses, score them (with a model of human preference, a verifier, or the outcome of a task), and push probability toward the responses that beat a baseline, while staying close enough to the starting model that the scores still mean something.

1. Language as an MDP

Take Day 8's PPO and swap the robot for a Transformer. The state is the prompt plus every token generated so far. The action is the next token. The transition appends it. The reward arrives once, at the end of the response, and is zero everywhere else. Ahmadian 2024 (LLM School Day 8 tells the same story from the LLM side.)

Stated like that, it is a nasty RL problem: 50,000 to 150,000 discrete actions, a horizon of up to 10,000 tokens, and one sparse number for the whole trace. In Week 1 that combination meant "does not learn".

What saves it is the starting point. After SFT, a Llama model puts about 60% of its probability on the top token and over 90% on the top 16, so gradient variance is low. Ahmadian 2024 Because the reward only lands at the end, you can even treat the whole completion as one action; it works as well as token-level modelling. Ahmadian 2024

Analogy

Three eras, one recipe, three judges. RLHF (2017–2023): the judge is a model trained to imitate human taste. RLVR, RL with verifiable rewards (2024–): the judge is a program, the answer key at the back of the maths book. Agentic RL (2025–): the judge is the world: did the multi-turn, tool-using episode reach the goal? Each era swapped a judge that could be fooled for one that is harder to fool.

2. RLHF: InstructGPT

Learning a reward from pairwise human comparisons dates to 2017. Christiano 2017 InstructGPT (March 2022) applied it to GPT-3 in three steps: SFT on about 13k labeler-written demonstrations; a reward model, where labelers rank K = 4 to 9 sampled outputs for about 33k prompts and a 6B model learns a scalar rθ(x, y) (6B even for the 175B policy); then PPO on about 31k prompts with a KL penalty to the SFT model. Ouyang 2022

The reward model is trained with the Bradley–Terry loss: the probability that the human preferred yw over yl is a sigmoid of the score difference, and the loss is its negative log.

loss(θ) = −1/C(K,2) · E[ log σ( rθ(x, yw) − rθ(x, yl) ) ]

The 1/C(K,2) divides by the number of pairs a ranking of K yields, so every prompt counts equally. By hand: scores 2.0 and 0.5 give σ(1.5) = 0.818 and loss −ln 0.818 = 0.201; backwards, σ(−1.5) = 0.182 and loss 1.70. Ouyang 2022 The RL objective (PPO-ptx) is

objective(φ) = E(x,y)~πφ[ rθ(x,y) − β · log( πφ(y|x) / πSFT(y|x) ) ] + γ · Ex~pretrain[ log πφ(x) ]

The first term is the reward minus a KL penalty toward the frozen SFT model, weighted by β: larger β means less reward hacking but less improvement. The γ term mixes in pretraining loss against the "alignment tax"; plain PPO has γ = 0. Ouyang 2022

Count the networks: the policy (trained), the frozen reference, the frozen reward model, and PPO's value model (trained). Four copies of a large model, two with optimizer state; OpenRLHF places "the Actor, Reward, Reference, and Critic models on separate GPUs". OpenRLHF 2026 The payoff: "outputs from the 1.3B parameter InstructGPT model are preferred to outputs from the 175B GPT-3, despite having 100x fewer parameters". Ouyang 2022 See the InstructGPT review.

Try it: step through one RLHF cycle. Each step lights up the models that are busy and shows its numbers.

Notice that the reward model is trained once, before any RL, and that the only per-token signal during RL is the KL penalty; the reward lands on the last token and the value model spreads it backwards.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Imagine a spelling-bee judge who cannot tell you the right word but can always say which of two attempts sounded better. First you build a robot that copies her taste. Then you practise against the robot thousands of times, doing more of what it likes. One rule: you may get better, but you may not turn into a completely different kid overnight. That rule is the KL leash.

3. DPO: skip the reward model

Direct Preference Optimization (May 2023) starts from the same objective, maxπ E[r(x,y)] − β·KL(π ‖ πref), whose optimum has a closed form: πr(y|x) = πref(y|x)·exp(r(x,y)/β) / Z(x), where Z(x) sums over every possible response and cannot be computed. Read it backwards: r = β·log(πr/πref) + β·log Z(x). Put that into the Bradley–Terry loss. Both responses in a pair share the prompt, so they share Z(x), and it cancels. Rafailov 2023

LDPO = −E[ log σ( β·log πθ(yw|x)/πref(yw|x) − β·log πθ(yl|x)/πref(yl|x) ) ]

Each β·log(πθ/πref) is an implicit reward: "your language model is secretly a reward model". With β = 0.1, winner log-ratio +0.5 and loser −0.3, the argument is 0.08, σ(0.08) = 0.520, loss 0.654; DPO keeps pushing until the margin is large. Rafailov 2023 Two models instead of four, no sampling, and results that match or beat PPO-RLHF on sentiment, summarisation and dialogue. Rafailov 2023

What it gives up is what made it cheap. DPO is off-policy: it learns only from the given pairs and cannot explore. Its experiments stop at 6B and flag generalisation and over-optimisation as open. Rafailov 2023 In 2024 an on-policy REINFORCE variant (RLOO) beat it on TL;DR summarisation, 77.9 vs 66.6 win rate. Ahmadian 2024 And it cannot do the next section: a verifier gives a 0/1 on a fresh sample, not a pair. See the DPO review.

4. RLVR and reasoning models

OpenAI's o1 (September 2024) was "trained with large-scale reinforcement learning to reason using chain of thought", and that is all its system card says. OpenAI 2024 The recipe became public in January 2025 with DeepSeek-R1 (LLM School Day 9 covers reasoning models from the user's side). DeepSeek-AI 2025

DeepSeek-R1-Zero is pure RL on the DeepSeek-V3 base model: no SFT, no human-written reasoning traces. The algorithm is GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization), introduced in DeepSeekMath in February 2024 as "a variant of PPO" that saves memory. Shao 2024 For each question q, sample G outputs from the old policy, score each, and use the group's own mean and standard deviation as the baseline:

JGRPO(θ) = E[ (1/G) Σi=1..G ( min( ρiAi, clip(ρi, 1−ε, 1+ε)Ai ) − β·DKL(πθ ‖ πref) ) ]

ρi = πθ(oi|q) / πold(oi|q)    Ai = ( ri − mean{r1..rG} ) / std{r1..rG}

DKL = πref(oi|q)/πθ(oi|q) − log( πref(oi|q)/πθ(oi|q) ) − 1

The clipped ratio is PPO's. New is Ai: the group-relative advantage replaces the value model. In code the ratio is applied per token and averaged with a 1/|oi| per response (section 5). R1-Zero used G = 16 and β = 0.001. DeepSeek-AI 2025 The reward is a rule: accuracy (the boxed answer matches, or the code passes its tests) plus format (reasoning inside <think>…</think> tags). Neural process reward models were tried and dropped. DeepSeek-AI 2026

Try it: four answers to "What is 17 × 23?" (truth 391). Toggle correctness and format, change G, and watch the advantages.

Notice that rewards [2, 1, 1, 0] have mean 1.0 and population std 0.7071, so GRPO gives [+1.414, 0, 0, −1.414]: answers 2 and 3 get zero gradient although one is right and one is wrong. They are average for this group. Make every answer correct and every advantage is 0; the prompt teaches nothing, which is what DAPO's dynamic sampling throws away. (TRL uses the sample std, giving ±1.225; the R1 paper does not say which.) Hugging Face 2026

Over training, R1-Zero's AIME 2024 pass@1 rose from 15.6% to 71.0% (86.7% with majority vote over 64 samples) and its responses grew steadily longer: it learned to think for longer. DeepSeek-AI 2025 The Nature version reports 77.9% under a different evaluation. DeepSeek-AI 2026 The "aha moment" is an intermediate checkpoint that writes, mid-solution, "Wait, wait. Wait. That's an aha moment I can flag here" and re-derives. DeepSeek-AI 2025

R1-Zero's traces were unreadable and mixed languages, so the released DeepSeek-R1 adds a cold start: SFT on thousands of human-polished long reasoning examples, then reasoning RL with a language-consistency reward, then rejection sampling and SFT on about 800k samples, then a final RL stage for helpfulness and harmlessness. R1 scores 79.8 on AIME 2024 and 97.3 on MATH-500. DeepSeek-AI 2025 One more number matters if you do not own a 671B model: distilling R1's 800k samples into Qwen-32B by plain SFT gives AIME 72.6; R1-Zero-style RL run directly on Qwen-32B gives 47.0. DeepSeek-AI 2025 See the DeepSeek-R1 review.

5. GRPO's 2025–26 fixes

Dr. GRPO ("GRPO Done Right", March 2025) names two biases. The 1/|oi| normaliser gives a long wrong answer a smaller per-token penalty than a short one, so the policy drifts toward longer incorrect responses. Dividing by the std over-weights lopsided groups: rewards [1, 0, 0, 0] have std 0.433 and advantages [+1.73, −0.58, −0.58, −0.58], while [1, 1, 0, 0] has std 0.5 and gets [+1, +1, −1, −1], although the raw reward gaps are 0.75 and 0.5. The fix removes both terms: a constant normaliser, and Ai = ri − mean. Their minimal recipe reaches 43.3% on AIME 2024 with a 7B base in about a day on 8 A100s, and they found DeepSeek-V3-Base already produces "aha"-style self-reflection before any RL. Liu 2025

DAPO (ByteDance Seed, March 2025) is an open recipe of four changes, each ablated on AIME 2024 with Qwen2.5-32B: Yu 2025

ChangeWhat it doesAIME 2024 avg@32
Naive GRPObaseline, KL term removed30
+ Overlong filteringmask the loss on truncated samples36
+ Clip-Higherεlow = 0.2, εhigh = 0.28: lets rare tokens grow, fights entropy collapse38
+ Soft overlong punishmentgraded penalty in a 4,096-token buffer before the 16,384 cap41
+ Token-level lossnormalise by all tokens in the batch, not per sample42
+ Dynamic samplingdrop all-right and all-wrong groups; resample to fill the batch50

The last step is the largest: the widget's zero-variance case made policy. DAPO reaches 50 against 47 for DeepSeek's R1-Zero-Qwen-32B in half the steps, with G = 16 and no KL term: a long-reasoning policy is supposed to drift far from its start. Yu 2025 See the DAPO review.

GSPO (Qwen, July 2025) fixes the ratio instead: "the unit of optimization objective should match the unit of reward", so one length-normalised ratio per sequence, si = (πθ(yi|x)/πold(yi|x))1/|yi|, clipped once. In the mixture-of-experts Qwen3-30B-A3B about 10% of activated experts change after each update, making per-token ratios jump; GRPO needed a "Routing Replay" patch, GSPO does not. Zheng 2025 Two cousins: RLOO (2024) uses the mean reward of the other k−1 samples as baseline and found PPO's clip active under 5% of the time; Ahmadian 2024 REINFORCE++ (2025) keeps PPO's per-token clip and KL but normalises advantages over the whole batch. Hu 2025 And the critic is not dead: VAPO (April 2025), PPO with a value model plus length and sparse-reward fixes, reaches 60.4 on AIME 2024 with a Qwen 32B base, ten points above DAPO. Yue 2025

MethodBaseline for advantageRatio unitKL to reference
PPO-RLHFlearned value model (GAE)tokenyes, β
GRPO (R1)group mean, ÷ group std; 1/|oi| per responsetokenyes, β = 0.001
Dr. GRPOgroup mean, no std; constant normalisertokenno
DAPOgroup mean, ÷ std; dynamic sampling; batch-token normalisertoken, εhigh = 0.28no
GSPOgroup mean, ÷ stdsequenceoptional
RLOOmean of the other k−1none (REINFORCE)yes
REINFORCE++batch mean, ÷ batch stdtokenyes

Common misunderstandings

  • "GRPO has no reference model." The R1 paper has β = 0.001. DAPO and TRL's default (β = 0, reference not loaded) remove it. Both are called GRPO. Hugging Face 2026
  • "The advantage is (r − mean)/std everywhere." Dr. GRPO drops the std, REINFORCE++ normalises over the batch, RLOO uses a leave-one-out mean.
  • "RL created the aha moment." The vocabulary is already in DeepSeek-V3-Base; RL raised its frequency. Liu 2025
  • "Longer answers mean better reasoning." Length is a known RLHF reward hack and a GRPO normalisation artefact.

6. What scaling RL compute looks like

Pretraining has scaling laws; until late 2025 RL post-training had folklore. "The Art of Scaling Reinforcement Learning Compute for LLMs" (October 2025; an oral at ICLR 2026 on 25 April 2026) spent over 400,000 GPU-hours of ablations on an 8B dense model and Llama-4 Scout to fit one curve: Khatri 2025 ICLR 2026

RC − R0 = (A − R0) · 1 / ( 1 + (Cmid/C)B )

RC is the pass rate after compute C, R0 the start, A the asymptote (the ceiling this recipe can ever reach), B the exponent (how fast it gets there), Cmid the half-way compute. A sigmoid, not a power law, because it fits robustly at low compute. The useful finding is which knobs move which. Moving A: the loss type (CISPO and GSPO beat DAPO), FP32 logits at the LM head (A rose from about 0.52 to 0.61), larger batches, longer generations, zero-variance filtering. Moving mostly B: asynchronous generation (PipelineRL vs PPO-off-policy: same ceiling, faster), loss aggregation, the advantage-normalisation variant, curriculum. Khatri 2025

The ScaleRL recipe: async PipelineRL eight steps off-policy, CISPO loss, FP32 head, prompt-level loss aggregation, batch-level advantage normalisation, zero-variance filtering, dropping prompts with a historical pass rate ≥ 0.9, and a forced end-of-thinking phrase for length control. A 100,000 GPU-hour run validated it: the curve fitted on the early portion predicted the later points. Khatri 2025 The practical lesson: find your A on small runs first, because no amount of compute moves a recipe past its ceiling. See the ScaleRL review.

7. Does RL add capability or sharpen it? And what gets hacked

Yue et al. (April 2025) compared base and RLVR models on pass@k, the chance that at least one of k samples is right, for k up to 1,024. RLVR wins at k = 1; at large k the base wins. On AIME 2024 at k = 1,024, 13.3% of problems were solved only by the base and 0.0% only by the RL model, and six RLVR algorithms behaved alike. Their reading: RLVR improves sampling efficiency on what the base could already do, while distillation from a stronger teacher adds new reasoning patterns. Yue 2025 Ni et al. (October 2025) supply the theory: GRPO is "a conservative reweighting scheme bounded by the base model's distribution"; it cannot find a solution the base gives zero probability. Ni 2025

The counter-claim is ProRL (NVIDIA, May 2025): over 2,000 RL steps on 136k verifiable problems, with a KL penalty and periodic resets of the reference policy and optimizer, a 1.5B model beat its starting point on pass@k everywhere, with pass@1 gains from +14.7% on math to +54.8% on logic puzzles. Liu 2025 Caveats: the start model was itself distilled, and the biggest gains are on tasks far from its training distribution. Honest summary as of October 2026: short RL runs sharpen; whether long, diverse RL with resets truly expands what a model can do is contested.

Whatever the judge, the policy learns to please it. Sycophancy: across five production assistants, responses matching the user's view were likelier to be preferred, and "both humans and preference models sometimes prefer convincing sycophantic responses over correct ones". Sharma 2023 Length: most of RLHF's reward gain comes from longer outputs, and a reward based purely on length recovers most of the improvement over SFT. Singhal 2023 RLVR adds format gaming and exploited verifiers. In September 2026 Anthropic's Opus 5.5 post said the company was "tightening how we filter the environments used in reinforcement learning", linking flawed environments to misaligned behaviour. Anthropic 2026

Going deeper (optional): process versus outcome rewards

An outcome reward model (ORM) scores the final answer; a process reward model (PRM) scores every step. "Let's Verify Step by Step" (2023) found process supervision significantly beat outcome supervision on MATH, with PRM-guided search solving 78% of a test subset, using 800k human step labels (PRM800K). Lightman 2023 DeepSeek-R1 reports the opposite at scale: steps are hard to define and label, and the policy hacks the PRM. DeepSeek-AI 2026 The 2025 reasoning wave is overwhelmingly outcome-verified; for domains with no exact checker, DeepSeek-V4's report lists a generative reward model, an LLM that writes a judgement. DeepSeek-AI 2026

8. Agentic RL: when the episode is a conversation

An agent episode is a conversation with tools. The policy emits tokens; some form a tool call; an environment (sandbox, API, browser, simulated user) returns an observation that is appended to the context; the policy continues; at the end the environment reports whether the goal was met. One detail every system shares: tool outputs and user turns are masked out of the loss. They are observations, not actions, and the trainer must see exactly the tokens the policy produced, which is why verl's agent loop generates at the token level rather than round-tripping through text. verl 2026

The benchmarks define the rewards. τ-bench (June 2024): a simulated user, domain APIs, policy rules; success means the final database state matches the goal. GPT-4o succeeded on under 50% of tasks, and its pass^k, the chance that all k trials succeed, was below 25% at k = 8 in retail. Yao 2024 τ²-bench (June 2025) gives the user tools too, so the agent must guide a person, with "significant performance drops". Barres 2025 SWE-RL (Meta, February 2025) trains on open-source software history with a rule-based reward, similarity to the real patch, and takes Llama3-70B to 41.0% on SWE-bench Verified. Wei 2025 Agent World Model (February 2026, ICML 2026) builds 1,000 synthetic, code-driven, database-backed environments whose inspectable state makes rewards reliable; training only on them generalised to three held-out benchmarks. Wang 2026 ToolVerse (July 2026) turns about 400 real MCP servers, about 4,500 tools, into environments with long-horizon tasks generated from a tool-dependency graph. Zhou 2026

The open problem is credit assignment: one terminal reward over 20 to 50 turns and 10,000+ tokens. GRPO gives every token in a trajectory the same sign, so a successful episode's one bad tool call is rewarded too. ToolVerse's answer is a Turn-Aware Relative Advantage that varies across turns; Zhou 2026 Agent World Model's is per-step rewards read off the database; Wang 2026 VAPO's is a value model.

Try it: step through a six-turn episode, flip the terminal reward, and compare three ways of spreading it over the turns.

Notice that "uniform over turns" is plain GRPO: the first thought and the final answer get identical credit. Tool results are greyed out because they are never in the loss.

What frontier labs say in public, as of 25 October 2026, is thin. DeepSeek-V4 (released 24 April 2026) trains domain experts "through SFT and RL with GRPO", then merges them into one model by on-policy distillation, the student minimising a reverse KL to the teachers. DeepSeek-AI 2026 DeepSeek 2026 DeepSeek-V3.2 (December 2025) credits "a robust RL protocol and scaling post-training compute" for matching GPT-5. DeepSeek 2025 Anthropic's statement is the environment-filtering sentence above; OpenAI's remains the o1 system card. OpenAI 2024

9. Architecture

Left half, top to bottom: prompts enter the trainable policy, which generates rollouts. Three scorers look at each: the frozen reward model returns one number at the final token, the frozen reference returns per-token log-probabilities for the KL penalty, and the trainable value model returns per-token values. GAE turns these into advantages, and a PPO clipped update flows back into both trained models. The right half deletes two boxes: the policy samples G = 16 responses, a rule scores each, and the group's mean and std give the advantage. The reference survives only if β > 0; in DAPO and TRL's default it does not.

Left to right: inference workers generate; in the agentic case an agent loop on top executes tool calls, appends observations, and records which tokens were the policy's. Trajectories (tokens, log-probabilities, loss mask, reward) go into a queue. The trainer pool recomputes log-probabilities, forms the advantage, takes a clipped step, and ships the new weights back. Synchronous: the pools take turns and each idles half the time. Asynchronous: they overlap, rollouts may be a few updates stale, and the ratio ρ with its clip (or a truncated importance weight) keeps the off-policy update honest.

Systems view

Generation "takes about 80% of RLHF time", hence the two engines. OpenRLHF 2026 verl implements HybridFlow (September 2024), whose 3D-HybridEngine reshards the actor between training and generation layouts without an extra copy, for 1.53× to 20.57× throughput. Sheng 2024 Its fully asynchronous mode puts rollouter and trainer on separate GPU pools with a staleness_threshold (0 is synchronous, about 1 is one step off-policy). NCCL weight sync fell from 15.76 s to 4.38 s per step for Qwen3-30B-A3B and from 58.57 s to 23.70 s for Qwen3-235B-A22B; end-to-end speedup was 2.35× to 2.67× on Qwen2.5-Math-7B with 128 GPUs (64 rollout, 64 training) and about 1.55× for multi-turn tool calling. verl 2026 PipelineRL (September 2025) updates weights in flight, continuing half-finished sequences on the new policy: about 2× faster learning on 128 H100s while nearly on-policy. Piché 2025 TRL's single-machine GRPOTrainer defaults to G = 8, β = 0 and the DAPO token-level loss. Hugging Face 2026

Check yourself

Q1. In InstructGPT, what did labelers prefer over the outputs of the 175B GPT-3?

The abstract's headline result. The 6B reward model scores responses; it does not write them.

Q2. Why can DPO drop the reward model?

Inverting the closed-form optimum gives r = β·log(π/π_ref) + β·log Z(x); the shared Z(x) cancels. DPO still needs the reference and never samples.

Q3. A GRPO group scores [2, 1, 1, 0]. What advantage do the two answers scoring 1 receive?

Mean 1.0, std 0.7071, A = [+1.414, 0, 0, −1.414]. Advantage is relative to the group, not to correctness.

Q4. Which single DAPO change produced the largest AIME 2024 gain in its ablation?

Dropping all-right and all-wrong groups took the score from 42 to 50. Removing KL is part of the 30-point baseline, not a measured step.

Q5. "RLVR teaches a model to reason in new ways." What did Yue et al. find at large k?

At k = 1,024 the base covered more problems. RLVR concentrated probability on solutions the base could already find; distillation stayed above the base at every k.

Q6. Why are tool results masked out of the loss in agentic RL?

Only the policy's own tokens are actions. Training on tool output would teach the model to predict the environment rather than act in it.

Recap: five things to remember

  1. Language is an MDP with a token action space, a long horizon and one terminal reward; tractable because the SFT model is already a strong policy.
  2. RLHF = a reward model trained with the Bradley–Terry loss, then PPO against it with a β·KL leash to the SFT reference; four models in memory; 1.3B beat 175B.
  3. DPO deletes the reward model because Z(x) cancels; GRPO deletes the value model because the group mean is the baseline. DPO cannot explore; GRPO's std and length normalisers bias the update.
  4. Rule rewards took R1-Zero from 15.6 to 71.0 on AIME 2024; DAPO's four fixes took 30 to 50; distillation beat RL on small models, 72.6 vs 47.0.
  5. RL compute follows a sigmoid: some knobs (FP32 head, loss type) raise the ceiling, others only reach it faster. Short RL sharpens; whether long RL expands capability is contested as of October 2026.
