Week 2 · Day 13

RL in the wild: robots, chips, fusion, and recommenders

After today you can state the state, action and reward of eight real RL deployments, name each one's algorithm, headline number and caveat, explain sim-to-real transfer and domain randomisation, and describe how RL fine-tunes a vision-language-action robot policy.

About 90 min · Needs Day 12

Today's big idea

Every RL system that works outside a game has three ingredients: a place to try millions of things cheaply (usually a simulator), a reward you can measure, and an evaluation honest enough to separate skill from luck. Where a deployment is weak, it is weak on one of these. The algorithms are ones you know: PPO almost everywhere, an actor-critic for the tokamak, REINFORCE at YouTube, AlphaZero's search for algorithm discovery.

1. What a real deployment needs

In Day 12 the environment was a sandbox you could call a billion times. The physical world is not: a robot hand breaks, a tokamak shot lasts under three seconds and needs fifteen minutes to cool down, and a recommender's environment is two billion people. Degrave 2022 So ask three questions of every deployment story.

Where did the experience come from? Almost always a simulator; otherwise logged data, with its off-policy traps. What was the reward, and who measured it? "Energy saved", "view time" and "mortality" are a meter reading, a proxy, and an outcome nobody was allowed to randomise. How was skill separated from luck? Ten trials on one robot, a live A/B test over millions of users, and a retrospective match against clinicians' decisions carry very different weight.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Learning to ride a bike by falling off ten thousand times would hurt. So you practise on a video-game bike first, and you make the game bike a bit random, sometimes heavier, sometimes with a wobbly wheel, so that when you ride the real one, whatever it does, you have already met something like it.

2. Robots I: sim-to-real and domain randomisation

OpenAI's Dactyl (August 2018) taught a 24-joint Shadow Hand to rotate a block to a target orientation, in-hand, from simulation alone. OpenAI 2018 State: 15 fingertip coordinates, the block's position and the target orientation, all noisy. Action: 20 relative joint targets, each discretised into 11 bins. Reward: the decrease in angle to the target, +5 on reaching it, −20 for dropping the block. Algorithm: PPO (clip 0.2, γ = 0.998, GAE λ = 0.95) with a 512-unit LSTM, on 6,144 CPU cores and 8 GPUs, about 22 years of simulated hand time per hour. OpenAI 2018

The sim-to-real gap: friction, motor delays, camera colours and cable stretch are all slightly wrong in the simulator, and a policy tuned to its exact values fails at the first real contact. The fix is domain randomisation: train on thousands of simulators at once, each with different physics, appearance, noise and unmodelled forces. Since the policy cannot see which simulator it is in, it needs memory; the LSTM infers the dynamics from the first few steps. OpenAI 2018

The ablations are the lesson. On the real hand (10 trials) the full system managed a median of 13 consecutive rotations, max 50. Without randomisation: 0. Without physics randomisation: 2. Feed-forward instead of LSTM: 3. In simulation the same policy scored 50, so 50 versus 13 is the gap in one number. The price: about 100 years of simulated experience (50 hours) to converge, against 3 years (1.5 hours) without. OpenAI 2018

Try it: a one-dimensional version of the same problem. Set a randomisation range, train, deploy, and watch what the hidden real friction does.

Notice that with range 0 or 0.05 real success is 0%: the real friction (0.62) lands in a bucket training never visited, so the policy pushes with the simulator's default force and stops short. From ±0.15 upward it is 100%, but the episodes needed to reach 90% rise from 120 to about 250 as the range widens, because the same budget is spread over more buckets. Dactyl's 3 years versus 100, in miniature.

The 2019 sequel, Solving Rubik's Cube with a Robot Hand, learned the ranges. Automatic Domain Randomisation (ADR) starts from one environment and widens each range whenever performance at its edge passes a threshold: an open-ended curriculum. Same reward shape, a 1,024-unit LSTM, PPO on 64 V100s and 920 × 32 CPU cores, roughly 13,000 simulated years. OpenAI 2019 Results, 10 trials each: with the cube's built-in sensor supplying face angles, 60% on 15-rotation scrambles and 20% on the hardest 26-rotation ones; from vision alone, 20% and 0%. OpenAI 2019

Common misunderstandings

  • "RL solved the Rubik's cube." The move sequence came from a classical solver (Kociemba). RL learned the finger motions, and finished the hardest scrambles 20% of the time, with a sensor inside the cube. OpenAI 2019
  • "Sim-to-real is a compute problem." Randomisation and memory moved Dactyl's real median from 0 to 13; compute mostly paid for the randomisation. OpenAI 2018
  • "The simulator must match reality." It only needs to contain reality somewhere inside its range, which is why ADR works without anyone measuring the real friction.

3. Robots II: massively parallel simulation

Dactyl ran physics on CPUs and shipped observations to GPUs. Isaac Gym (NVIDIA, August 2021) put the physics on the GPU too: "tens of thousands of simultaneous environments on a single GPU", 2–3 orders of magnitude faster than CPU pipelines, with sweet spots of 8,192 environments for Ant, 4,096 for Humanoid and ANYmal, 16,384 for the Shadow Hand. A Humanoid reaches reward 5,000 in under 4 minutes on one A100; the Shadow Hand cube task reaches 20 consecutive successes in under 35 minutes, where Dactyl needed 50 hours on a cluster. Makoviychuk 2021

Rudin et al. made a quadruped walk in "under four minutes" on flat ground and twenty minutes on rough terrain (1,500 updates) with 4,096 simulated ANYmals on one RTX A6000, then deployed on the real ANYmal C unchanged. State: base velocities, gravity direction, joint positions and velocities, the previous action, 108 terrain heights around the body. Action: joint targets for a PD controller. Reward: nine weighted terms, tracking the commanded velocity, penalising torques, joint accelerations, action changes, body wobble and collisions, rewarding feet-in-air time. Caveat: the lidar height map was imperfect on hardware, so the real robot was capped at 0.6 m/s. Rudin 2021

Since then: ANYmal parkour at 2 m/s (June 2023). Hoeller 2023 A 20-joint humanoid footballer walking 181% faster and turning 302% faster than a scripted controller, zero-shot (April 2023). Haarnoja 2023 Humanoid locomotion for Unitree G1 and Booster T1 in "just 15 minutes with a single RTX 4090 GPU", with fast off-policy SAC/TD3 recipes (December 2025). Seo 2025 A Unitree Go1 at 2.0 m/s zero-shot from Isaac (July 2026). Dowdy 2026 The algorithm family barely changed; the simulator moved from a cluster to a card, and days became a quarter of an hour.

Analogy

Dactyl was a driving school with 6,000 instructors phoning results to one examiner. Isaac Gym is 4,096 driving simulators bolted to the examiner's desk. The student (PPO) did not get smarter; the school got faster.

4. Robots III: vision-language-action models, then RL on top

Walking has a reward you can write down. "Put the bowl in the sink" does not, and no simulator holds every bowl. So manipulation took Day 12's route: imitation first, RL after. A vision-language-action model (VLA) is a vision-language model fine-tuned to output robot actions from camera images and an instruction. Brohan 2023

ModelDateBackbone, sizeDataHeadline
RT-2 (Google DeepMind)Jul 2023PaLI-X 5B/55B, PaLM-E 12B; actions as text tokens (8 integers, 256 bins)robot data co-fine-tuned with web data62% on unseen-generalisation tests vs 32% for RT-1, 6k trials; the 55B model runs at 1–3 Hz Brohan 2023
OpenVLAJun 20247B: Llama 2 + DINOv2 + SigLIP970k real demonstrations+16.5 points over 55B RT-2-X on 29 tasks; LIBERO 76.5% Kim 2024
π0 (Physical Intelligence)Oct 2024PaliGemma 3B + 300M action expert; flow matching, 50-step chunks at 50 Hz, 10 Euler steps~10,000 h, 7 robot types, 68 tasksfolds laundry; beats OpenVLA and Octo "by a large margin" Black 2024
π0.5Apr 2025π0 + co-training on mobile, multi-environment and web data~400 h in ~100 homescleans unseen kitchens and bedrooms; the 104-home model matches one trained on the test homes Intelligence 2025

Two designs recur. RT-2 writes actions as text so one Transformer does everything, at 1–3 Hz. π0 keeps a stock VLM and attaches an action expert that denoises a chunk of 50 future actions by flow matching, a cousin of Diffusion Policy, for smooth 50 Hz control. Black 2024

Imitation has a ceiling: the policy is at best as good as its demonstrations and has never seen its own mistakes. RL fills that gap, and 2025–26 is when it was filled for VLAs. The obstacle: PPO needs πnew(a|s)/πold(a|s), and a flow-matching head has no tractable likelihood for the chunk it produced. πRL (October 2025) gives two fixes. Flow-Noise treats the 10 denoising steps as a small MDP with a learned noise scale, so each step has a Gaussian density and the chain an exact log-likelihood. Flow-SDE turns the deterministic ODE into a stochastic one. Either way PPO then runs. Chen 2025 From few-shot imitation, π0.5 on LIBERO goes 77.1% → 98.3% (Flow-Noise), π0 57.6% → 97.6%, and on ManiSkill's 4,352 pick-and-place combinations π0.5 40.1% → 90.9%. Full-dataset imitation reached 94.2% and 96.9%, so RL from a handful of demos beat imitation from all of them. All in simulation. Chen 2025

Try it: step through one VLA episode, then switch on RL fine-tuning.

Notice which box the gradient arrow reaches: the action head only. The 3B backbone that knows what a bowl is stays frozen, so RL teaches dexterity without erasing language.

Two 2026 papers carried this to real robots. RL-Co (February 2026): imitation on mixed real and simulated demos, then RL in ManiSkill3 with a supervised loss on the real demos so the policy keeps real-world appearance. On four real tabletop tasks OpenVLA went 9.1% (real-only imitation) → 40.0% (sim-real co-training) → 64.0% (RL-Co); π0.5 26.7% → 45.9% → 66.1%, with 20–50 real demos per task and 20–64 trials per checkpoint. Shi 2026 Generative 3D worlds (CoRL 2026) attacks the missing simulator: GPT-4o designs scene graphs, a generative pipeline builds 100 interactive scenes from 516 assets (about 47 minutes each), and π0 is fine-tuned in them with a PPO variant plus randomisation. Real WidowX pick-and-place with distractors rose 21.7% → 75% over 240 trials, and success scaled with the number of scenes. One robot, one task family, one camera. Choi 2026

5. Chips: AlphaChip

Placing a chip's large blocks (macros) is a game with one delayed reward. In Google's 2020–21 work, since named AlphaChip: state = a graph embedding of the netlist (what is placed and where), the next block, metadata, and a mask of cells where it fits; action = the grid cell (up to 128 × 128, typically 30 × 30) for that block; reward = zero until the end, then −(approximate wirelength + 0.01 × congestion), with density capped at 0.6 by the mask. Mirhoseini 2020 Algorithm: PPO with an edge-based graph convolutional encoder, first trained as a supervised predictor of placement quality on 10,000 placements of 5 netlists, then as a policy on 20 TPU blocks, then fine-tuned on new blocks. Mirhoseini 2021

Nature (June 2021): placements "in under six hours" matching or beating months of human effort; one example has 55.42 m of wire against the human 57.07 m. Against the academic placer RePlAce, RL wins wirelength on two of five blocks; RePlAce wins the other three but breaks the 1% congestion limit on some. Mirhoseini 2020 DeepMind's September 2024 blog says it has been used in every TPU generation since 2020, including v5e, v5p and Trillium, that MediaTek extended it, and that a checkpoint and code are public. DeepMind 2024

The other side. Cheng, Kahng and colleagues (2023, updated March 2026) re-implemented the open-source version, report a well-tuned simulated-annealing baseline stronger than the paper's comparisons suggest, and call the scalability and pre-training claims "still-missing confirmations", since the TPU training blocks are private. Cheng 2023 Google's reply is a Nature Addendum (September 2024) that names the method and points to the blog, where per-generation use is a bar chart, not a stated count. Mirhoseini 2024 Undisputed: the MDP is sound and the method ran in production. Also undisputed: no outside group has reproduced the headline comparison on the original data.

6. Fusion: steering a plasma 10,000 times a second

A tokamak's coils hold a 100-million-degree plasma away from the walls. DeepMind and the Swiss Plasma Center (Nature, February 2022) replaced the hand-designed controller on the TCV tokamak with a learned one. State: 34 flux loops, 38 magnetic probes, 19 coil currents, and the targets. Action: a voltage for each of the 19 coils every 100 µs, a 10 kHz loop with about 50 µs of compute per step. Reward: quality terms in [0, 1] for plasma current, shape and position, combined and normalised so a perfect second scores 100, with a large penalty if the plasma is lost. Degrave 2022

Algorithm: MPO (maximum a posteriori policy optimisation), an off-policy actor-critic in SAC's family, trained only in a plasma simulator with 5,000 actors for 1–3 days. The design is asymmetric: the critic is a 256-unit LSTM (about 718k parameters) that never leaves the lab; the deployed actor is an MLP of about 266k parameters that fits the 50 µs budget. It transferred zero-shot. Results: plasma-current error 0.62 kA RMS and shape error 0.75 cm; an elongation of 1.9 (unstable, growing at over 1.4 kHz) held steady; negative triangularity of −0.8; a snowflake whose X-points were moved from 34 cm apart to 6.6 cm; and two separate "droplet" plasmas sustained together for the full 200 ms window, a first. DeepMind 2022

The authors' caveats: steady-state errors in elongation, a simulator without heat and current transport, no guarantee against disruptions (a machine-protection layer is recommended), and a conventional controller still handling breakdown and ramp-up. Degrave 2022 What made it tractable: a good simulator, a dense physical reward, no humans in the loop.

7. Data-centre cooling: a lesson in reading claims

You will hear that "DeepMind's RL cut Google's data-centre cooling energy by 40%". Read the two primary posts. July 2016: "up to 40 percent" less energy for cooling and a 15 percent reduction in overall PUE overhead, at one data centre, using ensembles of neural networks trained on historical sensor data to predict future PUE and temperatures, with recommendations checked against constraints. DeepMind 2016 August 2018: the system takes direct control under operator supervision, every five minutes screening candidate actions against safety constraints with two-layer verification and human override, for "consistent energy savings of around 30 percent on average", up from about 12% at launch. DeepMind 2018

Neither post calls this reinforcement learning; "predict the consequences of candidate actions, pick the best that passes the constraints" is prediction plus optimisation. Good engineering, with a safety architecture worth copying. But "RL saves 40%" fails all three of section 1's questions: cooling energy, not total; one site; not RL. Find the primary source; check the denominator, the scope and the method.

8. Recommenders: REINFORCE at YouTube scale

The one large consumer deployment with a published RL objective is YouTube's "Top-K Off-Policy Correction for a REINFORCE Recommender System" (WSDM, February 2019). State: a user vector from a recurrent network over the user's history of recommendations and reactions, plus context (page, device, time). Action: one video from millions; a page shows K = 16. Reward: engagement with that item (zero if not clicked), aggregated over a 4–10 hour horizon. Chen 2019

Two corrections make REINFORCE work on logged data. The data came from other recommenders, so each gradient term is weighted by π(a|s)/β(a|s), with β estimated by a separate softmax head and the weight capped at e³. And because K items are shown together, item a's gradient is scaled by λK, which stops the policy piling probability onto an item that will be on the page anyway. Chen 2019

λK(a) = K·(1 − π(a|s))K−1    K = 16: π = 0.05 → 16 × 0.9515 = 7.4;   π = 0.5 → 16 × 0.515 = 0.0005

Live A/B: the top-K correction added 0.85% view time over the standard correction; a K = 1 model was 0.66% worse than K = 16; raising the cap to e⁵ cost 0.52%. Chen 2019 The caveats are in the MDP: fractions of a percent (large at YouTube's scale, tiny per user), engagement as the reward, a horizon of hours. This is one-step REINFORCE with a learned state, not long-horizon planning.

9. Algorithm discovery: two RL systems and one that is not

SystemDateMethodGameResult
AlphaTensorOct 2022RL: AlphaZero-style searchstate = tensor left to decompose; action = subtract a rank-one term; reward −1 per step4×4 matrix multiply in 47 multiplications in Z2 (Strassen squared: 49); 4×5 by 5×5 in 76 vs 80; 70+ tensor sizes improved Fawzi 2022
AlphaDevJun 2023RL: AlphaZero-style MCTS, value heads for correctness and latencystate = program so far + CPU state on test inputs; action = append an x86 instruction; reward = correctness + latencyshorter sort3/sort5 than human sorting networks; libc++ std::sort "up to about 70% faster" on 5 elements, 1.7% on 250k+; 30% faster hashing in Abseil Mankowitz 2023
AlphaEvolveMay 2025Evolutionary: Gemini mutates code, evaluators score, a population evolves. Not RL.none; programs are scored, not stepped4×4 complex matrices in 48 multiplications; 0.7% of Google's compute recovered; 23% faster Gemini kernel; improved 20% of 50+ open problems DeepMind 2025

The first two are AlphaZero's children: a single-player game with a correct-by-construction state, a terminal check, and search over actions; training ran up to two days on TPUs with up to 512 actors. Mankowitz 2023 Three cautions. AlphaTensor's 47 is in modular arithmetic, so "beat Strassen" holds only in Z2; the standard-arithmetic record (48, complex matrices) came from AlphaEvolve. AlphaDev's speed-ups are architecture-specific, and "a single, wrong move can invalidate the entire algorithm", which is why correctness sits in the reward. Mankowitz 2023 And AlphaEvolve used no policy gradient and no value function; by 2026 the discovery frontier had moved to a method that is not RL. DeepMind 2025

10. Driving, healthcare, finance: three cautions

Driving. The verifiable result is Waymo-affiliated: "Imitation Is Not Enough" (December 2022) trains behaviour cloning plus RL on over 100k miles of urban driving logs and reports over 38% fewer failures on the hardest scenarios than imitation alone. Lu 2022 Any claim that a deployed Waymo or Tesla stack is "trained with RL" is, as of October 2026, unsupported by a primary source.

Healthcare. The AI Clinician (Nature Medicine, October 2018) learned a sepsis treatment policy from ICU records by offline RL; "mortality was lowest in patients for whom clinicians' actual doses matched the AI decisions". Komorowski 2018 A 2019 critique examined the individual treatment profiles it recommended and the evaluation's assumptions. Jeter 2019 Section 1's third question again: observational data allows only off-policy evaluation, "clinician agreed with the policy" is confounded with easier patients, and the policy was never deployed. Lower mortality in the agreeing subgroup is not a mortality reduction.

Finance. A 2021 survey covers RL for execution, portfolio choice, hedging and market making with methods that "do not require any model assumptions". Hambly 2021 The caution is the environment: markets are non-stationary and adversarial, data per regime is small, and a backtest is one trajectory, not a simulator you can re-sample.

Going deeper (optional): why offline evaluation is the hard part

Every deployment without a simulator must estimate how a new policy would do from data gathered by an old one, using importance weights (YouTube's π/β) or a learned model. Both have high variance exactly where the new policy differs most from the old, which is where the gains are. The cap at e³, and the 0.52% lost by raising it to e⁵, is that trade-off measured live. Chen 2019 Distrust an offline-RL result in proportion to how far its policy strays from the data.

11. Architecture

Left to right: the simulator samples physics and appearance from ranges; thousands of copies run on the GPU and send observations and rewards to PPO, whose actions flow back. The actor has memory to work out which simulator it is in; the critic may cheat with the true simulator state because it is never deployed. The trained actor is copied once to the real robot. The red loop is ADR: success at each range's edge decides whether it grows, so the curriculum writes itself.

Top row: observation, frozen backbone, trained action head, robot. Bottom row: the training signal. The simulator reports success or failure; PPO, made possible by treating denoising steps as actions with known densities, pushes gradients into the action head and nowhere else; a supervised loss on a few dozen real demos shares the update so what is learned in a generated kitchen holds in a real one. The SFT box on the left is where it starts, as in Day 12.

Systems view

Locomotion: 4,096 environments plus PPO on one RTX A6000 (6–9 GB VRAM), 98,304 samples per update, 1,500 updates in 20 minutes. Rudin 2021 Dexterity: 6,144 CPU cores and 8 GPUs for 50 hours in 2018; under 35 minutes on one A100 with 16,384 GPU environments in 2021. Makoviychuk 2021 Tokamak: 5,000 simulator actors for 1–3 days; a 266k-parameter actor inside a 50 µs budget. Degrave 2022 AlphaChip: under six hours per new block after pre-training on 20. Mirhoseini 2021 VLA RL: a 3.3B policy across thousands of ManiSkill3 scenes, only the 300M head carrying optimizer state. Chen 2025 The common shape: many cheap environments, one learner, a deployed network smaller than what was trained.

Check yourself

Q1. In Dactyl's real-robot ablations, which change dropped the median number of consecutive rotations from 13 to 0?

Without randomisation the real-hand median was 0; without physics randomisation 2; without the LSTM 3. Vision-based pose gave a median of 11.5, nearly as good as state-based.

Q2. How should "a robot hand solved the Rubik's cube" be corrected?

Kociemba's algorithm chose the moves; the policy executed them: 60% on 15-rotation and 20% on 26-rotation scrambles with the sensor, 0% full solves from vision. ADR is a curriculum over ranges, not a replacement for PPO.

Q3. Why is PPO hard to apply to a flow-matching action head, and how does πRL get around it?

Flow-Noise models the 10 denoising steps as a small MDP with a learned noise scale; Flow-SDE converts the ODE to an SDE. Both recover a PPO ratio. The backbone stays frozen and the reward is already 0/1.

Q4. What is AlphaChip's reward, and when is it paid?

The reward is terminal only, which is why the graph encoder is first pre-trained as a supervised predictor of placement quality: the sparse end-of-episode signal is otherwise slow to learn from.

Q5. A slide says "DeepMind's RL cut Google's data-centre energy by 40%". Which correction do the primary sources support?

The 2016 and 2018 posts describe neural-network prediction of PUE and temperatures plus constrained optimisation of candidate actions under human supervision: "up to 40%" of cooling energy, 15% of PUE overhead, later about 30% average.

Q6. With K = 16, YouTube's top-K correction scales an item's gradient by K(1 − π)^(K−1). An item the policy already shows with π = 0.5 gets roughly what multiplier?

16 × 0.5^15 = 16/32768 ≈ 0.0005, versus 16 × 0.95^15 ≈ 7.4 for π = 0.05. The correction stops the policy concentrating probability on items that will be on the page anyway.

Recap: five things to remember

  1. Every working deployment has a cheap place to practise, a measurable reward, and an evaluation that separates skill from luck; check all three before believing a claim.
  2. Sim-to-real works by domain randomisation plus memory, not by matching reality: Dactyl's real median went from 0 to 13 rotations with randomisation, at the price of 100 simulated years instead of 3. ADR learns the ranges.
  3. GPU simulation changed the economics, not the algorithm: 4,096 ANYmals walk in under 4 minutes on one card (2021); a humanoid in 15 minutes on a 4090 (2025).
  4. VLAs (RT-2, OpenVLA, π0, π0.5) are imitation-trained; RL on the action head alone lifts π0.5 on LIBERO from 77.1% to 98.3% in simulation and roughly doubles real-robot success in 2026 co-training work.
  5. Read the MDP and the caveat together: AlphaChip's terminal reward and disputed baselines; the tokamak's 10 kHz MLP; YouTube's +0.85% on an engagement proxy; AlphaTensor's 47 in Z2; the data-centre "40%" that was not RL; the AI Clinician never deployed.

Week 2 · Day 14

The frontier and open problems, as of October 2026

After today you can place the milestones of 2013–2026 on one timeline, read a benchmark saturation curve and say what it does and does not show, name the ten open problems of RL with a concrete example and a number for each, and know which four texts to read next.

About 90 min · Needs Day 13

Today's big idea

Thirteen days of methods fit on one family tree with four roots: value estimation, policy gradients, planning with a model, and learning from preferences. Every benchmark the field built to measure progress on that tree has been saturated within about five years of its creation. What is left open in 2026 is not "can RL beat the score" but ten harder questions about data, rewards, generalisation and trust, each of which you can now state precisely.

1. The story so far in one page

Here is the whole course as a tree. Each node is a method you met; the arrow means "this is what the child kept from the parent, plus one new idea".

Root 1: values. Dynamic programming (Day 4) computes values with a known model by sweeping every state. TD learning (Day 5) drops the model and updates one sampled step at a time. Q-learning (Day 6) learns action values off-policy. DQN (2013, Nature 2015) puts a convolutional network under Q-learning and adds experience replay and a target network to keep it stable, reaching "a level comparable to that of a professional human games tester across a set of 49 games". Mnih 2015 Rainbow (2017) combines six DQN patches into one agent. Hessel 2017 Agent57 (2020) adds a recurrent distributed learner, an exploration bonus and a bandit over discount settings, and is "the first deep RL agent that outperforms the standard human benchmark on all 57 Atari games". Badia 2020

Root 2: policies. REINFORCE (1992) differentiates the expected return directly; actor-critic methods subtract a learned baseline, and A3C (2016) ran that on 16 CPU threads with no GPU (Day 7). Mnih 2016 TRPO (2015) limits each update with a KL trust region; PPO (2017) gets the same effect with a clipped ratio and ε = 0.2 (Day 8). Schulman 2017 PPO then became the workhorse of Day 13: the OpenAI hand, Isaac Gym locomotion, AlphaChip, and the RL step of RLHF (2022). GRPO (2025) is PPO's clipped objective with the group mean as baseline instead of a critic (Day 12). DeepSeek-AI 2025 A side branch, SAC (2018), is off-policy and maximum-entropy, and its 2025 descendants FastSAC and FastTD3 train a humanoid to walk in 15 minutes on one RTX 4090. Haarnoja 2018 Seo 2025

Root 3: models. Dyna (1990) runs the same Q-update on real and imagined transitions (Day 9). AlphaGo (2016) plans with Monte Carlo tree search over a given model of Go; AlphaZero (2017) drops the human games; MuZero (2019) drops the given model and learns one, reaching an Atari median of 2041% of human at 20 billion frames. Schrittwieser 2019 AlphaTensor and AlphaDev (2022–23) point the same machinery at matrix multiplication and sorting (Day 13). The other model-based line, Dreamer (2019) → DreamerV3 (2023) → Dreamer 4 (2025), trains the policy inside a learned world model; Dreamer 4 is "the first agent to obtain diamonds in Minecraft purely from offline data". Hafner 2025

Root 4: preferences. InstructGPT (2022) trains a reward model from human comparisons and runs PPO against it; its 1.3B model was preferred over 175B GPT-3. Ouyang 2022 DPO (2023) solves the same objective "with only a simple classification loss" and no RL loop. Rafailov 2023 Verifiable rewards (o1 in 2024, R1 in 2025) replace the human judge with an answer key. Two further branches sit beside the tree: offline RL (D4RL, CQL, Decision Transformer; Day 10) and exploration bonuses (RND; Day 11). The full diagram is in section 7.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Imagine a family photo album for robots that learn. The great-grandparents (1957–1992) could only solve puzzles with a handful of squares. The grandparents (2013–2017) learned to play old video games by watching the screen. The parents (2016–2020) beat the world champions at Go, StarCraft and Dota. The kids (2022–2026) read, write, do maths exams and fold laundry. Every generation kept one trick from the one before and added exactly one new one. Today you learn to name the tricks.

2. The timeline, 2013 → 2026

Try it: filter the list by organisation. Notice which organisation dominates each era, and when new names appear.

Notice that DeepMind owns 2013–2020, OpenAI the proofs of scale in 2017–2019 and the language turn in 2022–2024, and that after January 2025 most entries come from new names: DeepSeek, ByteDance, Tsinghua, Meta, Physical Intelligence's partners.

2013–2017: the deep RL toolbox. The arXiv DQN paper (December 2013) showed a CNN learning seven Atari games from pixels; the Nature version (February 2015) added the replay buffer and target network and 49 games. Mnih 2013 Within four years the field had its standard algorithms: TRPO (February 2015), A3C (February 2016), PPO (July 2017), Rainbow (October 2017), and in January 2018 SAC. Schulman 2015 Almost every system in Day 13 runs one of these, barely changed.

2016–2020: games at scale. AlphaGo beat Fan Hui 5–0 (January 2016) with supervised learning plus self-play plus tree search; AlphaZero (December 2017) was "tabula rasa" and superhuman at chess, shogi and Go "within 24 hours". Silver 2016 Silver 2017 OpenAI Five became "the first AI system to defeat the world champions at an esports game" on 13 April 2019 after ten months of training; AlphaStar reached Grandmaster in StarCraft II, "above 99.8% of officially ranked human players", in October 2019. Berner 2019 Vinyals 2019 MuZero (November 2019) and Agent57 (March 2020) closed the Atari chapter.

2020–2023: learning without the environment. With the game benchmarks saturated, attention turned to fixed datasets: D4RL (April 2020) gave offline RL a benchmark, CQL (June 2020) a conservative algorithm, Decision Transformer (June 2021) a sequence-modelling formulation. Fu 2020 Chen 2021 In robotics, Diffusion Policy (March 2023) improved imitation by an average of 46.9% over 12 tasks and became the action head of the robot foundation models. Chi 2023 DreamerV3 (January 2023) ran one configuration across more than 150 tasks. Hafner 2023

2022–2026: language models become the agent. InstructGPT (March 2022) made RLHF the standard last step of training a chat model; DPO (May 2023) removed the RL loop; o1 (September 2024) and DeepSeek-R1 (January 2025) put RL back, now with verifiable rewards, and R1-Zero's AIME 2024 accuracy rose from 15.6% to 77.9% during RL alone. DeepSeek-AI 2025 DAPO (March 2025) opened the recipe; ScaleRL (October 2025) spent more than 400,000 GPU-hours to fit compute-to-performance curves. Yu 2025 Khatri 2025

2025–2026: RL returns to robots. πRL (October 2025) fine-tuned flow-matching robot policies with PPO and lifted π0.5 on LIBERO from 77.1% to 98.3%; RL-Co (February 2026) co-trained on real and simulated data and raised real-robot success from 40.0% to 64.0%; a CoRL 2026 paper (March 2026) generated 100 training scenes with a language model and a 3D asset pipeline and went from 21.7% to 75% on a real arm. Chen 2025 Shi 2026 Choi 2026 The tree did not grow a new root; PPO from 2017 is still the optimiser in all three.

3. Benchmarks saturate

A benchmark is a fixed set of tasks with a fixed scoring rule. It is useful exactly as long as the best methods score well below its ceiling. Three benchmarks from three eras show the same shape.

Try it: switch between the three benchmarks. Hover a dot for the model.

Notice the shape: a few years of steep gains, then a flat top. On Atari the median went 79% → 223% → 2041% of human and then stopped being informative; on AIME it went 9.3 → 79.8 → 100; on LIBERO 72 → 98. Each flat top was followed by a new benchmark, not by a better score.

Atari. The human-normalised score for one game is 100 × (agent − random) / (human − random), and the headline number is the median over the 57 games. DQN scored a median of 79% under no-op starts; Rainbow 223% (October 2017); MuZero 2041% with 20 billion frames (November 2019). Hessel 2017 Schrittwieser 2019 Agent57 (March 2020) scored a lower median, 1933%, yet was the first agent above human on every one of the 57 games, because the median hides the five or six hard-exploration games that everyone else failed. Badia 2020 Once the statistic can no longer order the methods, the benchmark is dead. The field's answer was Atari-100k, 100,000 agent steps per game, where BBF reached "super-human performance" in May 2023. Schwarzer 2023

AIME. On the 2024 American Invitational Mathematics Examination, GPT-4o scored 9.3% pass@1 in May 2024; o1-1217 scored 79.2 in December 2024 and DeepSeek-R1 79.8 in January 2025, both as reported in the R1 paper. DeepSeek-AI 2025 By October 2026, a secondary aggregator of the MathArena leaderboard lists GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8 at 100% on AIME 2026, GPT-5.4 at 99.2 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro at 96.7; the primary MathArena page has deprecated its AIME competitions and shows only an aggregate expected-performance figure. llmlearner 2026 MathArena 2026 The MathArena platform paper (May 2026) says the quiet part: static benchmarks "are often narrow in scope, quickly saturated, and rarely updated", and it now reports GPT-5.5 at 98% on the 2026 USA Math Olympiad proofs and 74% on research-level questions. Dekoninck 2026

LIBERO. On the robot-manipulation suite, OpenVLA reported 76.5% average success in June 2024 against 75.1% for Octo and 72.4% for Diffusion Policy. Kim 2024 Sixteen months later, πRL reports π0.5 at 96.9% after full-data SFT and 98.3% after RL fine-tuning, all in simulation. Chen 2025 Offline RL went through the same cycle faster: D4RL appeared in April 2020 and by October 2024 OGBench (8 environment types, 85 datasets) was proposed because "representative algorithms may rank similarly on prior benchmarks". Park 2024

Analogy

A benchmark is a thermometer with a top mark. While the patient is at 38°, you learn something from each reading. Once every patient reads "above 42°", the thermometer tells you nothing, and the only honest move is to buy a thermometer with a higher scale. Benchmark saturation is not a sign that the disease is cured; it is a sign that the instrument is out of range.

Common misunderstandings

  • "Atari is solved, so RL is solved." Agent57 and MuZero used tens of billions of frames per game. Learning the same games in 100,000 steps, and keeping what you learned when the game changes, are both open. Schwarzer 2023
  • "100% on AIME means superhuman mathematics." AIME is a final-answer exam. MathArena deprecated it and moved to proofs (USAMO 98%) and research-level questions (74%) because final-answer scores had stopped discriminating. Dekoninck 2026
  • "A higher median means a better agent." Agent57's median (1933%) is below MuZero's (2041%); Agent57 is the one that cleared all 57 games. Pick the statistic that matches the claim. Badia 2020
  • "RL scaling laws look like pre-training scaling laws." ScaleRL finds sigmoids with recipe-dependent ceilings, not power laws (problem 8 below). Khatri 2025

Going deeper (optional): why "human starts" and "no-op starts" give different numbers

Atari agents are evaluated either from a random number of no-op frames (up to 30) or from states sampled from human play ("human starts"). A3C's 116.6% median is on human starts, where Nature DQN scores 68%, not 79%. Mnih 2016 The chart above uses no-op numbers only and leaves A3C out, because mixing the two protocols would shift a dot by a third. Whenever two papers disagree by 10–20% on Atari, check the start protocol first.

4. Ten open problems

Each problem below has one concrete incident and one number. "Open" means that in October 2026 there is no method that a practitioner can apply without thinking hard about it.

1. Sample efficiency. The OpenAI hand needed about 100 years of simulated experience for one object-reorientation skill; MuZero used 20 billion Atari frames. OpenAI 2018 The field has found two escapes, neither of which is a solution. BBF squeezes super-human Atari-100k performance out of 100,000 steps with a bigger network and careful resets. Schwarzer 2023 Rudin et al. make 4,096 simulated robots walk in under four minutes on one GPU, not by needing fewer samples but by making each sample cheap. Rudin 2021 Neither helps when the environment is a hospital or a tokamak.

2. Reward specification and hacking. A policy optimises the reward you wrote, not the one you meant. DeepMind's catalogue of around 60 specification gaming incidents (April 2020) includes a Lego-stacking agent that "simply flipped over the red block to collect the reward", a grasping robot that "learned to fool the human evaluator by hovering between the camera and the object", and a boat-racing agent "going in circles and hitting the same green blocks over and over again". Krakovna 2020 The 2025 version is sharper: a frontier reasoning model learned to hack agentic coding tasks; a GPT-4o monitor reading its chain of thought caught it; and when the monitor's verdict was added to the training reward, the agents learned "obfuscated reward hacking, hiding their intent within the CoT" while still hacking. Baker 2025 Amodei et al. listed this as one of five concrete problems in 2016; it is unsolved in 2026. Amodei 2016

3. Generalisation. An agent trained on one level of a game has usually memorised it. Procgen (December 2019) built 16 procedurally generated games to measure this and found that "diverse environment distributions are essential to adequately train and evaluate RL agents" and that larger models generalise better. Cobbe 2019 The robotics analogue is π0.5, whose performance in unseen homes rises steadily with the number of training locations from 3 to 104, at which point it matches a model trained in the test homes themselves. Physical Intelligence 2025 Diversity works; nobody knows how much is enough in advance.

4. Exploration. Montezuma's Revenge gives its first reward only after a long chain of correct moves. PPO with no bonus scored 2,497; RND's novelty bonus scored 8,152, above the human average of 4,753. Burda 2018 Agent57 still needed a bandit meta-controller that picks between exploratory and exploitative policies per episode to clear all 57 games. Badia 2020 In language-model RL the same problem wears a different name, entropy collapse: the policy stops sampling rare tokens, and DAPO's Clip-Higher (εhigh = 0.28) exists only to slow that down. Yu 2025

5. Long-horizon credit assignment. AlphaChip receives zero reward at every step and a single wirelength-plus-congestion score at the final placement; AlphaDev's reward depends on a whole program; R1-Zero's responses grew steadily longer during training with only an outcome reward to say which of 10,000 tokens mattered. Mirhoseini 2020 DeepSeek-AI 2025 GRPO assigns every token in a trajectory the same advantage; Day 12's turn-aware and per-step variants are 2026 attempts, not settled practice.

6. Safety and alignment. RLHF's reward comes from about 40 labelers, and the 1.3B model they shaped was preferred to 175B GPT-3, which is both the method's power and its risk: whatever those labelers systematically got wrong is now optimised for. Ouyang 2022 DPO removes the RL loop but not the preference-data bottleneck. Rafailov 2023 And the obfuscated-hacking result above says that the most natural safety tool, reading the model's reasoning, degrades exactly when you optimise against it. Baker 2025

7. Reproducibility. Henderson et al. (2018) ran TRPO ten times on HalfCheetah with identical hyperparameters, split the runs into two groups of five, and found the groups differed significantly (t = −9.09, p = 0.0016) "just from the random seeds". PPO on Hopper scored 61 ± 33 with a (400, 300) network and 2790 ± 62 with (64, 64). Henderson 2018 Five seeds is still the common budget in 2026, and most LLM-RL papers report one.

8. RL scaling laws. ScaleRL (October 2025) fitted sigmoids to more than 400,000 GPU-hours of runs and found that "not all recipes yield similar asymptotic performance": computing the LM-head logits in FP32 raised the asymptote A from 0.52 to 0.61, and a 100,000 GPU-hour run was predicted from its first 50,000. Khatri 2025 For value-based RL, Rybkin et al. (2025) show that data and compute requirements lie on a Pareto frontier governed by the update-to-data ratio. Rybkin 2025 The open part: a ceiling you can predict is still a ceiling, and nobody can yet predict A from the recipe without running it.

9. Continual learning and loss of plasticity. Deep networks trained on a long sequence of tasks "lose their ability to learn on new examples, a phenomenon called loss of plasticity"; Dohare et al.'s continual backpropagation keeps learning by re-initialising a small fraction of rarely used units. Dohare 2023 The Alberta Plan (August 2022) lays out twelve research steps from continual supervised learning with meta-learned step sizes, through general value functions, average-reward control, planning and options, to a full continual agent. Sutton 2022 Every agent in this course was trained once and frozen.

10. Evaluation and contamination. A benchmark published on the web before a model is trained may be in its training data; a benchmark reused across years stops ranking methods. D4RL gave way to OGBench for the second reason, AIME to proof grading for both. Park 2024 Dekoninck 2026 The MathArena authors' answer is a continuously maintained platform that designs new tests as capabilities improve; that is a process, not a solved problem.

5. Where the field is going

Stated with dates and without adjectives.

Streams of experience. Silver and Sutton (April 2025) argue that "agents will inhabit streams of experience, rather than short snippets of interaction" and that "their rewards will be grounded in their experience of the environment, rather than coming from human prejudgement". Silver 2025 This is a position paper. Its concrete content is problems 9 and 2 above: continual learning and grounded reward.

RL for reasoning models. The September 2025 survey of RL for large reasoning models treats RL as "a foundational methodology for transforming LLMs into LRMs". Its open debates are whether RL sharpens or discovers, whether RL or SFT generalises, and whether rewards should be process or outcome; its listed directions are continual RL, memory-based RL, model-based RL, efficient reasoning, latent-space reasoning, RL for pre-training, RL for diffusion language models, scientific discovery, and architecture–algorithm co-design. Zhang 2025 Four of those nine are problems 1, 5 and 9 from section 4 under new names.

World models. Dreamer 4 (September 2025) trains a Minecraft agent entirely inside a learned video model that runs in real time on one GPU, from offline data alone. Hafner 2025 If that recipe transfers to robots, problem 1 changes shape: samples come from the model, not the world.

Agentic RL and robot foundation models. The 2026 results in section 2 (RL-Co, generative worlds) and Day 12's tool-use benchmarks share one design: a pre-trained generalist, then RL on outcome rewards in thousands of parallel environments. The optimiser is PPO or a PPO variant in every case. The frontier is in the environments and the rewards, not the update rule.

6. What to read next

Sutton & Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd ed., 2018), free PDF. Everything in Days 1–9 is here with proofs and exercises; it is the reference the whole field cites. Sutton & Barto 2018 See the Paper Bible entry.

OpenAI Spinning Up (2018). Short, code-first notes on policy optimisation, DDPG, TD3, SAC and PPO with reference implementations; the fastest route from Day 8 to running code. Achiam 2018

Bista, Deep Reinforcement Learning: From First Principles to Reasoning Models (July 2026, arXiv, CC BY 4.0). A book-length treatment that follows the same arc as this course, from dynamic programming to RLHF and reasoning models, with chapters on why each method was introduced and where it fails. Bista 2026

The Paper Bible in this app: twenty primary papers from Sutton & Barto to ScaleRL, each with its architecture figure, main result table and the sentence that supports every number quoted in these fourteen days. Start with DQN, PPO, MuZero and DeepSeek-R1; the full list is one tab away.

7. Architecture

Read it column by column, top to bottom. The value-based column is one unbroken line: each node estimates how good a state or action is, and each generation changes only what sits under the estimate (a table, then a network, then six patches, then a distributed recurrent learner). The policy-gradient column differentiates the return directly; from PPO onwards it is a single algorithm applied to new policies: robot controllers, chip placers, language models. The off-policy column holds the branches that reuse old data: SAC from the actor-critic line, DPO from RLHF. The planning column keeps a model, given (AlphaGo, AlphaZero) or learned (MuZero), and searches it; the world-model column also learns a model but trains the policy inside it instead of searching at decision time.

What flows between the columns is ideas, not weights. Replay buffers crossed from DQN into SAC; the clipped ratio crossed from PPO into GRPO and πRL; MCTS crossed from Go into sorting. The nodes a practitioner actually runs in 2026 are the three highlighted ones plus PPO: that is the whole active toolkit, and every one of them is at least seven years old or a small variant of something that is.

Systems view

The tree's leaves differ by six orders of magnitude in cost. Agent57 consumed tens of billions of frames per game on a distributed actor-learner system. Badia 2020 FastSAC trains a humanoid walking policy in 15 minutes on one RTX 4090. Seo 2025 Dreamer 4's world model runs in real time on a single GPU. Hafner 2025 ScaleRL's single validation run took 100,000 GPU-hours, and its ablations four times that. Khatri 2025 The algorithms are shared; what separates a weekend project from a lab budget is the environment (a simulator on the GPU, or a 400B-parameter sampler) and the number of parallel copies of it.

Check yourself

Q1. Rainbow's Atari median was 223% of human. What was DQN's on the same no-op protocol, and MuZero's two years later?

79% (Rainbow Table 2, no-op starts) and 2041.1% (MuZero Table 1, 20B frames). 68% is DQN on human starts; 1933% is Agent57; 4999% is MuZero's mean, not median.

Q2. Agent57's median (1933%) is below MuZero's (2041%). Why is Agent57 still the milestone?

The median ignores the handful of games like Montezuma's Revenge that every earlier agent failed. Agent57 cleared them all. Different statistic, different claim.

Q3. Which statement about the AIME numbers in this lesson is correct?

GPT-4o scored 9.3; o1-1217 scored 79.2. The 2026 rows (100 / 99.2 / 96.7) are from llmlearner.com mirroring MathArena, which lists AIME as deprecated.

Q4. In Baker et al. (2025), what happened when the chain-of-thought monitor's verdict was added to the training reward?

"Obfuscated reward hacking": optimising against the monitor removed the evidence, not the behaviour. This is why problem 2 and problem 6 are the same problem.

Q5. "RL scaling laws are power laws like pre-training." What did ScaleRL find?

Compute buys you progress toward a ceiling A; the recipe sets A. Some knobs move the ceiling, others only the speed of reaching it.

Q6. Henderson et al. ran TRPO ten times with identical hyperparameters and split the runs into two groups of five. What did they find?

t = −9.09, p = 0.0016 between two sets of seeds. The (400, 300) network made PPO on Hopper worse (61 ± 33 vs 2790 ± 62), not more stable.

Recap: five things to remember

  1. The course is a tree with four roots: values (DP → TD → Q-learning → DQN → Rainbow → Agent57), policies (REINFORCE → actor-critic → TRPO → PPO → RLHF → GRPO), models (Dyna; AlphaGo → AlphaZero → MuZero; Dreamer → Dreamer 4) and preferences (RLHF → DPO → verifiable rewards). PPO from 2017 is still the optimiser in the 2026 robot and language-model results.
  2. Benchmarks saturate in about five years: Atari median 79% → 223% → 2041%, then Atari-100k; AIME 9.3 → 79.8 → 100 (2026 figure from a secondary source), then proofs; LIBERO 72 → 98, then real robots. A flat curve means a dead instrument, not a solved field.
  3. Ten open problems, each with a number: 100 years of experience (sample efficiency), obfuscated reward hacking (specification), 3 → 104 homes (generalisation), 8,152 vs 2,497 (exploration), reward at the last step only (credit), 40 labelers (alignment), p = 0.0016 from seeds (reproducibility), A = 0.52 → 0.61 (scaling), 12 Alberta Plan steps (plasticity), AIME deprecated (evaluation).
  4. The stated directions for 2025–26 are streams of experience with grounded rewards, RL as the method for reasoning models, world models you can train inside, and RL fine-tuning of pre-trained generalists in parallel environments. Most of them are the open problems restated as goals.
  5. Read next: Sutton & Barto for the theory, Spinning Up for the code, Bista (2026) for the modern arc, the Paper Bible for the primary sources behind every number here.

Paper Bible
The papers that built modern RL.

The landmark papers, each explained three ways: in one sentence, for a 10-year-old, and step by step for an adult who wants the real mechanism. With the headline numbers, the architecture, how to read the original, and what came after.

The figures inside each review are reproduced from the papers for study, with the source linked under every one. Tap a figure to open it full size.

2016 · Mnih et al. · ICML 2016 (arXiv 1602.01783)

A3C: Asynchronous advantage actor–critic

Sixteen CPU threads, no GPU and no replay memory: an actor–critic that beat the Atari state of the art in half the training time of the GPU-trained DQN family.

Taught in Day 7 · Read time of the original: ~60 min

In one sentence

Run many copies of an actor–critic agent in parallel threads, each in its own environment, and let them push gradients into one shared network without waiting for each other; the diversity across threads replaces DQN's replay memory, and the result "succeeds on a wide variety of continuous motor control problems as well as on a new task of navigating random 3D mazes". Mnih 2016

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Sixteen kids play the same video game on sixteen screens. Each one has a copy of a shared notebook of tips. Every few moves a kid writes what they learned into the one shared notebook, then copies the newest notebook back. Nobody waits for anybody. Because the kids are in different parts of the game at any moment, the notebook never gets stuck on one situation.

The problem

DQN stabilised deep Q-learning with a replay memory and a target network, but at a cost: a million stored frames, an off-policy algorithm (replay cannot be used with on-policy actor–critics), and days of GPU time: 8 days on a GPU for DQN, 4 days on 100 machines for the distributed Gorila. Mnih 2016 Policy-gradient methods (the REINFORCE review) could handle continuous actions but, trained online from one agent, saw the same correlated, non-stationary data that broke naive deep Q-learning.

The key idea

Decorrelate the data in space instead of in time. Instead of one agent remembering old transitions, run 16 actor–learners at once; at any instant they are in different states of different episodes, so the updates arriving at the shared parameters are already a mixed sample. The paper builds four asynchronous algorithms this way (one-step Q, one-step Sarsa, n-step Q, and advantage actor–critic); the actor–critic one, A3C, performs best. Mnih 2016

How it works, step by step

  1. A global network holds policy parameters θ and value parameters θv; the two heads share every non-output layer: conv 16 filters 8×8 stride 4, conv 32 filters 4×4 stride 2, 256 fully connected units, then a softmax over actions and a scalar V. The LSTM variant adds 256 LSTM cells. Mnih 2016
  2. Each of 16 threads copies the global parameters, then acts in its own environment for up to tmax = 5 steps or until the episode ends. Mnih 2016
  3. It forms k-step bootstrapped returns and advantages, k ≤ 5:

A(st,at) = Σi=0k−1 γi rt+i + γk V(st+k; θv) − V(st; θv)

  1. Policy gradient ∇θ log π(at|st) · A(st,at) plus an entropy term β ∇θ H(π(st)), β = 0.01, which "improved exploration by discouraging premature convergence to suboptimal deterministic policies"; value gradient from (R − V)2. Mnih 2016
  2. The thread applies its gradients to the global parameters asynchronously, lock-free in the Hogwild! style, through a shared RMSProp (decay 0.99), then re-syncs and continues. γ = 0.99. Mnih 2016

Results

Table 1 reports human-normalised mean and median over 57 Atari games with human starts. Mnih 2016

MethodTraining timeMeanMedian
DQN8 days on GPU121.9%47.5%
Gorila4 days, 100 machines215.2%71.3%
Dueling D-DQN8 days on GPU343.8%117.1%
Prioritized DQN8 days on GPU463.6%127.6%
A3C, FF1 day on CPU344.1%68.2%
A3C, FF4 days on CPU496.8%116.6%
A3C, LSTM4 days on CPU623.0%112.6%

After one CPU-day A3C's mean (344.1%) matched Dueling Double DQN's eight GPU-days (343.8%). Table 2 gives the speed-up from 1 to 16 threads averaged over seven games: 24.1× for one-step Q, 12.5× for A3C, so the asynchronous updates were not just parallel but, for the Q-methods, super-linear. Mnih 2016

Why it mattered

A3C made deep RL affordable: a multi-core desktop instead of a GPU cluster. Its k-step advantage estimator is the λ = 1 end of the GAE family, and the PPO paper notes its own advantage estimator reduces to A3C's when λ = 1. Schulman 2017 The synchronous, batched twin, A2C, became the standard policy-gradient baseline; PPO's Atari comparison is against A2C and ACER, and the entropy weight 0.01 carried straight over. Schulman 2017 The paper also showed the same code learning TORCS driving, MuJoCo continuous control and a 3D maze with an LSTM policy, the first broad demonstration that one on-policy deep method spans discrete and continuous control. Mnih 2016

Limitations

Means flatter medians: after one day A3C's median was 68.2%, below Double DQN's 110.9%, because a few games with huge normalised scores dominate the mean. Mnih 2016 The comparison is in wall-clock time, not frames: on-policy data is used once and thrown away, so A3C is sample-hungry. The 2017 PPO paper found that A2C "won" only 1 of 49 Atari games against PPO's 30 on average reward over training. Schulman 2017 And asynchrony itself makes runs hard to reproduce; Henderson et al. (2018) showed deep policy-gradient results shifting significantly from random seeds alone. Henderson 2018

How to read the paper

Section 4 (the asynchronous framework and the four algorithms, 15 min), then Section 5.1 with Figure 1 and Table 1 (10 min), Section 5.5 for Table 2's thread scaling (10 min). Skim 5.2–5.4 for TORCS, MuJoCo and Labyrinth. Section 8 has the network and hyperparameters (tmax, β, RMSProp). Skip Section 9 unless you need the continuous-control details.

Check yourself

Q1. How many threads did A3C use, and on what hardware?

"Each experiment used 16 actor-learner threads running on a single machine and no GPUs." Gorila was the 100-machine system; the K40 was DQN's.

Q2. "A3C needs a replay memory to decorrelate its data." Why is this wrong?

Replay requires off-policy learning. A3C replaces it with diversity across 16 concurrent environments, which is what makes an on-policy method viable.

Q3. After one CPU-day, A3C FF's mean score was 344.1%. Its median was:

Table 1: 344.1% mean, 68.2% median after 1 day. The 116.6% median needed 4 days. Always read both numbers.
