  3. Schulman, J. et al. (2016). High-Dimensional Continuous Control Using Generalized Advantage Estimation. arXiv:1506.02438.
  4. Schulman, J. et al. (2017). Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms. arXiv:1707.06347.
  5. Henderson, P. et al. (2018). Deep Reinforcement Learning that Matters. AAAI 2018. arXiv:1709.06560.
2016 · Silver et al. · Nature 529:484–489

AlphaGo: Mastering the game of Go with deep neural networks and tree search

Policy and value networks steering Monte Carlo tree search won 99.8% of games against other Go programs and beat the European champion 5–0; its descendant AlphaGo Zero, trained from random play, beat the Lee Sedol version 100–0.

Taught in Day 11 · Read time of the original: ~45 min

In one sentence

AlphaGo replaced the random rollouts and hand-written evaluation of earlier Go programs with a policy network that says which moves are worth considering and a value network that says who is winning, making Monte Carlo tree search both narrower and shallower than brute force.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Go has more possible games than atoms in the universe, so nobody can check every move. AlphaGo has two helpers: one whispers "only these three moves look sensible", the other looks at the board and says "you are probably winning". It plays many quick imaginary games with those hints and picks the move it tried most. AlphaGo Zero later learned both helpers by playing only against itself.

The problem

Chess fell in 1997 to deep search plus a hand-crafted evaluation function. Go resisted: a 19×19 board, hundreds of legal moves per position, and no simple formula for who is ahead. Monte Carlo tree search, which evaluates positions by playing random games to the end, had carried programs to strong amateur level, but beating a professional on a full-size board had not been done. Silver 2016

The key idea

Learn the two things search cannot brute-force. A policy network p(a|s) cuts the breadth of the search by giving each move a prior. A value network v(s) cuts the depth: the search can stop at a leaf and ask who is winning instead of playing out a random game. The networks alone, with no search, already played at the level of the best MCTS programs. Silver 2016

How it works, step by step

  1. Supervised policy network. A convolutional network is trained on positions from human expert games to predict the expert's move (Figure 1 shows the pipeline). Silver 2016
  2. RL policy network. The same network is improved by self-play with the REINFORCE gradient of Day 7: reward +1 for a win, −1 for a loss, at the end only.
  3. Value network. A second network is regressed onto self-play outcomes, vθ(s) ≈ E[z | s].
  4. Search. Each simulation descends the tree choosing the move with the best value plus an exploration bonus that scales with the prior and shrinks with visits; a new leaf is expanded with the policy's priors, scored by mixing the value network with a fast rollout, and the score is backed up. The most-visited root move is played (Figure 3). Silver 2016

    at = argmaxa [ Q(st,a) + u(st,a) ], u(s,a) ∝ P(s,a) / (1 + N(s,a))

    V(sL) = (1−λ) vθ(sL) + λ zL

  5. AlphaGo Zero (2017). One residual network fθ(s) = (p, v), no human data, no rollouts; the search's visit counts π become the policy target and the game outcome z the value target. DeepMind 2017

    loss = (z − v)² − πT log p + c‖θ‖²

  6. AlphaZero (2017/2018). The same algorithm, "starting from random play, and given no domain knowledge except the game rules", for chess and shogi as well as Go. Silver 2017

Results

The 2016 paper reports a 99.8% win rate against other Go programs and a 5–0 win over the European champion Fan Hui, the first defeat of a professional on a full-size board (Figure 4, "Tournament evaluation of AlphaGo"). Silver 2016 Two months after publication AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol 4–1 in Seoul (March 2016), watched by over 200 million people; move 37 of game two had a 1-in-10,000 chance of being played by a human, and the win earned an honorary 9-dan ranking. DeepMind 2016

AlphaGo Zero (Nature 550:354–359, October 2017) learned "solely from self-play" and won "100–0 against the previously published, champion-defeating AlphaGo"; its 3-day run used a 20-block residual network, its 40-day run 40 blocks. Silver 2017a It passed AlphaGo Lee after 3 days and AlphaGo Master after 40, on 4 TPUs where AlphaGo Lee had used 48; the Elo chart puts it above 5000 against roughly 4800 for Master. DeepMind 2017

AlphaZero's preprint claims superhuman chess, shogi and Go "within 24 hours". Silver 2017 The 2018 evaluation has it overtaking Stockfish after 4 hours, Elmo after 2 and AlphaGo Lee after 30; it won 155 and lost 6 of 1,000 games against Stockfish, won 91.2% against Elmo and 61% against AlphaGo Zero, while searching about 60 thousand positions per second to Stockfish's 60 million, on 4 first-generation TPUs and 44 CPU cores. DeepMind 2018

Why it mattered

AlphaGo made "deep RL plus search" the template for every later planning system here. MuZero (November 2019) kept the search but learned the model, so rules no longer had to be given (the MuZero review). Schrittwieser 2019 AlphaTensor (2022) and AlphaDev (2023) reused the AlphaZero loop to find faster matrix-multiplication and sorting algorithms, treating algorithm design as a single-player game. Fawzi 2022 Mankowitz 2023 Self-play as an automatic curriculum is the standard answer to "where does the opponent come from" in Day 11.

Limitations

The 2016 system was not tabula rasa: it started from human games, used hand-designed features for its fast rollouts, and ran as a distributed system; AlphaGo Zero removed the human data and the rollouts. DeepMind 2017 All three systems are handed a perfect simulator, the rules of a two-player, zero-sum, perfect-information game; MuZero dropped that assumption. Schrittwieser 2019 Training compute stayed large: the later MuZero board-game runs, which inherit the setup, used 16 TPUs for training and 1000 for self-play. Schrittwieser 2019

How to read the paper

The Nature text is paywalled, but the abstract and figure captions are free: Figure 1 (pipeline), Figure 3 (the four MCTS steps), Figure 4 (tournament); the formulas are in Methods. Then the AlphaGo Zero abstract plus the DeepMind blog for the 3-day and 40-day numbers, and the first two pages and Table 1 of the AlphaZero preprint. About 45 minutes.

Check yourself

Q1. What does the value network change about the search?

The value network reduces search depth; the policy network's priors reduce breadth.

Q2. After how many days of self-play did AlphaGo Zero beat the Lee Sedol version 100–0?

3 days to pass AlphaGo Lee, 40 to pass Master. The 24-hour and 30-hour figures belong to AlphaZero.

Q3. "AlphaGo learned Go without any human data." Which is right?

The 2016 pipeline begins with supervised learning on expert positions; learning from "completely random play" arrived with AlphaGo Zero.

References

  1. Silver et al. Mastering the game of Go with deep neural networks and tree search. Nature 529:484–489, 27 Jan 2016. nature.com
  2. Silver et al. Mastering the game of Go without human knowledge. Nature 550:354–359, 19 Oct 2017. nature.com; blog: AlphaGo Zero: starting from scratch
  3. Silver et al. Mastering Chess and Shogi by Self-Play with a General RL Algorithm. 2017. arXiv 1712.01815; blog: AlphaZero (Dec 2018)
  4. DeepMind. AlphaGo breakthrough page. deepmind.google
  5. Schrittwieser et al. Mastering Atari, Go, chess and shogi by planning with a learned model. 2019. arXiv 1911.08265
2020 · Kumar et al. · arXiv 2006.04779 (Berkeley / Google)

CQL: Conservative Q-learning for offline RL

A Q-learning regulariser that pushes Q down on the actions the policy likes and up on the actions in the dataset, so the learned value lower-bounds the truth: 2–5× the return of prior offline methods on mixed data, and 61.2 on antmaze-medium-play where every baseline scored 0.0.

Taught in Day 10 · Read time of the original: ~60 min

In one sentence

CQL adds one term to the ordinary Bellman loss, α times (soft-maximum of Q over all actions minus average Q over dataset actions), which makes the Q-function pessimistic exactly where the data is silent, and this is enough to turn SAC into a strong offline learner with "only 20 lines of code".

Explain it to a 10-year-old

You learn to cook only from a recipe book and cannot taste anything until the exam. A careless cook thinks "chocolate in the soup could be amazing!" just because the book never says it is bad. CQL's rule: if the book never tried it, assume it is worse than it looks, and trust the recipes the book did use a bit more. You end up combining the best bits of many so-so recipes instead of inventing disasters.

The problem

Offline RL learns from a fixed dataset collected by some behaviour policy, with no further interaction. Standard off-policy methods fail here because the Bellman target maxa' Q(s', a') queries actions the data never covered; their values are guesses, the max picks the most over-estimated guess, and the error propagates. Fujimoto et al. named this extrapolation error in 2018. Fujimoto 2018 In CQL's own tables, SAC trained offline scores 3.5 on hopper-mixed and 1.9 on walker2d-mixed, below plain behaviour cloning (11.8 and 11.3). Kumar 2020

The key idea

Do not constrain the policy; make the Q-function pessimistic. If Q's expected value under the learned policy is a lower bound on the true value, a policy that maximises it cannot be fooled by phantom values on unseen actions. The regulariser is a soft-max over all actions minus the mean over dataset actions: non-negative, and small only when unseen actions are not valued above seen ones.

How it works, step by step

  1. Penalise the policy's actions. Equation 1 adds α·Es~D, a~μ[Q(s,a)] to the Bellman error, with μ the distribution of actions being evaluated. Theorem 3.1: the result lower-bounds the true Q pointwise, for large enough α. Kumar 2020
  2. Give back on dataset actions. Equation 2 subtracts α·Ea~π̂β[Q(s,a)]. The bound is now on the policy's expected value, not pointwise, and is tighter (Theorem 3.2). Kumar 2020
  3. Choose μ by a regulariser. CQL(R) maximises over μ with a regulariser R(μ); using entropy gives CQL(H), the version used in the experiments. Kumar 2020

    minQ α · Es~D[ log Σa exp Q(s,a) − Ea~π̂β[Q(s,a)] ] + ½ E(s,a,s')~D[ (Q(s,a) − B̂πQ̂(s,a))² ]

    Check it by hand with three actions and Q = [1, 2, 5], where only action 2 appears in the data: log(e1 + e2 + e5) ≈ 5.07, minus 2 gives a penalty of 3.07, almost all of it from the unseen action with Q = 5. If that action's value is pulled down to 1.5, the penalty falls to log(e + e2 + e1.5) − 2 ≈ 0.68.
  4. Train the policy as usual. For continuous control, CQL sits on top of SAC and α "is automatically tuned via Lagrangian dual gradient descent"; for Atari it sits on QR-DQN. Kumar 2020

Results

On the D4RL gym tasks (normalised so 0 is random and 100 is expert), CQL(H) scored 48.6 on hopper-mixed against 25.3 for the best prior method (BEAR), 26.7 on walker2d-mixed against 11.3 (BC), and 98.7 on walker2d-medium-expert against 11.3; its Table 1 caption says it "greatly outperforms prior methods with complex distributions". Kumar 2020 It did not win everywhere: on hopper-medium-expert, BC scores 111.9 to CQL's 111.0. Kumar 2020 On antmaze-medium-play, where the agent must stitch together segments of undirected trajectories, CQL(H) reached 61.2 while BC, SAC, BEAR, BRAC-p and BRAC-v all scored 0.0. Kumar 2020 On Adroit, CQL variants "are the only methods that improve over BC". Kumar 2020 On Atari with 1% of the DQN replay data, Q*bert went from 383.6 (QR-DQN) to 14,012.0. Kumar 2020

Why it mattered

CQL made offline RL a one-line change to an existing algorithm, and it became the baseline every later method is measured against: IQL (October 2021) beat it on AntMaze, 378.0 total to 303.6, by never querying unseen actions at all, while tying on locomotion (692.4 to 698.5). Kostrikov 2021 Decision Transformer (June 2021) reported its numbers against CQL (the DT review). Chen 2021 In Day 10 it is the canonical answer to "why not just run DQN on the dataset".

Limitations

Pessimism costs performance on clean expert data (hopper-medium-expert), and α must be set or dual-tuned. The authors leave "a rigorous theoretical analysis of CQL with deep neural nets" to future work and flag that offline methods can overfit, so finding "simple and effective early stopping methods" is open. Kumar 2020 CQL still evaluates Q on unseen actions in order to penalise them; IQL's expectile trick avoids that query entirely, and the D4RL-gym tasks it was tuned on later stopped separating methods, which motivated OGBench in 2024. Park 2024

How to read the paper

Section 3.1 (Equations 1–2, theorem statements only), 3.2 for CQL(H), Section 4 for the 20-line recipe; Tables 1–2 and Figure 1 for results. Skip 3.3 and the proofs in Appendix C unless you need guarantees. About 60 minutes; it is long.

Check yourself

Q1. What does the CQL(H) regulariser compute per state?

Soft-max over all actions minus the average over seen actions: non-negative, and zero only when unseen actions are not over-valued.

Q2. On antmaze-medium-play, CQL(H) scored 61.2. What did BC, SAC, BEAR and both BRAC variants score?

All five baselines scored 0.0; the task needs stitching sub-trajectories, which naive methods and BC cannot do.

Q3. "Offline RL is just behaviour cloning with extra steps." Which fact contradicts this?

BC copies the average demonstrator; CQL uses rewards and Bellman backups to combine the best fragments, which is how it solves a task BC cannot.

References

  1. Kumar, Zhou, Tucker, Levine. Conservative Q-Learning for Offline Reinforcement Learning. Jun 2020 (v3 Aug 2020). arXiv 2006.04779
  2. Fujimoto, Meger, Precup. Off-Policy Deep RL without Exploration (BCQ). 2018. arXiv 1812.02900
  3. Fu et al. D4RL: Datasets for Deep Data-Driven RL. 2020. arXiv 2004.07219
  4. Kostrikov, Nair, Levine. Offline RL with Implicit Q-Learning (IQL). 2021. arXiv 2110.06169
  5. Park, Frans, Eysenbach, Levine. OGBench. 2024. arXiv 2410.20092
2025 · Yu et al. · ByteDance Seed / Tsinghua

DAPO: an open-source LLM reinforcement learning system at scale

Four fixes to GRPO, each ablated in the open, took a Qwen2.5-32B base model from 30 to 50 on AIME 2024 and beat DeepSeek-R1-Zero-Qwen-32B's 47 with half the training steps, with code, data and recipe released. Yu 2025

Taught in Day 12 · Read time of the original: ~30 min

In one sentence

GRPO as written collapses its own exploration, wastes compute on questions where every sample agrees, under-weights long answers and punishes truncation randomly; DAPO fixes each with one change and shows the ladder of gains. Yu 2025

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Same classroom as DeepSeek-R1: 16 students answer a question and get compared with the class average. DAPO adds four house rules. If everyone gets a question right or everyone gets it wrong, swap it out, it teaches nothing today. Let rare good ideas grow a bit faster than usual. Grade every sentence equally, not every student equally, so long careful answers count. And warn a student who is running out of paper before cutting them off.

The problem

When R1 appeared, the recipe was described but the training details were not, and the authors of DAPO report that naive GRPO on Qwen2.5-32B reached only 30 on AIME 2024 and suffered entropy collapse, reward noise and training instability. Yu 2025 Entropy collapse means the policy's distribution sharpens early; the 16 samples become near-copies, the group has no variance, and the advantages go to zero (see the worked example in Day 12).

The key idea

Keep GRPO's group-relative advantage and PPO's clipped ratio (review), drop the KL term, and change four details that each attack a named failure. The paper's contribution is as much the open ablation ladder as the algorithm. Yu 2025

How it works, step by step

The objective (Eq. 12):

JDAPO(θ) = E[ 1/(Σi|oi|) · Σi Σt min( ρi,t Âi,t, clip(ρi,t, 1−εlow, 1+εhigh) Âi,t ) ]   s.t.   0 < |{ oi : correct }| < G

  1. Clip-Higher. PPO's symmetric clip ε = 0.2 caps how fast a rare token can grow: a token at probability 0.01 can reach at most 0.012 in one update, while a token at 0.9 can move to 1.0. DAPO decouples the bounds, εlow = 0.2 and εhigh = 0.28, so low-probability tokens get room and entropy stays up. Yu 2025
  2. Dynamic sampling. Drop prompts whose G = 16 samples are all right or all wrong (zero advantage, zero gradient) and keep sampling until the batch is full of informative prompts. That is the constraint under the expectation. Yu 2025
  3. Token-level loss. GRPO averages per response then across responses, so a 10,000-token answer and a 100-token answer weigh the same and each token in the long one barely counts. DAPO divides by the total token count Σ|oi| instead, so long reasoning is weighted in proportion and long rambling gets penalised in proportion. Yu 2025
  4. Overlong reward shaping. Truncated answers used to get the same −1 as wrong ones, which is noise. Soft punishment: a 4,096-token buffer before the 16,384-token expected maximum (20,480 total) in which the penalty grows with length; first they simply masked truncated samples out of the loss. Yu 2025
  5. Setup. No KL term, because a long-CoT policy legitimately drifts far from its initialisation; rule-based reward on the DAPO-Math-17K dataset, whose answers were rewritten as integers so a string match is the verifier; prompt batch 512, learning rate 1×10−6; built on verl. Yu 2025

Results

Table 1, all on AIME 2024 avg@32 with Qwen2.5-32B: naive GRPO 30; + overlong filtering 36; + Clip-Higher 38; + soft overlong punishment 41; + token-level loss 42; + dynamic sampling 50. The biggest single step is the last one. Yu 2025 The 50 beats DeepSeek-R1-Zero-Qwen-32B's 47 using "50% of the training steps". Yu 2025 The training-dynamics section shows entropy staying higher with Clip-Higher and response length growing steadily; the case study shows checking behaviour appearing during RL that the base model did not produce. Yu 2025

Why it mattered

DAPO was the first complete, reproducible RLVR system at the 32B scale: algorithm, verl training code and the DAPO-Math-17K dataset, released together in March 2025. Yu 2025 Its four fixes spread quickly. Hugging Face TRL made the token-level loss its default loss_type and recommends εhigh = 0.28; Hugging Face 2026 ProRL kept dynamic sampling and Clip-Higher (with εhigh = 0.4) for 2,000+ steps; Liu 2025 and the ScaleRL study (review) used DAPO as a named baseline recipe and kept zero-variance filtering, its cousin of dynamic sampling. Khatri 2025

Limitations

There is no limitations section. The evaluation is maths only, on one base model, with one metric; the authors say the method "can be readily transferred to other tasks" but do not test it, and they leave the study of emerging reflective behaviour to future work. Yu 2025 Removing the KL term is asserted, not ablated. Yu 2025 A month later a value-based counterpoint from the same lab, VAPO, reached 60.4 on the same setup in 5,000 steps with a critic and no crashes, so the critic is expensive rather than useless. Yue 2025 And ScaleRL found that DAPO's loss reached a lower asymptote than CISPO or GSPO when compute was scaled. Khatri 2025

How to read the paper

Read Figure 1 and Table 1 first; they are the paper. Then Sections 3.1–3.4, one page each, with the entropy and length plots in Section 4.3. Section 2 is a compact restatement of PPO and GRPO worth skimming if the R1 review was unclear. Skip Appendix A. About 25 minutes.

Check yourself

Q1. Which single change gave the largest jump in the ablation ladder?

Removing all-right and all-wrong groups added 8 points, more than any other step.

Q2. Why raise only the upper clip bound to 0.28?

With a symmetric 0.2, a token at p = 0.01 can only reach 0.012 per step; the asymmetric bound gives exploration headroom.

Q3. "DAPO keeps the KL penalty to the reference model." True or false?

Section 2.3 removes it without an ablation; there is no critic either.

References

  1. Yu, Zhang, Zhu, Yuan, Zuo et al. (ByteDance Seed, Tsinghua AIR). DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale. 2025. arXiv 2503.14476 · full text
  2. DeepSeek-AI. DeepSeek-R1. 2025. arXiv 2501.12948
  3. Yue et al. VAPO: Efficient and Reliable Reinforcement Learning for Advanced Reasoning Tasks. 2025. arXiv 2504.05118
  4. Khatri, Madaan et al. The Art of Scaling Reinforcement Learning Compute for LLMs. 2025. arXiv 2510.13786
2025 · DeepSeek-AI · Nature 645, 633–638 (Sept 2025)

DeepSeek-R1: incentivizing reasoning capability in LLMs via reinforcement learning

Pure RL with a rule-based 0/1 reward and no human reasoning traces took a base model's AIME 2024 score from 15.6% to 77.9%, and the released DeepSeek-R1 reached 79.8% on AIME 2024 and 97.3% on MATH-500. DeepSeek-AI 2025

Taught in Day 12 · Read time of the original: ~45 min (v1); the Nature version moves most detail to appendices

In one sentence

Sample 16 answers per maths question, grade each with an answer key, push probability toward the above-average answers and away from the below-average ones, and the model teaches itself to write long chains of thought, check its work and say "wait" without ever being shown an example. DeepSeek-AI 2025

Explain it to a 10-year-old

A class of 16 students all answer the same maths problem. There is no teacher grading style, only the answer key at the back of the book: right or wrong. Each student is compared with the class average. Beat the class, do more of that; fall below, do less. After thousands of problems the students start writing out their steps and double-checking, because that is what kept winning.

The problem

OpenAI's o1 (September 2024) showed that a model trained "with large-scale reinforcement learning to reason using chain of thought" jumped on maths and code, but published no recipe. OpenAI 2024 The open question was whether reasoning needs human-written reasoning traces for SFT, process reward models that grade each step, or search at inference time. DeepSeek-AI 2025 RLHF-style PPO (the InstructGPT review) also kept a value model the size of the policy, which for a 671B-parameter base is a serious cost.

The key idea

Two moves. First, verifiable rewards: for maths and code, a program can check the final answer, so no learned reward model is needed and there is nothing to game except the checker. Second, GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization, from DeepSeekMath, February 2024): replace PPO's value model with the mean and standard deviation of rewards inside a group of samples for the same question. Shao 2024 Apply both to the base model directly, with no SFT, and see what emerges. That model is DeepSeek-R1-Zero. DeepSeek-AI 2025

How it works, step by step

  1. Sample. For each question q, draw G = 16 outputs o1..G from the old policy. DeepSeek-AI 2025
  2. Grade. Reward = accuracy (boxed answer matches, or code passes tests) + format (reasoning inside <think>…</think>), equally weighted. DeepSeek-AI 2025
  3. Advantage and update (Eqs. 1–3):

JGRPO(θ) = E[ (1/G) Σi=1..G ( min( ρiAi, clip(ρi, 1−ε, 1+ε)Ai ) − β·DKL(πθ ‖ πref) ) ]

ρi = πθ(oi|q) / πold(oi|q)    Ai = ( ri − mean{r1..rG} ) / std{r1..rG}

DKL = πref(oi|q)/πθ(oi|q) − log( πref(oi|q)/πθ(oi|q) ) − 1

The clipped ratio is PPO's (the PPO review). The new part is Ai: the group-relative advantage needs no critic. R1-Zero used β = 0.001; in practice the ratio is applied per token and averaged with a 1/|oi| per response. DeepSeek-AI 2025 Worked example, rewards [2, 1, 1, 0]: mean 1.0, population std 0.7071, advantages [+1.414, 0, 0, −1.414]; the two middle answers get no gradient.

  1. From R1-Zero to R1. R1-Zero's traces were hard to read and mixed languages, so the released model adds four stages: a cold-start SFT on thousands of human-polished long reasoning examples; reasoning RL with an extra language-consistency reward; rejection sampling and SFT on about 800k samples (about 600k reasoning, 200k not); and a final RL stage for helpfulness and harmlessness using reward models. DeepSeek-AI 2025

Results

R1-Zero's AIME 2024 pass@1 rose from 15.6% to 77.9% over RL, and to 86.7% with majority voting; the v1 preprint reported 71.0% under its evaluation setup. DeepSeek-AI 2025 DeepSeek-AI 2025 Response length grew steadily during training: the model learned to think for longer, and an intermediate checkpoint wrote "Wait, wait. Wait. That's an aha moment I can flag here" before re-deriving a solution. DeepSeek-AI 2025 DeepSeek-R1: AIME 2024 79.8, MATH-500 97.3, Codeforces rating 2029 (96.3rd percentile), SWE-bench Verified 49.2, GPQA Diamond 71.5. DeepSeek-AI 2025 Distilling R1's 800k samples into Qwen-32B by SFT alone gave AIME 72.6, while running R1-Zero-style RL directly on Qwen-32B gave 47.0. DeepSeek-AI 2025

Why it mattered

R1 (January 2025) was the first open recipe and open weights for an o1-class reasoner, and GRPO with verifiable rewards became the default for the 2025 "RLVR" wave: DAPO (March 2025, review), Dr. GRPO, GSPO and ScaleRL (October 2025, review) are all edits to the objective above. Yu 2025 Khatri 2025 Its distillation result set the pattern for small models: RL makes the teacher, SFT makes the students.

Limitations

The authors list weak tool use and structured output, overthinking on simple questions, language mixing outside Chinese and English, sensitivity to few-shot prompts, limited software-engineering gains, and the difficulty of building reliable rewards for tasks such as writing. In the discussion they report that process reward models and MCTS both failed at scale: steps are hard to define and label, PRMs get hacked, and the token search space explodes. DeepSeek-AI 2025 Two months later, Dr. GRPO ("GRPO Done Right") argued the objective itself is biased: the 1/|oi| length normalisation gives long wrong answers a smaller per-token penalty, so responses drift longer; and dividing by the group std over-weights questions that are nearly all right or all wrong. Removing both terms reached 43.3% AIME 2024 with a 7B base in about a day on 8 A100s. The same paper found "aha"-style self-reflection already in DeepSeek-V3-Base before any RL. Liu 2025 Whether RLVR adds ability or only sharpens it is still contested: at k = 1024 samples the base model solved 13.3% of AIME24 problems the RL model never did, and 0.0% the other way. Yue 2025

How to read the paper

Read the v1 preprint, not the Nature version: Section 2.1 (GRPO), 2.2 (rewards), 2.3 with Figures 2–3 and Table 3 (the aha moment), then Section 2.3 of the R1 pipeline and Tables 4–5. Finish with Section 4 (distillation vs RL, and the unsuccessful attempts). Skip the safety and evaluation appendices. About 40 minutes.

Check yourself

Q1. What replaces PPO's value model in GRPO?

Ai = (ri − mean)/std over the G = 16 samples; no critic.

Q2. With rewards [2, 1, 1, 0], which answers get zero gradient?

They equal the group mean, so Ai = 0, even though one is correct and the other is not.

Q3. For a 32B model, which gave the higher AIME 2024 score?

Distillation from a larger model beat large-scale RL on the smaller model.

  2. Shao et al. DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning in Open Language Models (introduces GRPO). 2024. arXiv 2402.03300

2023 · Chi et al. · RSS 2023 / IJRR

Diffusion Policy: visuomotor policy learning via action diffusion

A robot policy that denoises a sequence of actions out of Gaussian noise, the way an image diffusion model denoises pixels, beat the best prior imitation methods by 46.9% on average across 12 simulated tasks and reached 95% success on a real Push-T task. Chi 2023

Taught in Day 10 · Read time of the original: ~60 min (the IJRR version is long; the RSS core is ~35 min)

In one sentence

Instead of outputting one action, the policy outputs a 16-step block of actions by running a learned denoiser from random noise, conditioned on the last two camera frames, which lets it copy demonstrations that go left or right without averaging them into "go straight". Chi 2023

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Imagine learning to draw an arm movement by starting from a page of scribbles and erasing the scribble a little at a time until a clean line appears. The eraser has watched thousands of good movements, so it knows which bits are noise. If the teacher sometimes went around the left of a cup and sometimes around the right, the eraser can produce either path, but never the silly one straight through the cup.

The problem

Behaviour cloning (Day 10) fits a network to "state → action" from human demonstrations. Humans are inconsistent: for the same scene one demo pushes a block from the left, another from the right. A Gaussian or mean-squared-error policy averages the two and pushes straight ahead, which fails. The standard fixes, mixture models (LSTM-GMM) and energy-based implicit policies (IBC), favour one mode or fail to commit, and IBC is unstable to train. Chi 2023 On the real Push-T task, the baselines scored 20% (LSTM-GMM) and 0% (IBC). Chi 2023

The key idea

Treat the action as something to generate, not to regress. A denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) learns to turn noise into samples from a data distribution in K small steps. Apply it to a short sequence of future actions, conditioned on recent observations, and you get a policy that can represent any shape of action distribution, including several separate modes, and that is trained with a plain regression loss. Chi 2023

How it works, step by step

  1. Inputs. The last To = 2 observations (camera images through a ResNet encoder, or low-dimensional state). Chi 2023
  2. Training. Take a ground-truth action block A0 of Tp = 16 steps from the demos, pick a noise level k, add Gaussian noise εk, and train the network εθ to predict the noise that was added. Chi 2023

L = MSE( εk, εθ(Ot, A0t + εk, k) )

  1. Inference. Start from AK ~ N(0, I) and repeat for k = K … 1 (Eq. 4 of the paper): Chi 2023

Ak−1 = α ( Ak − γ εθ(Ot, Ak, k) + N(0, σ2I) )

  1. Act. Execute the first Ta = 8 actions of the 16, then observe and re-plan (receding horizon). Training uses 100 diffusion iterations; at test time a DDIM sampler needs only 10, giving 0.1 s latency on an RTX 3080. Chi 2023
  2. Two backbones. A 1-D temporal U-Net with FiLM conditioning on the observation in every convolution layer, or a Transformer with cross-attention to observations and causal attention among action tokens. Chi 2023

Results

Across 12 tasks from 4 benchmarks (Robomimic, Push-T, Block Pushing, Franka Kitchen), the average improvement over the best prior method was 46.9%. Chi 2023 The journal version adds real-world tasks: Push-T 95% success and 0.80 IoU against 100% and 0.84 for the human demonstrator, with LSTM-GMM at 20% and IBC at 0%; plus mug flipping, sauce pouring and three bimanual tasks (egg beater, mat unrolling, shirt folding). Chi 2023 The encoder matters: with a frozen R3M encoder real Push-T drops to 80%, with ImageNet weights to 15%. Chi 2023 Figure 3 of the paper is the one to remember: on Push-T the policy takes the left route in some rollouts and the right in others, and commits to one per rollout. Chi 2023

Why it mattered

Diffusion Policy made generative action models the default head for robot imitation. π0 (Physical Intelligence, October 2024) kept the idea but swapped diffusion for flow matching: the network predicts a velocity field and 10 Euler steps carry noise to a 50-step action chunk, on top of a 3B vision-language model trained on more than 10,000 hours of robot data across 7 robot configurations and 68 tasks. Black 2024 Then came RL on top. Because a diffusion or flow policy's final-action likelihood is intractable, DPPO (September 2024) treats each denoising step as an action in an inner MDP and runs PPO there. Ren 2024 πRL (October 2025) does the same for flow policies with Flow-Noise and Flow-SDE, lifting π0 on LIBERO from 57.6% to 97.6% after few-shot fine-tuning. Chen 2025

Limitations

The authors say the method inherits behaviour cloning's limits: it cannot do better than the demonstrations and degrades when they are scarce, and they point to RL as the way to use suboptimal and negative data. Inference costs more than an LSTM-GMM, which action chunking only partly hides at high control rates. Chi 2023 The task count is quoted inconsistently across versions (11 in v1, 12 in v5, 15 in the full text once the bimanual tasks are counted); the 46.9% figure is the same in all. Chi 2023

How to read the paper

Read the abstract and Figure 1 (explicit vs implicit vs diffusion policies), then Section 2.3 for Eq. 4, Figure 2 for the two backbones, and Section 4.1 with Figure 3 for multimodality. Skim Tables 1–2 and read Table 6 (real Push-T). Skip Sections 6.2–7 unless you care about the bimanual hardware. About 40 minutes.

Check yourself

Q1. Why does a mean-squared-error policy fail on Push-T when demos go both left and right?

MSE regression predicts the mean action, which lies between the two modes and drives into the block.

Q2. What does the network εθ learn to predict during training?

Standard DDPM training: add noise εk, predict it back with an MSE loss.

Q3. Which numbers describe the receding-horizon setup?

To = 2, Tp = 16, Ta = 8; then re-plan.

References

  1. Chi, Xu, Feng, Cousineau, Du, Burchfiel, Tedrake, Song. Diffusion Policy: Visuomotor Policy Learning via Action Diffusion. RSS 2023; extended IJRR version. arXiv 2303.04137 · project page
  2. Black et al. π0: A Vision-Language-Action Flow Model for General Robot Control. 2024. arXiv 2410.24164
  3. Ren et al. Diffusion Policy Policy Optimization (DPPO). 2024. arXiv 2409.00588
  4. Chen et al. πRL: Online RL Fine-tuning for Flow-based Vision-Language-Action Models. 2025. arXiv 2510.25889
2023 · Rafailov et al. · Stanford (NeurIPS 2023)

DPO: Direct Preference Optimization, your language model is secretly a reward model

The RLHF objective has a closed-form optimum, and substituting it into the preference loss gives a plain classification loss on the policy, with no reward model and no sampling, that matched or beat PPO-RLHF on sentiment control, summarisation and dialogue at up to 6B parameters. Rafailov 2023

Taught in Day 12 · Read time of the original: ~40 min

In one sentence

Because the best KL-regularised policy for any reward can be written as the reference policy times exp(reward/β), you can run the equation backwards, read the reward off the policy, and train the policy directly to rank the human-preferred answer above the rejected one. Rafailov 2023

Explain it to a 10-year-old

In InstructGPT you first build a robot judge that copies the real judge, then practise against the robot. DPO skips the robot. It reads the judge's old scorecards ("this answer beat that one") and nudges you straight toward the winners and away from the losers, a little harder on the pairs you currently have backwards.

The problem

RLHF with PPO is expensive and fiddly. Four copies of a large model sit in memory (policy, value model, reference, reward model), the loop needs fresh samples from the policy at every step, and PPO is sensitive to hyperparameters. Rafailov 2023 The paper's abstract calls the standard pipeline "complex and often unstable". Rafailov 2023 Most of that machinery exists only to turn a dataset of pairwise preferences into a policy.

The key idea

Start from the RLHF objective (Eq. 3): maximise expected reward minus β times the KL divergence from the reference πref. Its optimum is known in closed form (Eq. 4):

πr(y|x) = (1/Z(x)) · πref(y|x) · exp( r(x,y) / β )

Z(x) sums over every possible response, so it cannot be computed. Invert it (Eq. 5):

r(x,y) = β·log( πr(y|x) / πref(y|x) ) + β·log Z(x)

Plug this into the Bradley–Terry preference model. Both answers in a pair share the prompt x, so they share Z(x), and it cancels in the difference r(x,yw) − r(x,yl). The reward model has vanished; what is left is a loss on the policy. Rafailov 2023

How it works, step by step

  1. Data. A fixed dataset of (prompt x, preferred yw, rejected yl) triples, usually produced by sampling from an SFT model and asking humans to choose. Rafailov 2023
  2. Two models. The trainable policy πθ, initialised from the SFT model, and a frozen copy πref.
  3. Loss (Eq. 7), minimised by ordinary gradient descent:

LDPO(πθ; πref) = −E(x,yw,yl)~D[ log σ( β·log πθ(yw|x)/πref(yw|x) − β·log πθ(yl|x)/πref(yl|x) ) ]

  1. Read the gradient. Each β·log(πθ/πref) is an implicit reward r̂θ. The gradient raises log πθ(yw|x), lowers log πθ(yl|x), and weights the pair by σ(r̂θ(x,yl) − r̂θ(x,yw)): how wrongly the implicit reward currently ranks it. The paper notes an unweighted version degenerates. Rafailov 2023
  2. Check by hand. β = 0.1, winner log-ratio +0.5, loser log-ratio −0.3: argument 0.1·0.8 = 0.08, σ(0.08) = 0.520, loss 0.654. Far from zero, so DPO keeps pushing until the margin is large. Rafailov 2023

Results

Three tasks. Controlled sentiment on IMDb with GPT-2-large: DPO reaches a strictly better reward-vs-KL frontier than PPO, even PPO given the ground-truth reward. Summarisation on Reddit TL;DR: about 61% win rate against human reference summaries at temperature 0, versus about 57% for PPO at its best temperature, judged by GPT-4. Single-turn dialogue on Anthropic HH with Pythia-2.8B: the only method to beat the preferred completions in the dataset. The paper did not meaningfully tune β for DPO and evaluates models "up to 6B parameters". Rafailov 2023

Why it mattered

DPO made preference tuning cheap enough for anyone with two copies of a model and a preference file, and became the default alignment step in open-weight releases through 2023–24. It also sharpened the vocabulary: "RLHF" is a KL-regularised objective, and DPO showed that solving it does not require RL. The counter-move came within a year: on-policy methods that do sample, such as RLOO (February 2024), beat DPO on TL;DR 77.9 vs 66.6 win rate with k = 4 samples. Ahmadian 2024 And the 2024–25 reasoning wave needed a verifier's 0/1 on fresh samples, which DPO cannot use (the DeepSeek-R1 review).

Limitations

Section 7 lists them: how DPO policies generalise out of distribution compared with an explicit reward model "needs more study"; whether the late-training decline in Figure 3 is reward over-optimisation; whether it works "orders of magnitude" beyond 6B; and that GPT-4 win rates depend on the judging prompt. Rafailov 2023 The structural limit is that DPO is off-policy: it only ever sees the pairs in the file, so it cannot explore, cannot improve on its data, and cannot use a programmatic reward (Day 12).

How to read the paper

Read the abstract and Figure 1, then Section 4 slowly (Eqs. 3–7 and the gradient paragraph); that is the whole paper. Look at Figure 2 and Section 6.1–6.2, then Section 7. Skip Section 5 and Appendix A unless you want the proof that the reparameterisation loses nothing. About 30 minutes.

Check yourself

Q1. Why does the intractable normaliser Z(x) not matter in DPO?

Z(x) depends only on x; the Bradley–Terry loss uses r(x,yw) − r(x,yl), so it drops out.

Q2. How many model copies does DPO need in memory?

No reward model and no value model; only πθ and πref.

Q3. Which statement about DPO is true?

DPO is off-policy and offline; experiments stop at 6B.

References

  1. Rafailov, Sharma, Mitchell, Ermon, Manning, Finn. Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model. 2023 (v3 July 2024). arXiv 2305.18290 · full text
  2. Ouyang et al. Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback. 2022. arXiv 2203.02155
  3. Ahmadian et al. Back to Basics: Revisiting REINFORCE-Style Optimization for Learning from Human Feedback in LLMs (RLOO). 2024. arXiv 2402.14740
  4. DeepSeek-AI. DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning. 2025. arXiv 2501.12948
2015 · Mnih et al. · Nature 518:529–533 (arXiv 1312.5602, Dec 2013)

DQN: Human-level control through deep RL

One convolutional network, one set of hyperparameters, 49 Atari games learned from pixels and score alone, at a level "comparable to that of a professional human games tester".

Taught in Day 6 · Read time of the original: ~40 min (5 pages plus Methods)

In one sentence

DQN is Watkins's Q-learning with a deep convolutional network as the Q table, kept stable by two tricks, a replay memory of past transitions and a slowly updated copy of the network for computing targets; it beat the best prior methods on 43 of 49 games and reached at least 75% of a professional tester's score on 29. Mnih 2015

Explain it to a 10-year-old

A computer learns to play old TV games by looking only at the screen and the score, the way you would. It keeps a diary of moments it has seen and re-reads random pages instead of only the last one, so it does not fixate on today. And it grades its new guesses against a photocopy of its older self, taken every so often, so the target it is chasing stays still long enough to hit.

The problem

Combining Q-learning with a neural network was known to be unstable. The Nature paper names the causes: consecutive observations are correlated; small changes to Q can change the policy and so the data distribution; and the Q values are correlated with their own targets r + γ maxa′ Q(s′,a′). Mnih 2015 In Sutton and Barto's terms, this is the deadly triad: function approximation, bootstrapping and off-policy learning all at once. Sutton & Barto 2018 The best Atari agents before DQN were linear learners over hand-built features (Bellemare et al. 2012, the baseline in Figure 3). The December 2013 arXiv version was the first crack: seven games, "outperforms all previous approaches on six of the games and surpasses a human expert on three of them". Mnih 2013

The key idea

Two stabilisers around a plain Q-learning loss. Experience replay stores transitions and trains on random minibatches drawn from the store, which "breaks these correlations and therefore reduces the variance of the updates" and averages the training distribution over many past behaviours. Mnih 2013 A target network with parameters θ−, copied from the online network only every C steps, computes the targets, so an update to Q no longer moves its own target immediately. Replay only works because Q-learning is off-policy: the replayed actions came from older policies. Mnih 2015

How it works, step by step

  1. Preprocess. Take the 210×160 colour frame, max over two consecutive frames to remove flicker, convert to luminance, rescale to 84×84, stack the last 4 frames: input 84×84×4. The agent acts every 4th frame. Mnih 2015
  2. Q-network. Conv 32 filters 8×8 stride 4, conv 64 filters 4×4 stride 2, conv 64 filters 3×3 stride 1, each with ReLU; fully connected 512 units; a linear output per valid action (4 to 18). One forward pass gives all Q values. Mnih 2015
  3. Act ε-greedily, ε annealed from 1.0 to 0.1 over the first million frames, then fixed. Mnih 2015
  4. Store (φt, at, rt, φt+1) in a replay memory holding the last 1 million frames. Rewards are clipped to +1, −1 or 0 during training. Mnih 2015
  5. Learn. Sample 32 transitions uniformly and minimise the squared TD error, with the target network held fixed between copies:

Li(θi) = E(s,a,r,s′)∼U(D) [ ( r + γ maxa′ Q(s′,a′; θi−) − Q(s,a; θi) )2 ]

  1. The error term is clipped to [−1, 1], which the authors found "further improved the stability"; the optimiser is RMSProp, γ = 0.99. Every C steps set θ− ← θ. Mnih 2015 The restated hyperparameters are C = 10,000 updates and learning rate 0.00025. van Hasselt 2015
  2. Train for 50 million frames per game, about 38 days of play; the 2013 version used 10 million. Mnih 2015 Mnih 2013

Results

Evaluation: 30 episodes of up to 5 minutes with ε = 0.05, against a professional tester who practised about 2 hours. Scores are normalised as 100 × (DQN − random)/(human − random). DQN beat the best existing RL methods on 43 of 49 games and scored at or above 75% of the human on 29. Mnih 2015 The spread is enormous; a few raw scores as restated in the Double DQN paper: van Hasselt 2015

GameRandomHumanDQNNormalised
Video Pinball16,256.917,297.642,684.1≈2,539%
Breakout1.731.8401.2≈1,327%
Pong−20.79.318.9≈132%
Montezuma's Revenge0.04,366.70.00%

Why it mattered

Spinning Up calls DQN "a classic which substantially launched the field of deep RL". Achiam 2018 Within a year the components were improved one at a time: Double DQN (September 2015) evaluated the arg-max with the target network and raised the median normalised score from 93.5% to 114.7%; prioritised replay (November 2015) improved 41 of 49 games; the dueling architecture (November 2015) split V and A. van Hasselt 2015 Schaul 2015 Wang 2015 Rainbow (2017) combined six of them for a median of 223% against DQN's 79%, and matched DQN's final score after 7 of its 200 million frames. Hessel 2017 Agent57 (2020) was the first to beat the human benchmark on all 57 games. Badia 2020

Limitations

Fifty million frames per game is about 38 days of play; a human needs hours. Mnih 2015 Exploration is ε-greedy, so sparse-reward games score zero (Montezuma's Revenge); RND's exploration bonus reached 8,152 there in 2018. Burda 2018 The max in the target overestimates: Double DQN measured overestimation in all 49 games. van Hasselt 2015 Reward clipping means the agent "cannot differentiate between rewards of different magnitude". Mnih 2015 Actions must be discrete and few. And "one network" means one architecture: weights were reset and trained separately for each game. Sutton & Barto 2018 Stability is empirical; the deadly triad has no convergence theorem here.

How to read the paper

Main text first (20 min): the opening page for the three instability causes, Figure 1, Figure 3, and Figure 2's learning curves. Then Methods (20 min): "Model architecture", "Training details", the loss with θ−, and Extended Data Table 3, the ablation that removes replay and the target network in turn. Skip the t-SNE figure. The 2013 arXiv paper is a good second read: its Algorithm 1 is the whole method in a dozen lines, before the target network was added. Mnih 2013

Check yourself

Q1. On how many of the 49 games did DQN reach at least 75% of the human tester's score?

29 of 49 at ≥75%; 43 of 49 beat the best previous RL methods; 7 was the 2013 game count.

Q2. "The target network is a second network trained on its own loss." What is it really?

θ⁻ ← θ every C steps; between copies it is frozen. Its job is to keep the regression target still.

Q3. Why does experience replay require an off-policy learner?

Q-learning's target uses max over next actions, so it does not care which policy produced the transition. An on-policy target like Sarsa's would be wrong for stale data.

2025 · Hafner et al. · Nature 640:647–653 (arXiv 2301.04104) · Dreamer 4: arXiv 2509.24527

DreamerV3 and Dreamer 4: learning inside a world model

One fixed configuration learned over 150 tasks across 8 domains and was the first to collect Minecraft diamonds from scratch; Dreamer 4 (2025) collected diamonds from 2,541 hours of offline video alone, in 0.7% of episodes.

Taught in Day 9 · Read time of the original: ~40 min (V3) + ~30 min (Dreamer 4)

In one sentence

Dreamer learns a compressed model of the world from replayed experience, then trains its actor and critic entirely on imagined rollouts inside that model; V3 made this work with the same hyperparameters everywhere by normalising every quantity, and Dreamer 4 scaled the model to a 2-billion-parameter transformer that learns from video.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Before you step onto ice you imagine slipping, and you walk differently because of it. Dreamer watches what happens when it acts, builds a small imaginary world in its head, and then practises thousands of futures there, which is much cheaper than practising for real. Dreamer 4 learned its imaginary Minecraft mostly by watching videos of other people playing, and then practised inside it until it could find diamonds, something no player manages by luck.

The problem

Model-free agents need huge numbers of real interactions, and every earlier model-based agent needed per-domain tuning: different reward scales, different loss weights, different horizons. DreamerV2 (2020) had reached a median of 2.15 gamer-normalised on 55 Atari games against Rainbow's 1.47, but only on Atari. Hafner 2020 Minecraft's diamond task, a 12-item chain with sparse rewards and episodes of up to 36,000 steps, had never been solved from scratch. Hafner 2023

The key idea

Make every signal the networks see live on the same scale, so one configuration fits all domains. V3 does this with symlog transforms of inputs and targets, a critic that predicts a distribution over bins instead of a number, returns normalised by their 5th–95th percentile range, and KL losses clipped below 1 nat so they switch off once small. Hafner 2023 Dreamer 4 keeps the imagination loop and swaps the recurrent model for a transformer trained with shortcut forcing, so it stays accurate over long rollouts and fast enough to run in real time. Hafner 2025

How it works, step by step

  1. World model (RSSM). An encoder maps the image xt to a discrete latent zt; a recurrent sequence model ht = f(ht−1, zt−1, at−1) carries memory; a dynamics predictor guesses ẑt from ht alone; heads from (ht, zt) decode the image, predict reward and predict whether the episode continues. Hafner 2023
  2. Loss. Prediction loss (decoder, reward, continue) with weight 1; dynamics loss, pulling the prior toward the posterior, weight 1; representation loss, pulling the posterior toward the prior, weight 0.1; both KL terms floored at 1 nat ("free bits") and smoothed with 1% uniform noise. Hafner 2023

    symlog(x) = sign(x) · ln(|x| + 1), symexp = its inverse

  3. Imagine. Start from replayed latent states and roll the dynamics predictor forward T = 16 steps, choosing actions with the actor. No pixels are produced. Hafner 2023
  4. Actor-critic. The critic predicts a categorical distribution over exponentially spaced bins with two-hot regression; returns are divided by max(1, S) where S is the 5th–95th percentile range; the actor uses the REINFORCE estimator for both discrete and continuous actions. Hafner 2023
  5. Dreamer 4. A ~400M-parameter tokenizer compresses frames; a ~1.6B block-causal transformer (spatial attention within a frame, temporal attention once every 4 layers) predicts the next tokens given interleaved actions. Shortcut forcing trains it on noised representations conditioned on noise level and step size and predicts the clean representation, so inference needs only K = 4 forward passes per frame. Three phases: pretrain on video (and actions when available), fine-tune policy and reward heads by behaviour cloning, then imagination training with the transformer frozen and a sign-of-advantage objective (PMPO). Hafner 2025

Results

With one set of hyperparameters, V3 covered 8 domains: Atari (57 games), ProcGen (16), DMLab (30), Atari100k (26), Proprio Control (18), Visual Control (20), BSuite (23 environments, 468 configurations) and Minecraft, "over 150 diverse tasks", outperforming the tuned specialist on each benchmark summary. Hafner 2023 Across six model sizes from 12M to 400M parameters, "increasing the model size directly translates to both higher task performance and a lower data requirement". Hafner 2023 Every Dreamer run discovered diamonds in Minecraft within 100M environment steps, with no human data or curriculum, on one A100 GPU for 9 days. Hafner 2023 The ablations rank the KL objective as the most important robustness technique, then return normalisation and the two-hot critic. Hafner 2023

Dreamer 4 trained on the 2,541-hour VPT contractor dataset (video plus actions) and never touched the game during training; it reaches diamonds in 0.7% of 60-minute episodes and the iron pickaxe in 29%, a task that takes humans about 20,000 to 24,000 mouse and keyboard actions. A fine-tuned VPT gets as far as sticks 53% of the time and a Gemma-3 vision-language-action baseline reaches the iron pickaxe in 11%. Hafner 2025 The authors call this "100x less data" than VPT's 270K hours of YouTube video; training ran on 256 to 1024 TPU-v5p chips, and the finished world model runs interactively in real time on a single GPU. Hafner 2025

Why it mattered

DreamerV3 was the first general RL algorithm whose selling point was "no tuning", and its 2025 Nature publication made world models respectable as a route to generality rather than a curiosity. Hafner 2025a DayDreamer (2022) had already put the loop on hardware, with a quadruped walking in about 1 hour without a simulator. Wu 2022 Dreamer 4 ties the line to video-trained generative models: if the model can be learned from recorded play, the agent can be trained before it ever acts, which is the setting robots live in. Hafner 2025

Limitations

Imagination is capped at 16 steps because model errors compound, so the agent cannot plan long chains explicitly; it relies on the critic to summarise them. Hafner 2023 V3 spends capacity reconstructing pixels, which MuZero and TD-MPC2 avoid (the MuZero review). Dreamer 4's diamond rate is 0.7%, a proof of existence rather than a reliable skill, and its "100×" counts only labelled hours. Hafner 2025 As of October 2026 there is no independent replication of the offline diamond result.

How to read the paper

V3: Figure 1 (the benchmark summary), then "Learning algorithm" for the world model, critic and actor, with Figure 3 beside you; the "Robust predictions" subsection is the heart of it. Skim "Ablations" and "Scaling properties". Dreamer 4: Figure 2 for the architecture, Section 3.3 for imagination training, Section 4.1 and Figure 3 for the challenge. About 70 minutes together.

Check yourself

Q1. What does symlog(x) = sign(x)·ln(|x|+1) buy DreamerV3?

Symlog compresses large magnitudes of either sign while staying near the identity around zero, so inputs and targets across domains land on comparable scales.

Q2. In what fraction of episodes did Dreamer 4 obtain diamonds, having never interacted with Minecraft during training?

0.7%. 29% is the iron pickaxe, 53% is fine-tuned VPT reaching sticks, 11% is the Gemma-3 baseline at the iron pickaxe.

Q3. Why does Dreamer stop imagined rollouts at 16 steps?

A one-step model feeds its own output back as input; small errors grow. Short horizons plus a learned critic is the standard remedy.

  2. Hafner, Yan, Lillicrap. Training Agents Inside of Scalable World Models (Dreamer 4). 29 Sep 2025. arXiv 2509.24527
  3. Hafner et al. Mastering Atari with Discrete World Models (DreamerV2). 2020. arXiv 2010.02193
