2021 · Chen, Lu et al. · arXiv 2106.01345 (Berkeley / Facebook AI / Google)

Decision Transformer: RL via sequence modelling

A causal GPT trained to predict actions given the return it should achieve: no value function, no policy gradient, yet 74.7 average on D4RL to CQL's 63.9 and 94.6% on Key-to-Door where CQL reached 13.3%.

Taught in Day 10 · Read time of the original: ~35 min

In one sentence

Decision Transformer turns offline RL into supervised sequence modelling: feed a Transformer the trajectory as (return-to-go, state, action) tokens, train it to predict the action, and at test time ask for a high return and let it autocomplete the actions that would earn it.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Your phone's autocomplete has read millions of game recordings where every move is labelled with "how many points were still to come". Now you type "this game ends with 1,000 points, the board looks like this, next move is…" and it fills in the move. It never learned what "good" means; it learned what players who went on to score 1,000 did next.

The problem

Offline RL methods of 2020 fight extrapolation error with conservatism or constraints and inherit the machinery of temporal-difference learning: bootstrapped targets, target networks, instability (the CQL review). Kumar 2020 GPT-style Transformers, meanwhile, were scaling smoothly on language. Can the supervised recipe replace TD learning when the data is fixed?

The key idea

Condition on the outcome you want. Replace rewards with the return-to-go R̂t = Σt'≥t rt', the reward still to come, and model the sequence (R̂1, s1, a1, R̂2, s2, a2, …) with a causally masked Transformer. The abstract puts it directly: "by conditioning an autoregressive model on the desired return (reward), past states, and actions, our Decision Transformer model can generate future actions that achieve the desired return". Chen 2021

How it works, step by step

  1. Tokens. Each timestep contributes three tokens, return-to-go, state and action, so the last K timesteps give 3K tokens. Each modality has its own linear embedding (a convolutional encoder for images) and a learned per-timestep embedding is added to all three tokens of a step. Chen 2021
  2. Model and loss. A GPT with a causal mask; the output at the state token predicts the action, with mean-squared error for continuous actions or cross-entropy for discrete ones. Predicting states or returns did not improve performance. Chen 2021

    R̂t = Σt'=tT rt'; loss = Σt ‖ at − DT(R̂≤t, s≤t, a<t) ‖²

  3. Rollout. Set a target return (for example the dataset's best, or more), generate an action, step the environment, subtract the reward received from the target, append the new tokens and repeat until the episode ends. Chen 2021
  4. Sizes. Atari: 6 layers, 8 heads, embedding 128, context K = 30 (50 for Pong). Gym: 3 layers, 1 head, embedding 128, K = 20 (5 for Reacher). Chen 2021

Results

On Atari with 1% of the DQN-replay data (gamer-normalised), DT beat CQL on Breakout (267.5 vs 211.1) and Seaquest (2.5 vs 1.7), lost on Qbert (15.4 vs 104.2) and roughly tied on Pong (106.1 vs 111.9). Chen 2021 On D4RL gym it averaged 74.7 to CQL's 63.9 without Reacher and 69.2 to 54.2 over all settings. Chen 2021 On Key-to-Door, a task that needs credit for an early pickup to reach a late reward, DT succeeded 71.8% of the time with 1K random trajectories and 94.6% with 10K, against 13.1% and 13.3% for CQL. Chen 2021 Context matters: with K = 1, Breakout fell from 267.5 to 73.9 and Pong from 106.1 to 2.5. Chen 2021 Figure 4 shows achieved return tracking the requested return, and on Seaquest the model could be asked for more than the dataset's best and sometimes delivered it. Chen 2021

Why it mattered

DT and the Trajectory Transformer, posted one day apart in June 2021, made "RL as sequence modelling" a research programme and gave offline RL a method that scales the way language models do. Janner 2021 The habit of writing actions as tokens in a Transformer stream is now the default in robot foundation models: RT-2 (July 2023) emits actions as 8 integer tokens in the same vocabulary as text. Brohan 2023 In Day 10 DT is the counterpoint to CQL: outcome conditioning instead of value estimation.

Limitations

There is no value function, so DT cannot in general stitch together sub-trajectories that never co-occurred; in the paper's shortest-path example only 15.8% of generated paths were stitched from suboptimal segments, and the Qbert result shows TD methods winning when the data is poor. Chen 2021 The target return is a knob the user must set, and asking for the impossible can produce arbitrary behaviour. The authors flag stochastic environments as a weakness (future work on return distributions) and warn that "reward design by nefarious actors can potentially generate unintended behaviors". Chen 2021 Later work found IQL and other TD methods ahead on the stitching-heavy AntMaze tasks. Kostrikov 2021

How to read the paper

Figure 1 and Section 3 (one page, with pseudocode) are the whole method. Then Tables 1–2 and Figure 4, and the Section 5 discussions: is it just behaviour cloning, long-term credit assignment, context length. Skip Section 6. About 35 minutes.

Check yourself

Q1. What are the three tokens per timestep in a Decision Transformer?

Return-to-go (the reward still to come), state and action; no values or advantages are ever estimated.

Q2. On Key-to-Door with 10K trajectories, DT vs CQL success rates were:

94.6% vs 13.3% at 10K; 71.8% vs 13.1% at 1K. The other pairs are D4RL averages and Breakout scores.

Q3. "Decision Transformer learns a value function implicitly." Which statement is accurate?

DT conditions on the desired return; predicting returns was tried and did not help. Without a learned value, combining never-seen fragments is not guaranteed.

References

  1. Chen, Lu, Rajeswaran, Lee, Grover, Laskin, Abbeel, Srinivas, Mordatch. Decision Transformer: Reinforcement Learning via Sequence Modeling. Jun 2021. arXiv 2106.01345
  2. Janner, Li, Levine. Offline RL as One Big Sequence Modeling Problem (Trajectory Transformer). 2021. arXiv 2106.02039
  3. Kumar, Zhou, Tucker, Levine. Conservative Q-Learning for Offline RL. 2020. arXiv 2006.04779
  4. Kostrikov, Nair, Levine. Offline RL with Implicit Q-Learning. 2021. arXiv 2110.06169
  5. Brohan et al. RT-2: Vision-Language-Action Models Transfer Web Knowledge to Robotic Control. 2023. arXiv 2307.15818
2022 · Ouyang et al. · OpenAI (NeurIPS 2022)

InstructGPT: training language models to follow instructions with human feedback

Three steps (supervised fine-tuning, a reward model trained on human rankings, PPO against that reward model) turned GPT-3 into a model whose 1.3B-parameter version humans preferred over the original 175B GPT-3, "despite having 100x fewer parameters". Ouyang 2022

Taught in Day 12 · Read time of the original: ~50 min (the main text; the appendices double it)

In one sentence

Humans cannot write a reward function for "helpful, honest and harmless", but they can say which of two answers is better; InstructGPT trains a network to imitate those judgements and then uses PPO, with a KL leash to the starting model, to make the language model score higher on it. Ouyang 2022

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Picture a spelling-bee judge who cannot tell you the right word but can always say which of two attempts sounded better. First you build a robot that copies the judge's taste. Then you practise against the robot thousands of times, doing more of what it likes. One rule: you may improve, but you may not turn into a completely different kid overnight. That rule is the KL leash.

The problem

GPT-3 predicted the next token of internet text. Asked "Explain the moon landing to a 6-year-old", it was as likely to produce more questions as an explanation. The paper's framing is that the language-modelling objective is misaligned with what users want: bigger models did not become more helpful, and they still produced untruthful, toxic or unhelpful output. Ouyang 2022 Learning a reward from pairwise human comparisons had already worked for Atari and simulated locomotion in 2017, using feedback on less than 1% of the agent's interactions. Christiano 2017 InstructGPT applied it to a 175B-parameter language model.

The key idea

Treat the language model as a policy (Day 12): state = prompt plus tokens so far, action = next token, one reward at the end of the response. Replace the missing reward function with a reward model learned from human rankings, and optimise it with PPO (the PPO review) while penalising distance from the supervised starting point so the policy cannot wander into regions where the reward model is wrong. Ouyang 2022

How it works, step by step

  1. SFT. About 40 contractors wrote demonstrations for roughly 13k prompts; GPT-3 is fine-tuned on them with ordinary supervised learning. Ouyang 2022
  2. Reward model. For about 33k prompts, labelers rank K = 4 to 9 sampled outputs. A 6B model (the paper only ever uses 6B reward models; the 175B one trained unstably) learns a scalar rθ(x, y) with the Bradley–Terry loss (Eq. 1): Ouyang 2022

loss(θ) = −1/C(K,2) · E(x,yw,yl)[ log σ( rθ(x, yw) − rθ(x, yl) ) ]

Each ranking yields C(K,2) pairs; dividing by that count gives every prompt equal weight. Check it by hand: winner scored 2.0, loser 0.5 gives σ(1.5) = 0.818 and loss 0.201; backwards, σ(−1.5) = 0.182 and loss 1.70. Ouyang 2022

  1. PPO. On about 31k prompts, sample a response, score it with rθ, and update with PPO. The objective (Eq. 2, "PPO-ptx"): Ouyang 2022

objective(φ) = E(x,y)~πφ[ rθ(x,y) − β·log( πφ(y|x) / πSFT(y|x) ) ] + γ·Ex~pretrain[ log πφ(x) ]

The β term is a per-token KL penalty toward the frozen SFT model. The γ term mixes in pretraining loss so the model keeps its general skills; plain "PPO" has γ = 0. Four networks live in memory: the policy and PPO's value model (trained), the reference and the reward model (frozen). Ouyang 2022

Results

Labelers preferred the 175B InstructGPT over 175B GPT-3 about 85% of the time (±3%), and preferred even the 1.3B PPO-ptx model over the 175B GPT-3. Ouyang 2022 On closed-domain tasks InstructGPT hallucinated about half as often (21% vs 41%), and produced about 25% fewer toxic outputs when told to be respectful; the toxicity gain vanished without that instruction and bias benchmarks did not improve. Ouyang 2022 Plain PPO regressed on some public NLP benchmarks (the "alignment tax"); PPO-ptx reduced the regression but still lagged GPT-3 on DROP, SQuADv2 and translation. Ouyang 2022

Why it mattered

InstructGPT is the recipe behind ChatGPT (November 2022) and, with small changes, behind most assistant models since. It also set the cost structure everyone then tried to escape: four large models in memory and a slow sampling loop. DPO (May 2023) removed the reward model and the sampling (the DPO review). Rafailov 2023 GRPO (2024–25) removed the value model and, for maths and code, replaced the learned reward with a verifier (the DeepSeek-R1 review). DeepSeek-AI 2025

Limitations

The authors say the models "are neither fully aligned nor fully safe": they still fabricate facts and follow harmful instructions. The preferences come from about 40 mostly English-speaking contractors, most comparisons were labelled by a single person, and the data is almost all English, so "aligned" means aligned to that group. Ouyang 2022 Later work found two systematic reward-model failures: preference data favours answers that agree with the user (sycophancy), and reward gains in RLHF mostly track response length. Sharma 2023 Singhal 2023

How to read the paper

Read the abstract, Figure 1 and Figure 2, then Section 3.5 (the three models and Eqs. 1–2) and Section 4.1. Section 5.3 (Limitations) is short and honest. Skip Section 3.4 (labeler recruitment) and the appendices unless you plan to run RLHF yourself. About 35 minutes.

Check yourself

Q1. Which of the three steps is reinforcement learning?

Steps 1 and 2 are supervised learning. Only step 3 samples from the policy and optimises a reward.

Q2. How large was the reward model used for the 175B policy?

The paper uses only 6B reward models; the 175B one trained unstably.

Q3. What does the β term in the PPO objective do?

β weights the KL penalty toward πSFT; γ is the pretraining-mix term.

References

  1. Ouyang, Wu, Jiang, Almeida, Wainwright, Mishkin, Zhang, Agarwal, Slama, Ray, Schulman, Hilton, Kelton, Miller, Simens, Askell, Welinder, Christiano, Leike, Lowe. Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback. 2022. arXiv 2203.02155 · full text
  2. Christiano, Leike, Brown, Martic, Legg, Amodei. Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences. 2017. arXiv 1706.03741
  3. Rafailov et al. Direct Preference Optimization. 2023. arXiv 2305.18290
  4. Sharma et al. Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models. 2023. arXiv 2310.13548; Singhal et al. A Long Way to Go: Investigating Length Correlations in RLHF. 2023. arXiv 2310.03716
2020 · Schrittwieser et al. · Nature 588 (arXiv 1911.08265, Nov 2019)

MuZero: Planning with a learned model

AlphaZero's search run inside a learned latent model, with no rules given: median 2041.1% human-normalised on 57 Atari games (R2D2: 1920.6%) and AlphaZero-level Elo in Go, chess and shogi.

Taught in Day 9 · Read time of the original: ~50 min

In one sentence

MuZero learns three networks, one that encodes observations into a hidden state, one that steps the hidden state forward given an action and predicts the reward, and one that reads a policy and value off any hidden state, and runs Monte Carlo tree search entirely in that hidden space, training the model only to be right about rewards, values and policies, never about pixels.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

AlphaGo was given the rulebook so it could imagine future moves. MuZero is not. It builds its own imaginary version of the game in its head, one that looks nothing like the real screen but is good at answering the questions that matter: "what score will I get?" and "which moves look good?" Then it plans inside that imaginary game.

The problem

AlphaZero planned with a perfect simulator: the rules of Go, chess and shogi. Silver 2017 Most problems have no such simulator, and learned pixel-space models had not matched model-free methods on Atari: a model that gets every pixel right wastes capacity on what does not affect the score and still drifts over long rollouts (the compounding error of Day 9). What must a model predict for planning to work?

The key idea

Only what the search uses. The hidden state is under no obligation to reconstruct the observation or match the true environment state; it may represent whatever helps predict rewards, values and policies. Schrittwieser 2019 Training the model end to end on those three targets, through the same unrolled search that will later use it, makes the model and the planner agree by construction.

How it works, step by step

  1. Three functions. Representation h: past observations o1..t → root hidden state s0. Dynamics g: (sk, a) → (reward rk, next hidden state sk+1). Prediction f: sk → (policy pk, value vk). Schrittwieser 2019
  2. Plan. From s0, run MCTS as in AlphaZero but every edge is one call to g and every new node one call to f. Selection uses a pUCT rule with constants c1 = 1.25 and c2 = 19652; because Atari values are unbounded, Q is rescaled to [0, 1] with the minimum and maximum seen in the tree so far. 800 simulations per move in board games, 50 in Atari. Schrittwieser 2019
  3. Act. Sample the real action from the root visit-count distribution πt; store the observation, action, reward and search statistics.
  4. Train. Pick a stored position, unroll the model K = 5 steps along the actions that were actually taken, and match each step's outputs to what happened. Schrittwieser 2019

    L = Σk=0..K [ ℓp(πt+k, pk) + ℓv(zt+k, vk) + ℓr(ut+k, rk) ] + c‖θ‖²

    Here z is the game outcome (board games) or an n-step return (Atari), u the observed reward, π the search policy.
  5. Networks. h and g each use 16 residual blocks with 256 planes, against 20 blocks in AlphaZero; Atari training uses batches of 1024 and a replay of the latest 125 thousand sequences of 200 steps. Schrittwieser 2019

Results

On Atari at 20.0 billion frames, MuZero reached a median human-normalised score of 2041.1% and a mean of 4999.2%, against 1920.6% and 4024.9% for R2D2 at 37.5 billion frames (Table 1). Schrittwieser 2019 In the small-data setting, MuZero Reanalyze, which re-runs search on stored trajectories to refresh their targets, reached a median of 731.1% at 200 million frames, against 231.1% for Rainbow and 431% for LASER. Schrittwieser 2019 In chess and shogi it matched AlphaZero's Elo and in Go slightly exceeded it while using less computation per node (16 residual blocks against 20). Schrittwieser 2019 Compute: 16 TPUs for training and 1000 for self-play per board game; 8 and 32 per Atari game. Schrittwieser 2019 Go strength rose by more than 1000 Elo as thinking time went from 0.1 to 50 seconds per move. DeepMind 2020

Why it mattered

MuZero settled what a world model is for: in late 2019 it showed that a model trained only on value-relevant targets can plan as well as the true rules. Schrittwieser 2019 The decoder-free idea returns in TD-MPC2 (2023); the Dreamer line kept a decoder and found it useful (the Dreamer review). Hansen 2023

Limitations

The dynamics function is deterministic, one (s, a) gives one next state, which fits board games better than stochastic worlds. The compute is enormous (20 billion frames per Atari game on 40 TPUs), and the model is trained only along actions actually taken, so its predictions on the untried branches the search visits are extrapolations. Schrittwieser 2019 Reanalyze cuts the data need by about 100× but not the compute. Schrittwieser 2019

How to read the paper

Figure 1 first, slowly; it is the whole method. Then Section 3 for the loss, Appendix B for the search, Table 1 and Figure 2 for results. Skip Appendices D–G unless implementing; read Appendix H (Reanalyze) if you care about sample efficiency. About 50 minutes.

Check yourself

Q1. What is MuZero's hidden state required to predict?

The paper imposes no reconstruction or state-matching constraint; the hidden state may be anything that predicts rewards, values and policies.

Q2. MuZero's Atari median human-normalised score at 20 billion frames was about:

2041.1% median (4999.2% mean). 731.1% is Reanalyze at 200M frames; 231.1% is Rainbow.

Q3. "MuZero and AlphaZero are the same algorithm." What is the real difference?

Both search with MCTS and train from self-play; MuZero replaces the rule-based simulator with learned h, g, f, and so also runs on Atari.

References

  1. Schrittwieser et al. Mastering Atari, Go, chess and shogi by planning with a learned model. Nature 588, 23 Dec 2020. arXiv 1911.08265 · nature.com
  2. DeepMind. MuZero: Mastering Go, chess, shogi and Atari without rules. Blog, 23 Dec 2020. deepmind.google
  3. Silver et al. Mastering Chess and Shogi by Self-Play with a General RL Algorithm (AlphaZero). 2017. arXiv 1712.01815
  4. Hansen, Su, Wang. TD-MPC2: Scalable, Robust World Models for Continuous Control. 2023. arXiv 2310.16828
2017 · Schulman et al. · OpenAI (arXiv 1707.06347)

PPO: Proximal policy optimization

Clip the new-to-old probability ratio to [1−ε, 1+ε] with ε = 0.2, run several epochs of minibatch SGD on each batch, and you keep most of TRPO's reliability in first-order code: 0.82 against −0.39 for the unclipped objective on seven MuJoCo tasks.

Taught in Day 8 · Read time of the original: ~45 min (8 pages plus appendix)

In one sentence

PPO replaces TRPO's KL constraint with a clipped surrogate objective that "removes the incentive for moving rt outside of the interval [1−ε, 1+ε]", which makes it safe to perform "multiple epochs of minibatch updates" on the same batch, something standard policy gradients cannot do. Schulman 2017

Explain it to a 10-year-old

A coach watches you practise and says "good, you've improved enough on that move for today, no extra credit for overdoing it". Because the coach stops you from changing too much at once, you can safely study the same practice video several times before the next game, instead of watching it once and throwing it away.

The problem

The paper opens with a scorecard. Deep Q-learning "fails on many simple problems and is poorly understood"; vanilla policy gradients "have poor data efficiency and robustness"; TRPO "is relatively complicated, and is not compatible with architectures that include noise (such as dropout) or parameter sharing". Schulman 2017 The root issue is the one the TRPO review describes: a policy gradient step of the wrong size collapses the policy, and vanilla methods take exactly one gradient step per sample, so they cannot reuse data without risking that collapse. TRPO's fix needs a conjugate-gradient solve every update.

The key idea

Write the surrogate in terms of the probability ratio rt(θ) = πθ(at|st) / πθold(at|st), so r = 1 at the start of each update. Then take the minimum of the unclipped term and a term whose ratio is clipped to [1−ε, 1+ε]. The minimum makes the objective "a lower bound (i.e., a pessimistic bound) on the unclipped objective": once the ratio has moved beyond the band in the direction the advantage favours, the gradient is zero, but a move that makes things worse is never ignored. Schulman 2017

How it works, step by step

  1. Each of N actors runs the frozen policy πθold for T steps (T = 2048 for MuJoCo with one actor; T = 128 with 8 actors for Atari). Schulman 2017
  2. Compute advantages Ât with truncated GAE, γ = 0.99, λ = 0.95; with λ = 1 this is A3C's k-step estimator. Schulman 2017
  3. Optimise the clipped surrogate over K epochs of minibatches (10 epochs of 64 for MuJoCo; 3 epochs for Atari):

LCLIP(θ) = Êt[ min( rt(θ) Ât , clip(rt(θ), 1−ε, 1+ε) Ât ) ]

  1. When the policy and value heads share parameters, use the combined loss with a value term and an entropy bonus (c1 = 1, c2 = 0.01 on Atari):

LtCLIP+VF+S(θ) = Êt[ LtCLIP(θ) − c1 (Vθ(st) − Vttarg)2 + c2 S[πθ](st) ]

  1. Set θold ← θ, discard the batch, repeat. Adam, learning rate 3 × 10−4 (MuJoCo) or 2.5 × 10−4 annealed to zero (Atari). Schulman 2017

Work one term by hand with ε = 0.2, so the band is [0.8, 1.2]. Â = +2, r = 1.5: unclipped 3.0, clipped 1.2 × 2 = 2.4, min = 2.4, flat in r, so no further push. Â = +2, r = 0.6: unclipped 1.2, clipped 1.6, min = 1.2, gradient active, pulling r back up. Â = −2, r = 1.5: unclipped −3.0, clipped −2.4, min = −3.0, gradient active, pushing the probability down. The objective is flat only when the update would move r further in the direction the advantage already favours (RL School arithmetic from eq. 7). Schulman 2017

Results

Table 1, seven MuJoCo tasks, 21 runs, scores normalised so random = 0 and the best result = 1: Schulman 2017

ObjectiveAvg. normalised score
No clipping or penalty−0.39
Clipping, ε = 0.10.76
Clipping, ε = 0.20.82
Clipping, ε = 0.30.70
Adaptive KL, dtarg = 0.010.74
Fixed KL, β = 30.72

The negative score comes from HalfCheetah, where the unclipped surrogate ends "worse than the initial random policy". Figure 3 then compares PPO against TRPO, CEM, vanilla policy gradient and A2C over one million steps on each environment. On 49 Atari games against tuned A2C and ACER, counting games "won" averaged over three seeds: on average reward over all of training, A2C 1, ACER 18, PPO 30; on the last 100 episodes, A2C 1, ACER 28, PPO 19, one tie. Schulman 2017

Why it mattered

PPO became the default optimiser for policies at every scale. OpenAI Five was "trained using Proximal Policy Optimization" with a 4096-unit LSTM, for 180 days spread over 10 months, and beat the Dota 2 world champions OG on 13 April 2019. Berner 2019 OpenAI's dexterous hand (2018) used PPO with the same clip, 0.2. OpenAI 2018 InstructGPT (2022) "fine-tuned the SFT model on our environment using PPO" with a per-token KL penalty, and its 1.3B model was preferred to 175B GPT-3. Ouyang 2022 DeepSeek-R1's GRPO (2025) keeps PPO's clipped objective and drops the critic for a group-mean baseline; DAPO (2025) tunes the clip asymmetrically. DeepSeek-AI 2025 Yu 2025

Limitations

Clipping is not a trust region: it removes the incentive to leave the band but does not bound the KL, which is why implementations add early stopping on an approximate KL (Spinning Up's target 0.01). Achiam 2018 Much of the performance lives in code, not equations: the reference implementation has 37 details absent from the paper, including Adam ε = 10−5, global gradient-norm clipping at 0.5, and value-loss clipping, for which later studies "find no evidence" of benefit. Huang 2022 Seeds and network sizes swing results: PPO on Hopper scored 61 ± 33 with a (400, 300) network and 2790 ± 62 with (64, 64). Henderson 2018 It is on-policy and sample-hungry; at one million steps on HalfCheetah, TD3 reported 9637 against PPO's 1795. Fujimoto 2018 And ACER still had slightly better final Atari scores (28 wins to 19). Schulman 2017

How to read the paper

Sections 1–3 with Figure 1 (15 min): the scorecard, the ratio, the clip. Section 5, Algorithm 1 (5 min): the whole method in nine lines. Section 6.1 and Table 1 (10 min): the one table that justifies the clip. Figure 3 and Table 2 (10 min). Skip Section 4 (adaptive KL) on a first pass; the authors found it "performed worse". Then read the 37-details blog before writing any code. Huang 2022

Check yourself

Q1. On the seven MuJoCo tasks, what did the unclipped, unpenalised surrogate score against clipping with ε = 0.2?

Table 1: −0.39 (worse than random on HalfCheetah) vs 0.82. ε = 0.1 gave 0.76 and ε = 0.3 gave 0.70.

Q2. With ε = 0.2, Â = +2 and r = 1.5, what is the gradient of the clipped term with respect to r?

Unclipped 3.0, clipped 1.2 × 2 = 2.4; min is 2.4 and constant in r, so this sample stops pushing the action's probability up.

Q3. "ε = 0.2 guarantees the policy changes by at most 20% per update." What is wrong?

The objective is flat beyond the band, but nothing stops r from being pushed there by other samples in the minibatch; the paper's own Figure 2 shows KL still growing along the update.

1992 · Watkins & Dayan · Machine Learning 8:279–292 (and Watkins's 1989 Cambridge thesis)

Q-learning: learn the optimal action values without a model

A one-line update that converges to the optimal action values with probability 1, however clumsily you explore, as long as you keep trying every action in every state.

Taught in Day 6 · Read time of the original: ~45 min (a 14-page technical note)

In one sentence

Keep a table Q(s,a); after each step move Q(s,a) a little toward "reward plus γ times the best Q in the next state", and the table converges to q* "so long as all actions are repeatedly sampled in all states and the action-values are represented discretely". Watkins & Dayan 1992

Explain it to a 10-year-old

You are in a maze and stick a note on every door saying how good it is to go through it. Each time you walk through a door, you rewrite its note: "what I got on the other side, plus the best note I can see in the next room". You can wander randomly and still, after enough wandering, the notes become exactly right, and the best path is just "follow the biggest note".

The problem

Dynamic programming (Bellman 1957; Howard's policy iteration, 1960) finds optimal policies, but only given the full rulebook p(s′,r|s,a), and only for small problems: backgammon alone has about 1020 states. Sutton & Barto 2018 Temporal-difference learning (Sutton 1988) learned without a model, but it learned the value of a fixed policy, and to act greedily from a state-value function you still need the model. Sutton 1988 Watkins's 1989 thesis reframed the whole problem as "learning to control a Markov Decision Process by incremental dynamic programming" and included a sketch of a convergence proof; the 1992 note with Dayan supplies the proof. Watkins 1989 Watkins & Dayan 1992

The key idea

Learn action values, and learn the optimal ones directly. The target uses the best action in the next state, maxa Q(S′,a), not the action you happen to take. So the table "directly approximates q*, the optimal action-value function, independent of the policy being followed". Sutton & Barto 2018 That is what off-policy means: the behaviour policy explores, the target policy is greedy, and the two never have to agree. Once Q is right, the policy is read off with no model and no search: act greedily.

How it works, step by step

  1. Initialise Q(s,a) arbitrarily for every pair; set Q(terminal, ·) = 0.
  2. In state S, choose A by any policy that keeps exploring, for example ε-greedy on Q.
  3. Take A; observe reward R and next state S′.
  4. Form the target: R + γ maxa Q(S′, a). This is a one-step sample of the Bellman optimality equation.
  5. Move Q(S,A) toward the target by a step size α (eq. 6.8 in Sutton & Barto):

Q(St,At) ← Q(St,At) + α [ Rt+1 + γ maxa Q(St+1,a) − Q(St,At) ]

  1. S ← S′; repeat until the episode ends, then start another.

The convergence theorem, in words. Run this forever. If every state–action pair is updated infinitely often, the values are stored exactly (a table, one cell per pair), and the step sizes shrink in the usual stochastic-approximation way (they add up to infinity, their squares do not), then Q converges to q* with probability 1. Watkins & Dayan 1992 Sutton & Barto 2018 Nothing is assumed about how you choose actions. The note also sketches two extensions: undiscounted problems with absorbing goal states, and updating many Q values per step rather than one. Watkins & Dayan 1992

Results

This is a theory paper: the result is the theorem, not a benchmark. The behaviour it predicts is visible in Sutton and Barto's cliff-walking gridworld (Example 6.6, ε = 0.1): Q-learning learns the values of the optimal cliff-edge path, while the on-policy Sarsa learns a longer, safer route. Because exploration keeps pushing the agent off the cliff, Q-learning's online return is worse, about −50 per episode against Sarsa's about −25 in the book's plot; RL School's replication (α = 0.5, 50 runs) gives −50.9 and −27.4. Sutton & Barto 2018 The book also shows the max in the target causing maximisation bias: in Example 6.7 Q-learning keeps picking a bad action about 5% too often even at convergence, which Double Q-learning removes. Sutton & Barto 2018 van Hasselt 2010

Why it mattered

Sutton and Barto date the moment the dynamic-programming and trial-and-error threads of RL were "fully brought together" to Watkins's 1989 thesis; the term "action value" is also his. Sutton & Barto 2018 Twenty-six years later the same update, with a convolutional network in place of the table, became DQN: 49 Atari games from pixels at a level "comparable to that of a professional human games tester" (Nature, February 2015). Mnih 2015 Every value-based deep RL method since, Double DQN, Rainbow, Agent57, is this update plus engineering (see the DQN review).

Limitations

The theorem needs a table. Replace it with a function approximator and you have all three ingredients of the deadly triad (approximation, bootstrapping, off-policy), under which instability "can" occur; "if any two elements of the deadly triad are present, but not all three", it can be avoided. Sutton & Barto 2018 The max over noisy estimates overestimates: Double DQN (2015) observed overestimation in all 49 Atari games and lifted the median normalised score from 93.5% to 114.7% by fixing it. van Hasselt 2015 The theorem gives no rate, and "infinitely often" is not a budget. And, as cliff walking shows, learning the optimal policy is not the same as behaving well while you learn.

How to read the paper

The note is short; the full text sits behind Springer's paywall, so we could verify only its abstract page. Read the abstract (5 min), then the theorem statement and the conditions on the step sizes, and skim the proof. Then read Sutton & Barto §6.5 for the modern statement and procedural box, §6.7 for maximisation bias, and §11.3 for why the table matters (45 min). The thesis chapter is gentler than the note. Watkins 1989

Check yourself

Q1. Which condition is NOT required by the Watkins–Dayan convergence theorem?

Q-learning is off-policy: the behaviour policy only has to keep visiting every pair. Greedy-in-the-limit is Sarsa's requirement, not Q-learning's.

Q2. On cliff walking with ε = 0.1, roughly what did Q-learning and Sarsa score per episode in the book's plot?

Q-learning finds the optimal cliff-edge path but falls off during exploration; Sarsa's safer path scores better online. Learning the optimal values and acting well are different things.

Q3. "Off-policy methods are inherently unstable." What does the deadly triad actually say?

Tabular Q-learning is off-policy and bootstraps, yet converges. The danger appears only when the table is replaced by a shared parameter vector.

References

  1. Watkins, C. J. C. H. & Dayan, P. (1992). Q-learning. Machine Learning 8(3–4):279–292. doi:10.1007/BF00992698 (abstract page opened; full text paywalled).
  2. Watkins, C. J. C. H. (1989). Learning from Delayed Rewards. PhD thesis, University of Cambridge. Author's thesis page.
  3. Sutton, R. S. & Barto, A. G. (2018). Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, 2nd ed., §6.5, §6.7, §11.3. PDF.
  4. van Hasselt, H. (2010). Double Q-learning. NIPS 23. proceedings.neurips.cc.
  5. van Hasselt, H., Guez, A. & Silver, D. (2015). Deep Reinforcement Learning with Double Q-learning. arXiv:1509.06461.
  6. Mnih, V. et al. (2015). Human-level control through deep reinforcement learning. Nature 518:529–533. nature.com.
1992 · Williams · Machine Learning 8:229–256

REINFORCE: climb the expected reward by sampling

A 28-page paper showing that a network of stochastic units can follow the gradient of expected reward by nudging up the log-probability of whatever it did, scaled by the reward it got, without ever computing that gradient explicitly.

Taught in Day 7 · Read time of the original: ~90 min

In one sentence

REINFORCE algorithms "make weight adjustments in a direction that lies along the gradient of expected reinforcement" for immediate-reward tasks and "certain limited forms of delayed-reinforcement tasks", and they do it "without explicitly computing gradient estimates". Williams 1992

Explain it to a 10-year-old

After each game of darts you remember every throw you made. If the game went well, you try to repeat all of those throws a little more often; if it went badly, a little less. You never need to know why a throw was good. It takes many games, because luck is mixed in with skill, and a good trick is to ask "did I do better than usual?" instead of "did I win?".

The problem

Value methods pick actions by an arg-max over Q(s,a). That needs a short list of actions and gives a deterministic policy. Both fail somewhere. Continuous actions have no list. And some problems want randomness: in Sutton and Barto's short-corridor gridworld, where two states look identical but have swapped actions, no ε-greedy policy scores better than about −44 per episode, while a policy that goes right with probability about 0.59 scores about −11.6. Sutton & Barto 2018 The obvious fix, give the policy its own parameters θ and do gradient ascent on expected reward J(θ), hits a wall: the reward comes from the environment as a number, and you cannot backpropagate through the environment. Williams's connectionist setting made this sharp: his units are stochastic (Bernoulli-logistic), so even the network's own output is a sample, not a differentiable function. Williams 1992

The key idea

The log-derivative trick: for any probability P(x|θ), ∇P = P · ∇log P. So the gradient of an expectation Ex∼P[R(x)] is itself an expectation, E[R(x) ∇log P(x|θ)], which you can estimate by sampling. Applied to a trajectory, the environment's transition probabilities appear inside log P but do not depend on θ, so they vanish under ∇θ; only Σt ∇log π(at|st,θ) survives. Achiam 2018 You differentiate only your own network, never the world.

How it works, step by step

  1. Run one episode with the current stochastic policy π(a|s,θ): S0, A0, R1, …, ST−1, AT−1, RT.
  2. For each step t compute the return from there, Gt = Σk>t γk−t−1 Rk.
  3. Update the parameters toward making At more likely, in proportion to Gt (Sutton & Barto eq. 13.8, with the γt of the boxed algorithm):

θ ← θ + α γt Gt ∇θ ln π(At|St,θ)

  1. Optionally subtract a baseline b(St) from Gt. Because Σa b(s) ∇π(a|s,θ) = b(s) ∇1 = 0, the baseline "leaves the expected value of the update unchanged, but it can have a large effect on its variance". Sutton & Barto 2018
  2. Discard the episode and go back to step 1. The data is on-policy; after θ moves, old episodes are from the wrong distribution.

Why the ∇ln π rather than ∇π? Dividing by π(At|St) stops frequently chosen actions from winning merely because they are updated more often. Sutton & Barto 2018 Check it by hand with a two-action softmax, logits [0, 0], so π(right) = 0.5. Take "right", observe G = +10, α = 0.01. The gradient of log π(right) with respect to the logits is [0.5, −0.5], so the logits become [0.05, −0.05] and π(right) rises to about 0.525. With a baseline b = 12 the same return counts as −2 and π(right) falls to about 0.495: the same episode is "good" or "bad" only relative to what you expected. (RL School arithmetic from eq. 13.8 and 13.11.) Sutton & Barto 2018

Results

Williams's paper is a theory paper. Its results are the proofs that the expected weight change of each REINFORCE rule is proportional to the gradient of expected reinforcement, the demonstration that the rules "can be naturally integrated with backpropagation", and a discussion of their limiting behaviour. Williams 1992 The GAE paper (2016) states the price in one line: the Monte Carlo estimator with λ = 1 is unbiased "regardless of the accuracy of V, but it has high variance due to the sum of terms". Schulman 2016 In practice the method is judged by its descendants; the short-corridor example above is the clean demonstration that a learned stochastic policy beats every ε-greedy one. Sutton & Barto 2018

Why it mattered

Every policy-gradient method is REINFORCE with a better weight on ∇log π. The list of valid weights, R(τ), reward-to-go, reward-to-go minus a baseline, Qπ, the advantage Aπ, is the spine of modern policy optimisation. Achiam 2018 A3C (2016) used a learned value baseline and 5-step returns on 16 CPU threads (the A3C review). Mnih 2016 PPO's surrogate, a probability ratio times an advantage, equals the policy gradient to first order around the old policy (the PPO review). Schulman 2017 Outside games: YouTube's 2019 recommender is literally a REINFORCE policy over millions of videos, with off-policy and top-K corrections, and lifted ViewTime by 0.85% in live A/B tests. Chen 2019 DeepSeek-R1's GRPO (2025) replaces the learned critic with a group-mean baseline, which is REINFORCE's baseline idea again. DeepSeek-AI 2025

Limitations

Variance: one return credits every action in the episode equally, so learning needs many episodes. The theory covers immediate reinforcement and only "certain limited forms" of delayed reinforcement. Williams 1992 You must wait for the episode to end, and each batch is used once. Later work attacked each: critics and k-step returns (A3C, 2016), the λ knob of GAE trading bias for variance (2016), and trust regions or clipping to allow larger, reusable updates (TRPO 2015, PPO 2017). Schulman 2016 Schulman 2017

How to read the paper

We could open only Springer's abstract page; the body is paywalled, so section-level advice below is for Sutton & Barto's treatment, which is the standard modern route. Read §13.1 (why parameterise the policy) and Example 13.1 (15 min), §13.2 for the policy gradient theorem (20 min), §13.3 for REINFORCE and the boxed algorithm (20 min), §13.4 for the baseline (15 min). Then the Spinning Up derivation for the trajectory form (20 min). Return to Williams's abstract last; it will read as a summary.

Check yourself

Q1. Starting from logits [0, 0], you take "right", get G = +10 and update with α = 0.01. What is π(right) afterwards?

∇ log π(right) = [0.5, −0.5]; logits become [0.05, −0.05]; the softmax of a 0.1 gap is σ(0.1) ≈ 0.525.

Q2. "Subtracting a baseline biases the gradient." Why is this wrong?

The identity holds because probabilities sum to one. A baseline that depended on the action would break it.

Q3. What does the log-derivative trick let you avoid?

Transition probabilities appear inside log P(τ|θ) but do not depend on θ, so they vanish under the gradient; only ∇ log π terms remain.

References

  1. Williams, R. J. (1992). Simple statistical gradient-following algorithms for connectionist reinforcement learning. Machine Learning 8(3–4):229–256. doi:10.1007/BF00992696 (abstract page opened; body paywalled; bibliographic data also as given in Sutton & Barto's bibliography).
  2. Sutton, R. S. & Barto, A. G. (2018). Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter 13. PDF.
  3. Achiam, J. (2018). Spinning Up: Intro to Policy Optimization. spinningup.openai.com.
  4. Schulman, J. et al. (2016). High-Dimensional Continuous Control Using Generalized Advantage Estimation. arXiv:1506.02438.
  5. Mnih, V. et al. (2016). Asynchronous Methods for Deep Reinforcement Learning. arXiv:1602.01783.
  6. Chen, M. et al. (2019). Top-K Off-Policy Correction for a REINFORCE Recommender System. arXiv:1812.02353.
2018 · Burda et al. · arXiv 1810.12894 (OpenAI / Edinburgh)

RND: Exploration by random network distillation

An exploration bonus equal to how badly a trained network predicts a frozen random network's features: 8,152 mean on Montezuma's Revenge against 2,497 for PPO and 4,753 for an average human, the first agent past the human average without demonstrations.

Taught in Day 11 · Read time of the original: ~40 min

In one sentence

RND pays the agent for visiting observations a predictor network has not yet learned to copy from a fixed random target network, which rewards novelty while being immune to unpredictable noise, and feeds that bonus to PPO through a second value head with its own discount.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

You get a sweet for walking into a room you have never seen. How does the game know? A scribble machine turns any picture into a fixed random scribble, and a copier learns to copy the scribbles. In familiar rooms the copier is good and you get nothing; in a new room it gets the scribble wrong and you get a sweet. A flickering TV cannot fool it, because the same picture always gives the same scribble.

The problem

In Montezuma's Revenge the first reward needs a long chain of precise moves past lethal traps, and random exploration essentially never finds it; DQN scored about zero and saw 2 rooms. Bellemare 2016 Curiosity bonuses based on prediction error help, but a forward model that predicts the next frame is drawn to anything unpredictable, "local sources of entropy in the environment" such as static on a screen or a coin flip, the so-called noisy-TV problem. Burda 2018 Count-based bonuses work in tables but every frame of a game is new.

The key idea

Predict something deterministic that you have never seen before. The paper lists four sources of prediction error: amount of training data, stochasticity, model misspecification and learning dynamics. Burda 2018 Only the first is novelty. If the thing being predicted is the output of a fixed random network, the target is a deterministic function of the observation (no stochasticity) in the same architecture family as the predictor (no misspecification), so what remains is mainly "have I trained on this before?"

How it works, step by step

  1. Two networks, same shape. A target f is randomly initialised and frozen forever; a predictor f̂ is trained by mean squared error to match f on observations the agent visits. Both use the convolutional encoder of the 2015 DQN followed by dense layers. Burda 2018

    rit = ‖ f̂(ot+1) − f(ot+1) ‖²

  2. Normalise. Observations are whitened with running statistics and clipped to [−5, 5] so the random target's outputs have a sensible scale; intrinsic rewards are divided by a running estimate of the intrinsic return's standard deviation. Burda 2018
  3. Two value heads. PPO fits VE to the extrinsic return (episodic, γE = 0.999) and VI to the intrinsic return (non-episodic, γI = 0.99), then uses V = VE + VI. The intrinsic return "is not truncated at 'game over'", so dying is not a way to escape boredom; raising γI to 0.999 hurt. Burda 2018
  4. Scale. Most runs use 128 parallel environments and about 1.97 billion frames, with sticky actions so the agent cannot memorise a deterministic sequence; the predictor trains on 25% of the experience so its update rate matches a 32-environment run. Burda 2018

Results

Table 1 (final mean score, RND / PPO / average human): Montezuma's Revenge 8,152 / 2,497 / 4,753; Gravitar 3,906 / 3,426 / 3,351; Venture 1,859 / 0 / 1,188. The dynamics-based curiosity baseline scored 400 on Montezuma. Burda 2018 The best agents "often find 22 out of the 24 rooms on the first level"; a scaled-up run with 1,024 parallel environments averaged 10,070 and one run passed the first level once for a best return of 17,500. Burda 2018 With no extrinsic reward at all, the non-episodic agent still explored up to 21 rooms. Burda 2018 The same table shows where it fails: Pitfall! −3, Private Eye 8,666 against a human 69,571, Solaris 3,282 against 12,327. Burda 2018

Why it mattered

RND was the first agent to beat the average human on Montezuma's Revenge "without using demonstrations or having access to the underlying state of the game", in October 2018. Burda 2018 Its bonus became a standard component: Agent57 (March 2020), the first agent above the human baseline on all 57 Atari games, uses RND as the lifelong-novelty factor of its Never Give Up reward. Badia 2020 It is also the cleanest example in Day 11 of separating "new" from "unpredictable".

Limitations

The bonus decays wherever the predictor has trained, so the agent can forget how to return to a frontier it found earlier; Go-Explore (January 2019) named this detachment, kept an explicit archive of states instead, and scored 43,763 on Montezuma without domain knowledge. Ecoffet 2019 RND needs about 2 billion frames, two discount factors to tune, and still leaves Pitfall!, Private Eye and Solaris far below human. Burda 2018 The abstract itself says it only "occasionally completes the first level". Burda 2018

How to read the paper

Sections 2.2–2.2.1 (the four error sources) are the idea, 2.3 the two-head trick, Figure 1 the bonus spiking along a real episode. Then Section 3.6, Table 1 and the pseudocode in Appendix A.2; skip the ablations in 3.2–3.5 on a first pass. About 40 minutes.

Check yourself

Q1. Which of RND's two networks is trained?

The target is fixed forever; the predictor learns to copy it. Novel observations give large copy errors.

Q2. RND's mean score on Montezuma's Revenge vs the average human was:

8,152 (RND) vs 4,753 (human); 2,497 is PPO; 17,500 is the best single return.

Q3. Why does a noisy TV not trap an RND agent?

Forward models chase irreducible stochasticity; RND predicts a fixed random mapping, so static becomes learnable and stops paying.

References

  1. Burda, Edwards, Storkey, Klimov. Exploration by Random Network Distillation. 30 Oct 2018. arXiv 1810.12894
  2. Bellemare et al. Unifying Count-Based Exploration and Intrinsic Motivation. 2016. arXiv 1606.01868
  3. Pathak et al. Curiosity-driven Exploration by Self-supervised Prediction (ICM). 2017. arXiv 1705.05363
  4. Ecoffet et al. Go-Explore: a New Approach for Hard-Exploration Problems. 2019. arXiv 1901.10995
  5. Badia et al. Agent57: Outperforming the Atari Human Benchmark. 2020. arXiv 2003.13350
2018 · Haarnoja et al. · ICML 2018

SAC: Soft actor-critic, off-policy maximum-entropy RL

An off-policy actor-critic that is paid for entropy as well as reward: one hyperparameter set learned six MuJoCo tasks on which DDPG made no progress on three, and the December 2018 version taught a real quadruped to walk in about 2 hours.

Taught in Day 8 · Read time of the original: ~40 min

In one sentence

SAC trains a stochastic policy to maximise reward plus α times its own entropy, using two Q-critics (the smaller one sets the target), a replay buffer and, in the follow-up paper, an automatically tuned α, which gives off-policy sample efficiency with the seed-to-seed stability DDPG lacked.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

A treasure hunter gets points for treasure and for trying new paths. The dial α says how much a new path is worth: if she wanders too much it turns down, if she always takes the same route it turns up. Two judges score her routes and she believes the stricter one, so she never gets over-confident.

The problem

On-policy methods like PPO are stable but discard their data after a few epochs, so every update costs fresh environment steps. Off-policy DDPG reuses a replay buffer but is brittle: in SAC's benchmark "DDPG fails to make any progress on Ant-v1, Humanoid-v1, and Humanoid (rllab)", three of six tasks, and a deterministic policy with a single critic "exhibits very high variability across seeds". Haarnoja 2018

The key idea

Put entropy into the reward, not just into the loss. The agent is paid for being random, with a temperature α that "determines the relative importance of the entropy term against the reward". Haarnoja 2018 Because entropy is part of the return, Q and V change too (the "soft" Bellman equation), so the critic itself prefers states where many actions remain good.

How it works, step by step

  1. Objective. Maximise expected reward plus entropy, H(π(·|s)) = E[−log π(a|s)]. Haarnoja 2018

    J(π) = Σt E(st,at)~ρπ[ r(st,at) + α H(π(·|st)) ]

  2. Critic update. Sample a replay batch, sample ã' from the current policy at s', and regress both critics onto a target built from the smaller target-critic minus the entropy term. Two Q-functions "significantly speed up training, especially on harder tasks". Haarnoja 2018

    y = r + γ(1−d) ( minj=1,2 Qtarg,j(s', ã') − α log π(ã'|s') ), ã' ~ π(·|s')

  3. Actor update. Write the action as a function of noise, ã = tanh(μ(s) + σ(s) ⊙ ξ), ξ ~ N(0, I), so the gradient flows from the critic into the policy; maximise E[ minj Qj(s, ã) − α log π(ã|s) ]. Haarnoja 2018
  4. Automatic temperature (the 2018-12 paper). Constrain entropy to be at least H̄ = −dim(A) and descend on a dual loss. Haarnoja 2018b

    J(α) = Ea~π[ −α log π(a|s) − α H̄ ]

    Check by hand: HalfCheetah has 6 action dimensions, so H̄ = −6. Haarnoja 2018b If current entropy is −4, ∂J/∂α = (−4) − (−6) = +2 and descent lowers α; at −8 the sign flips and α rises.
  5. Housekeeping. Polyak targets with τ = 0.005, one gradient step per environment step, replay 106, batch 256, two hidden layers of 256 ReLU units, Adam 3×10−4, γ = 0.99. Haarnoja 2018b

Results

The first paper trained "five different instances of each algorithm with different random seeds" on Hopper, Walker2d, HalfCheetah, Ant, Humanoid-v1 and Humanoid (rllab). Haarnoja 2018 Its one tuned knob was a per-task reward scale (5 for the first four, 20 for Humanoid-v1, 10 for Humanoid rllab); Figure 3 shows SAC "is particularly sensitive to the scaling of the reward signal". Haarnoja 2018 The December follow-up replaced that knob with the automatic temperature and dropped the separate state-value network after finding it "unnecessary". Haarnoja 2018b

Then it left the simulator. A Minitaur quadruped "successfully learns to walk from 160k environment steps, or approximately 400 episodes", about 2 hours of real-world training, and the gait generalised to slopes, steps and obstacles it never saw; a three-finger hand learned to rotate a valve in about 3 hours from the joint angle and in 20 hours (300k steps) from 32×32 pixels. Haarnoja 2018b

Why it mattered

SAC became the default for continuous control whenever samples are expensive: one gradient step per environment step means a robot is trained at the rate it moves, which is why it walked a real quadruped in 2 hours in 2018. Haarnoja 2018b Seven years later the same recipe, sped up as FastSAC and FastTD3, trained sim-to-real humanoid locomotion in "just 15 minutes with a single RTX 4090 GPU". Seo 2025 See Day 8 for when to pick SAC over PPO.

Limitations

As published, SAC is continuous-action only. Its one-step-per-sample loop does not parallelise like PPO's rollout workers (Spinning Up notes it "does not support parallelization"), so with cheap simulators PPO often wins on wall-clock. Achiam 2018 The twin-critic minimum, inherited from TD3, is a deliberate pessimistic bias. Fujimoto 2018 And the first version's reward-scale sensitivity is fixed only by the automatic α of the second paper. Haarnoja 2018b

How to read the paper

Section 3.2 for Equation 1, Section 4.2 for the three updates and Algorithm 1, Figures 1–3, Appendix D for hyperparameters; skip the proofs in Appendix B. Then in arXiv 1812.05905 read only Section 5 (Equations 17–18) and Section 7 (the robots). About 40 minutes for both.

Check yourself

Q1. In SAC, what does the temperature α control?

α multiplies the entropy term in the objective; Polyak τ handles the target critics.

Q2. With automatic temperature, what is the entropy target for HalfCheetah, whose action has 6 dimensions?

The target is −dim(A) = −6. Entropy above it lowers α; below it raises α.

Q3. How does SAC's entropy term differ from PPO's entropy bonus?

SAC's return includes α H(π) at every step, giving the soft Bellman equation; PPO's c₂ term only regularises the policy update.

References

  1. Haarnoja, Zhou, Abbeel, Levine. Soft Actor-Critic: Off-Policy Maximum Entropy Deep RL with a Stochastic Actor. ICML 2018. arXiv 1801.01290
  2. Haarnoja et al. Soft Actor-Critic Algorithms and Applications. 2018 (v2 Jan 2019). arXiv 1812.05905
  3. Fujimoto, van Hoof, Meger. Addressing Function Approximation Error in Actor-Critic Methods (TD3). ICML 2018. arXiv 1802.09477
  4. Achiam. Spinning Up: Soft Actor-Critic. OpenAI, 2018. spinningup.openai.com
  5. Seo et al. Learning Sim-to-Real Humanoid Locomotion in 15 Minutes. 2025. arXiv 2512.01996
2025 · Khatri, Madaan et al. · Meta (ICLR 2026 oral)

ScaleRL: the art of scaling reinforcement learning compute for LLMs

More than 400,000 GPU-hours of ablations showed that RL training curves follow a sigmoid in compute whose ceiling depends on the recipe, and the resulting ScaleRL recipe predicted the outcome of a 100,000 GPU-hour run from its first half. Khatri 2025

Taught in Day 12 · Read time of the original: ~70 min (28 pages, 20 figures; the appendix is most of it)

In one sentence

Fit every RL run with RC − R0 = (A − R0) / (1 + (Cmid/C)B) and you can separate design choices that raise the ceiling A from those that only make you reach it faster (B), which turns out to be most of them. Khatri 2025

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Everyone training a reasoning model argues about the recipe: this loss, that batch size, this trick. ScaleRL ran hundreds of small bake-offs and found that most tricks only change how fast the cake rises, not how tall it can get. A few ingredients change the height. And if you watch the cake for the first half of the baking time, you can predict exactly how tall it will be at the end.

The problem

Pretraining has scaling laws: fit a power law on small runs and predict a big one. RL for LLMs had none. Recipes (GRPO, DAPO, Magistral, MiniMax-M1 and others) were compared at one small budget, and nobody knew whether a recipe that won at 1,000 GPU-hours would still win at 100,000, or how to tell a slow start from a low ceiling. Khatri 2025 Picking wrong at scale costs hundreds of thousands of GPU-hours.

The key idea

Measure every recipe the same way: run it on a fixed 8B dense model with maths prompts, record pass rate on a held-in validation set against GPU-hours spent, and fit a sigmoid, chosen over a power law because it fits more robustly in the low-compute regime and has a ceiling. Khatri 2025 Then ask of each design choice: did it move A, or only B and Cmid?

How it works, step by step

  1. The curve (Eq. 1): A is the asymptotic pass rate (0 ≤ A ≤ 1), B the scaling exponent (compute efficiency), Cmid the compute at which half the gain is reached, R0 the starting reward. Fits start after about 1,500 GPU-hours. Khatri 2025

RC − R0 = (A − R0) · 1 / ( 1 + (Cmid / C)B )

  1. The study. Leave-one-out and one-at-a-time ablations on the 8B model, each run to a few thousand GPU-hours, then confirmation on Llama-4 Scout (17B×16 MoE). In total more than 400,000 GPU-hours on GB200 GPUs. Khatri 2025
  2. What moves the ceiling A. The loss type (CISPO and GSPO beat DAPO's token-level clipped loss); computing the LM head's logits in FP32, which raised A from about 0.52 to about 0.61; larger batches and longer generation lengths, which start slower but end higher. Khatri 2025
  3. What mostly moves efficiency B. Asynchronous PipelineRL versus PPO-off-policy (same A, better B), loss aggregation, advantage normalisation, curriculum. Khatri 2025
  4. The recipe. ScaleRL = asynchronous PipelineRL with 8 off-policy steps; CISPO (a truncated-importance-sampling REINFORCE loss); FP32 LM head; prompt-level loss averaging; batch-level advantage normalisation; zero-variance filtering (drop prompts whose group all agree, DAPO's dynamic sampling in another coat); No-Positive-Resampling (drop prompts with historical pass rate ≥ 0.9); and interruption-based length control that forces an end-of-thinking phrase instead of truncating. Khatri 2025

Results

The fit made from the first 50,000 GPU-hours of a ScaleRL run on the 8B model predicted the validation pass rate of the full 100,000 GPU-hour run; a 50,000 GPU-hour run on Scout and a downstream AIME-24 curve followed the same shape. Khatri 2025 Against four published recipes re-implemented in the same harness, ScaleRL had the highest fitted asymptote, A = 0.61, and the others differed in A, not only in speed: "Not all recipes yield similar asymptotic performance". Khatri 2025

Why it mattered

It is the first paper to treat LLM-RL as something you can budget rather than gamble on, and it was accepted as an oral at ICLR 2026 (25 April 2026). ICLR 2026 Its negative result is as useful as its recipe: the 2025 objective papers (DAPO, Dr. GRPO, GSPO) were mostly arguing about B. It also made two systems ideas standard: PipelineRL's in-flight weight updates, where the inference engine pauses only to receive new weights and continues the same half-finished sequences, Piché 2025 and FP32 logits at the LM head, after the paper traced the gap between the sampler's and the trainer's probabilities to that layer. Khatri 2025

Limitations

The authors say the predictions are for in-distribution validation pass rate and generalisation to held-out tests is not fully characterised; the experiments are almost all maths, with maths-plus-code results called preliminary; effects of generations-per-prompt may only appear at batches of 2,000 or more; and ScaleRL "is not the final word" given how many design choices remain. Khatri 2025 Two models, one lab, one kind of prompt. Whether the sigmoid shape survives agentic multi-turn rewards (Day 12) is, as of October 2026, unanswered in print.

How to read the paper

Read Figure 1, Eq. 1 and Figure 3 (the A/B/Cmid schematic) first, then Section 3.2 one ablation at a time, looking only at whether A or B moved. Section 4 lists the recipe; Section 5 is the scaling confirmation. Skip Appendix A.1–A.17 unless you are reproducing a specific ablation. About 45 minutes for the main text.

Check yourself

Q1. In the fitted curve, which parameter does a "better recipe" in the authors' sense change?

Most choices only change efficiency B; the recipe-defining ones (loss type, FP32 head, batch and length) move the ceiling A.

Q2. What did switching the LM head logits to FP32 do?

A precision fix at one layer moved the ceiling, not just the speed.

Q3. Why fit a sigmoid rather than a power law?

Pass rate is bounded in [0, 1]; the sigmoid gives a ceiling A and was more stable to fit early.

References

  1. Khatri, Madaan, Tiwari, Bansal, Duvvuri, Zaheer, Dhillon, Brandfonbrener, Agarwal. The Art of Scaling Reinforcement Learning Compute for LLMs. 2025; ICLR 2026 oral. arXiv 2510.13786 · full text · ICLR page
  2. Piché, Kamalloo, Pardinas, Chen, Bahdanau. PipelineRL. 2025 (TMLR 2026). arXiv 2509.19128

2018 · Sutton & Barto · MIT Press, 2nd edition

Sutton & Barto: Reinforcement Learning, An Introduction

The textbook the field is written in: 17 chapters in three parts, given away as a free PDF by the authors, and the source of the notation every other entry in this Paper Bible uses.

Taught in Day 1 · Read time of the original: about a week at two chapters a day

In one sentence

Sutton and Barto define reinforcement learning as "learning what to do—how to map situations to actions—so as to maximize a numerical reward signal", then show how to do it exactly with tables (Part I), approximately with function approximation (Part II), and what it has to do with brains, psychology and real systems (Part III). Sutton & Barto 2018

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Imagine a thick guide for teaching a puppy tricks when nobody tells the puppy the rules, only when it gets a treat. The first part is for small games where you can keep score on one sheet of paper. The second part is for games with so many situations that you need a clever guesser instead of a sheet. The third part asks how real animals, and real brains, do the same thing. The two authors put the whole guide online for free.

The problem

Before this book, the ideas of RL lived in three separate literatures. Psychology had Thorndike's Law of Effect (1911), the "essence of trial-and-error learning". Control theory had Bellman's dynamic programming and Markov decision processes (1957). A third thread, temporal-difference learning, ran from Samuel's checkers player (1959) to Sutton's 1988 paper. The three were "fully brought together" only in Watkins's 1989 thesis on Q-learning. Sutton & Barto 2018 The book's job is to teach the unified subject with one notation: return Gt, discount γ, values vπ(s) and qπ(s,a), dynamics p(s′,r|s,a). The second edition is the one cited here; the authors' page lists the full PDF, errata, code and slides. Sutton & Barto 2018

The key idea

Two sentences carry the book. First, every estimate is updated the same way: NewEstimate ← OldEstimate + StepSize [Target − OldEstimate] (eq. 2.4); bandits, TD(0), Sarsa, Q-learning and semi-gradient methods only differ in what the target is. Second, generalised policy iteration: let policy evaluation and policy improvement interact at any granularity, because "almost all reinforcement learning methods are well described as GPI". Sutton & Barto 2018

How it works, step by step

The book is a course, so "how it works" means how to read it. This is the order RL School follows, with the chapter each Day leans on.

  1. Chapter 1 → Day 1. The agent–environment loop, trial-and-error search and delayed reward as the two defining features, the history section (§1.7). Sutton & Barto 2018
  2. Chapter 2 → Day 2. Bandits; the 10-armed testbed where greedy earns about 1.0 per step against a possible 1.54. Sutton & Barto 2018
  3. Chapter 3 → Day 3. Finite MDPs and the Bellman equations:

vπ(s) = Σa π(a|s) Σs′,r p(s′,r|s,a) [ r + γ vπ(s′) ]

  1. Chapter 4 → Day 4. Dynamic programming; in the 4×4 gridworld the greedy policy is already optimal after 3 sweeps. Sutton & Barto 2018
  2. Chapters 5, 6, 7, 12 → Day 5. Monte Carlo, TD(0), n-step returns, eligibility traces; the random walk with true values 1/6 … 5/6. Sutton & Barto 2018
  3. §6.4–6.7 and §16.5 → Day 6. Sarsa, Q-learning, maximisation bias, and the DQN case study (see the Q-learning review and the DQN review).
  4. Chapter 13 → Day 7. The policy gradient theorem and REINFORCE (the REINFORCE review).
  5. Chapters 9–11 are background for Days 6–8: function approximation and the deadly triad (§11.3). Chapters 14–17 feed Day 1's history and the applications days.

Results

A textbook's "results" are the worked examples you can reproduce. These are the ones RL School's widgets re-run; if your code does not print these numbers, your code is wrong.

ExampleWhereNumber to hit
10-armed testbed, greedy§2.3≈1.0 reward/step vs 1.54 possible; best arm found in ≈⅓ of tasks
Gridworld, random policy, γ=0.9Example 3.5v(A) = 8.8, below its +10 reward; v(B) = 5.3, above its +5
4×4 gridworld, policy evaluationFigure 4.1greedy policy optimal from sweep k = 3
Five-state random walkExample 6.2true values 1/6, 2/6, 3/6, 4/6, 5/6
Short corridor, policy gradientExample 13.1best ε-greedy ≈ −44; stochastic policy ≈ −11.6

All five come from the book's own text and figures. Sutton & Barto 2018

Why it mattered

The lineage of this Paper Bible runs through the book. Watkins's Q-learning (§6.5, 1989) is the update inside DQN (Nature, February 2015), which the book covers as a case study in §16.5. Mnih 2015 REINFORCE (§13.3, Williams 1992) is the ancestor of A3C, TRPO and PPO. Williams 1992 The authors are still setting the agenda: Sutton co-wrote the Alberta Plan (2022) and, with Silver, "Welcome to the Era of Experience" (2025), which argues agents "will inhabit streams of experience, rather than short snippets of interaction". Silver & Sutton 2025

Limitations

The book stops in 2018. The phrases "trust region" and "proximal policy" do not occur in it, so the whole of Day 8 (TRPO, PPO, SAC) is taught from the papers. Sutton & Barto 2018 Deep networks appear mainly in the Chapter 16 case studies; Part II is built around linear features and tile coding. One slip to know: §16.5 says DQN reached human level on "29 of the 46 games", where the Nature paper reports 49 games. Sutton & Barto 2018 Mnih 2015 For the post-2018 arc (DQN → PPO/SAC → MuZero → offline RL → RLHF and reasoning models) a 2026 book-length treatment exists. Bista 2026

How to read the paper

Budget one week. Day one: Chapter 1 and §3.1–3.6 (3 h). Day two: Chapter 2 with the testbed coded (3 h). Day three: Chapter 4 (2 h). Day four: §6.1–6.5 before Chapter 5; TD first, then MC as the λ=1 special case (3 h). Day five: §6.6–6.7, §11.3, §16.5 (3 h). Day six: Chapter 13 (3 h). Day seven: Chapter 17. Skip Chapters 14–15 and the starred sections on a first pass; do the exercises marked with a value table, because the tables are the answer key.

Check yourself

Q1. In the 4×4 gridworld of Chapter 4, after how many sweeps of policy evaluation is the greedy policy already optimal?

Figure 4.1: the values keep changing until k → ∞, but the arg-max arrows stop changing at k = 3. That gap is why value iteration can truncate evaluation.

Q2. "The Bellman equation is an algorithm." Why is this wrong, in the book's framing?

Chapter 3 presents the Bellman equations as equalities that v_π and v* must satisfy; Chapters 4–6 are three families of methods for finding functions that satisfy them.

Q3. Which of these is NOT covered in the 2018 second edition?

Q-learning is §6.5, REINFORCE with baseline is §13.4, DQN is §16.5. Neither "trust region" nor "proximal policy" appears in the text; PPO is a 2017 paper the book does not treat.

  2. Watkins, C. J. C. H. & Dayan, P. (1992). Q-learning. Machine Learning 8(3–4):279–292. doi:10.1007/BF00992698 (§6.5 of the book).

2015 · Schulman et al. · ICML 2015 (arXiv 1502.05477)

TRPO: Trust region policy optimization

A policy update with a proof that the true return cannot fall, approximated into an algorithm that learned to swim, hop and walk in simulation where unconstrained natural gradient produced only standing.

Taught in Day 8 · Read time of the original: ~2 h (16 pages with appendices)

In one sentence

Maximise a surrogate objective, the old policy's advantages re-weighted by the new-to-old probability ratio, subject to the constraint that the average KL divergence between new and old policies stays below δ = 0.01, which the theory shows guarantees monotonic improvement. Schulman 2015 Schulman 2015

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Learning to ride a bike, you lean a little at a time. Lean too far at once and you fall, and you have to start again from where you fell, which is worse than where you began. TRPO is a rule for the computer: "each practice session, change what you would do by no more than a small, fixed amount", with a bit of maths that says why that amount is safe.

The problem

A policy gradient is only a local direction. Take too big a step and the policy changes, the states it visits change, and the next batch of data comes from a worse policy; the loop can collapse and not recover. The PPO paper later measured it: on seven MuJoCo tasks an unconstrained surrogate scored −0.39 on a scale where random is 0 and the best run is 1, because on HalfCheetah it ended worse than random. Schulman 2017 Step size is also a hyperparameter you cannot set once: the same α is huge for one parameter and tiny for another. Natural gradient fixes the geometry but not the step length; in TRPO's own experiments, natural gradient without the trust region failed to produce hopping or walking. Schulman 2015

The key idea

Bound how much the policy may change, measured in behaviour (KL divergence between action distributions), not in parameters. Theorem 1 gives a lower bound on the new policy's return: the surrogate improvement minus a penalty C · DKLmax(π, π̃) with C = 4εγ/(1−γ)2, where ε is the largest advantage magnitude. Schulman 2015 Maximising that bound each step cannot decrease the true return. The penalty coefficient from the theory gives very small steps, so the practical algorithm swaps the penalty for a hard constraint on the average KL, with radius δ. Schulman 2015

How it works, step by step

  1. Collect trajectories with the current policy πθk (the "single path" scheme; "vine" branches extra rollouts from visited states). Estimate advantages A.
  2. Form the surrogate and the constraint:

maximise L(θ) = Es,a∼πθk[ πθ(a|s) / πθk(a|s) · A(s,a) ] subject to D̄KL(θk ‖ θ) ≤ δ

  1. Approximate: L ≈ gT(θ − θk) and D̄KL ≈ ½ (θ − θk)T H (θ − θk), where H is the Fisher information matrix. Achiam 2018
  2. Never invert H. Solve Hx = g by conjugate gradient, 10 iterations, using Fisher-vector products computed on 10% of the data. Schulman 2015
  3. Step to the edge of the trust region:

θk+1 = θk + sqrt( 2δ / (xTHx) ) · x

  1. Backtracking line search: shrink the step by a factor until the measured KL is ≤ δ and the surrogate actually improved. Achiam 2018

Check the arithmetic: with δ = 0.01 and xTHx = 4 the step scale is sqrt(0.02/4) = sqrt(0.005) ≈ 0.0707 along x. If the realised KL is 0.013, backtrack to 0.8 × 0.0707, then 0.64 × 0.0707, until KL ≤ 0.01 (RL School arithmetic from the formula above).

Results

Locomotion in MuJoCo: swimmer, hopper and walker, with "δ = 0.01 for all experiments". Figure 4 compares single-path and vine TRPO against natural gradient, CEM and CMA, "averaged across five runs of each algorithm with random initializations"; the caption warns that for hopper and walker "a score of −1 is achievable without any forward velocity, indicating a policy that simply learned balanced standing, but not walking", which is where the baselines sat. Schulman 2015 Atari from pixels, 7 games with a 33,500-parameter convolutional policy: TRPO "only outperformed the prior methods on some of the games" but "consistently achieved reasonable scores", beating DQN on Q*bert (vine) and Enduro (single path) in Table 1. Schulman 2015

Why it mattered

TRPO turned "how big a step?" from a tuning problem into a constraint with a meaning, and it worked on neural-network policies with tens of thousands of parameters. Its direct descendant is PPO (2017), whose stated aim is "the data efficiency and reliable performance of TRPO, while using only first-order optimization". Schulman 2017 The idea of bounding behaviour change by KL reappears wherever policies are fine-tuned from a reference: InstructGPT's RLHF adds "a per-token KL penalty from the SFT model at each token" to keep the language model close to its starting point. Ouyang 2022 See the PPO review for what replaced the constraint.

Limitations

The theory bounds the maximum KL over states; the algorithm constrains the average, and the authors say so. Schulman 2015 Each update needs a conjugate-gradient solve with Fisher-vector products, and the method "is not compatible with architectures that include noise (such as dropout) or parameter sharing (between the policy and value function, or with auxiliary tasks)". Schulman 2017 On Atari the authors "could not obtain error statistics due to time constraints". Schulman 2015 Reproducibility bit later: Henderson et al. split 10 identical TRPO runs on HalfCheetah into two groups of five and found them significantly different (p = 0.0016) from random seeds alone. Henderson 2018

How to read the paper

Sections 1–2 for notation (15 min). Section 3 for Theorem 1 and the bound; read the statement, skip Appendix A's proof the first time (20 min). Section 4 for the switch from penalty to constraint, Section 6 for the algorithm you would implement (30 min). Section 8.1 with Figure 4 (15 min). Then the Spinning Up TRPO page for the conjugate-gradient and line-search pseudocode. Achiam 2018 Appendix C is where the Fisher-vector product trick lives, if you need to implement it.

Check yourself

Q1. What value of the trust-region radius δ did the paper use?

"We used δ = 0.01 for all experiments." 0.2 is PPO's clip ε; 0.95 is GAE's λ.

Q2. "TRPO inverts the Fisher matrix H." What does it actually do?

Ten CG iterations with Fisher-vector products on a 10% subsample. For a network with many parameters, forming H would be impossible.

Q3. Theory and practice differ in TRPO. How?

The penalty coefficient from Theorem 1 gives tiny steps, so the authors replace it with a constraint, and the per-state max with an average that can be estimated from samples.
